<term>Coat of Arms</term>: A unique heraldic design on an escutcheon (shield), used to identify a person, family, or organization.

<term>Heraldry</term>: The profession, study, or art of devising, granting, and blazoning arms and ruling on questions of rank or protocol.

<term>Crest</term>: An ornament worn on top of the helmet in a coat of arms.

<term>Quarterly</term>: A method of dividing a shield into four or more sections to incorporate the arms of different families joined by marriage.

<term>Leopard's Faces</term>: In heraldry, a "leopard" often refers to a lion shown with its face turned toward the viewer.

<term>Scallop Shells</term>: A common heraldic symbol, often associated with pilgrimage (specifically the Shrine of St. James) or naval command.

# TRANSLATOR’S PREFACE.
<sig>v</sig>

---

I first began the translation of this, the earliest known published work dealing with both magnetism and electricity, at the beginning of 1889. It was then my intention to place it before the public during the following year, recognizing as I did the demand for an English version which had been frequently requested by scientists generally in this country, in England, and on the Continent of Europe. But the attention I was forced to give, both here and abroad, to the preparation of my “Chronological History of Electricity and Magnetism” has unavoidably delayed the publication of the present volume.

The translation of *De Magnete* has been a task of extraordinary difficulty; it has brought up innumerable problems, the solution of which has involved much laborious research—as the result was intended to be a clear and capable presentation of the author in idiomatic English and not simply a substitution of English words for Latin. Nor would I have dared to appear as the English interpreter of the great Gilbert, “father of the magnetic philosophy,” if not for the strong encouragement and very substantial help, in translating and otherwise, extended by many literary and scientific friends, among whom must be especially mentioned Mr. Joseph Fitzgerald, Mr. E. McMillan,

<summary>The translator discusses the origins of this English version of William Gilbert's *De Magnete*, noting that while he began in 1889, his other historical research delayed its completion. He emphasizes that the translation aims for idiomatic clarity rather than a literal word-for-word rendering of the original Latin.</summary>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the list of contributors and explains the specific difficulties regarding William Gilbert's unique terminology and his reliance on Scholastic philosophy, specifically the concepts of form and matter.</meta>

<page-num>vi</page-num>

# TRANSLATOR'S PREFACE.

Mr. Joseph Wetzler, Dr. Joseph V. Livingston, Hon. Park Benjamin, and Prof. Alfred M. Mayer. I am also indebted to Prof. Charles Sanders Peirce, to Mr. Latimer Clark, F.R.S., to Dr. Isaac H. Hall, and to Dr. Charlton T. Lewis for valuable suggestions regarding the general treatment of the work; and, in the words of the celebrated English mathematician Edward Wright, I do not doubt that our united efforts “will find the heartiest approval among all intelligent men and children of magnetic science.”

Not only does Gilbert frequently make use of what he calls “words new and unheard-of,” besides attaching to many others a meaning far different from that generally recognized today, but, what is worse, he retains to a great extent the terminology of the medieval scholastic philosophers. The translator must necessarily retain that terminology; no substitute is possible. Consequently, one finds a multitude of unfamiliar words which, for the modern reader, require explanation. It is unnecessary to make any special mention of them here, since the detailed general index to this work will very easily indicate where they can be found. It is known that in the philosophy of the Scholastics (as in that of Aristotle), form—*forma*—means that which, when added to matter—*materia*—constitutes the true nature of the thing. Matter *per se* (in itself) is indifferent and indefinite; form gives it definiteness. The earth is *informed* with <term>verticity</term> <note>The property of having magnetic poles or a specific direction.</note>—that is its primary distinction. When any portion of the earth loses verticity, it loses its *forma*—it is *deformate*. To restore verticity to it is to *reformate* it, or to *informate* it. Portions of the earth that are *deformate* are, as it were, worn out, waste matter. Gilbert states (Book II, Chapters II and IV) that the natural magnetic force (movement) comes from the primary *forma* of the earth, or rather the primary native strength (*vigor*). Elsewhere he tells

<summary>The translator acknowledges several scientific and academic contributors and explains the difficulty of Gilbert's terminology, which relies on medieval Scholastic concepts of "form" and "matter." He defines how Gilbert uses these terms to describe the magnetic properties (verticity) of the earth.</summary>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of William Gilbert’s specific Latin terminology and the philosophical concepts of form, while also citing John Dryden’s views on the challenges of translation.</meta>

<page-num>vii</page-num>

# TRANSLATOR'S PREFACE.

...us that the earth and the loadstone conform—*conformant*—magnetic movements (Book II, Chapter VI); and he speaks of substances conformated—*conformatum*—by the earth (Book III, Chapter IV), and of the globe of earth as of small account and deformate—*deformatum* (Book V, Chapter XII). He speaks besides of the formate soul—*formata anima* (Book V, Chapter XII); of air or water being informated—*informaren-tur*—by magnetic forms or spheres (Book V, Chapter XI); of iron being transformated—*transformatur* (Book III, Chapter XII); and he adds that iron will attract more properly if it is afformed—*afformatum* (Book II, Chapter IV); also that it will be better if the iron's "acquired verticity be, by some process, rather weakened or deformated"—*deformata* (Book III, Chapter XI).

England's great poet, John Dryden, tells us: "It is almost impossible to translate word-for-word and well at the same time; for Latin (a most rigorous and concise language) often expresses in one word what either the crudeness or the narrowness of modern tongues cannot provide in many. . . But since every language is so full of its own unique characteristics that what is beautiful in one is often crude, even nonsense, in another, it would be unreasonable to limit a translator to the narrow range of his author's words; it is enough if he chooses some expression that does not corrupt the meaning." While, in order to do this acceptably in the present instance, it has often been found necessary to adhere very closely (even literally) to the original lines, the "fair-minded reader" will naturally observe that greater clarity has been provided where paraphrasing has been used for better understanding, specifically regarding words of Gilbert's own invention.

Following Dryden, I have translated with freedom, keeping

<summary>The translator details William Gilbert’s specific Latin terminology regarding the concept of "form" and quotes John Dryden to justify using paraphrasing rather than literal translation for the sake of clarity.</summary>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page concludes the translator's preface by P. Fleury Mottelay, discussing his methodology for translating William Gilbert's work and his reliance on supporting historical sources.</meta>

<page-num>viii</page-num>
# TRANSLATOR’S PREFACE.

...keeping the author’s meaning in view more specifically than his words, and expanding upon the former without changing it. Nor have I, in doing so, attempted—any more than Gilbert did—to add “any rhetorical flourishes or verbal ornamentation” to the work. Like him, I have simply tried to address “difficult questions about which little is known in a style and with terms that are necessary to make what is said clearly understandable.”

The few passages of *De Magnete* that I have seen translated independently elsewhere are reproduced in their proper places. Wherever possible, I have followed the established plan used in my “Chronological History” by quoting many authorities and inserting numerous excerpts from the writings of different authors to support the original material. The extent to which this has been done is shown in the general index accompanying this work.

I should add that I would be grateful to those who call attention to any errors, typographical or otherwise, that may be found here, as well as to those whose helpful advice may make improvements possible in future editions.

->P. FLEURY MOTTELAY.<-

NEW YORK, March 10, 1892.

Immediately upon leaving college he traveled on the Continent, “where he probably had the degree of Doctor of Medicine conferred upon him, for he does not appear to have taken it either at Oxford or Cambridge,”<note>Philip Morant, *loc. cit.*, Vol. I, Book II, page 117. See also Ree’s Cyclopædia, 1819, Vol. XVI, article “Gilbert.”</note> and where, as well as in England, he is said to have “practiced as a physician with great success and applause.” In 1573, he was elected a Fellow of the Royal College of Physicians, and filled many important offices there, becoming, in turn, Censor (1581–1582, 1584–1587, 1589–1590), Treasurer (1587–1591, 1597–1599), Consiliarius (1597–1599), and President (1600). His skill had already attracted the attention of Queen Elizabeth, by whom he was appointed her physician-in-ordinary, and who showed him many marks of her favor, besides settling upon him an annual pension (said to be the only legacy she left to anyone) for the purpose of aiding him in the pursuit of his philosophical studies.

Gilbert’s move to the court led to the dispersion of the members of a society or college which, it appears, frequently met at his residence in Colchester (see illustration). This house, anciently known as “Lanseles,” “Timperley’s,” or “Tympornell’s” (Old Taxation),<note>Philip Morant, *loc. cit.*, Vol. I, Book II, page 117. See also Ree’s Cyclopædia, 1819, Vol. XVI, article “Gilbert.”</note> was located “on St. Peter’s Hill, between Upper Thames Street and Little Knight-Rider Street.”

The early investigations of Gilbert were centered almost exclusively upon chemistry, he “attaining great accuracy in it,” but this branch was soon made to yield to the study of the phenomena of electricity and of magnetism, the

<page-num>xii</page-num>

<header>BIOGRAPHICAL MEMOIR.</header>

guished man of science in England during the reign of the Virgin Queen.

“The year 1600,” observes the English historian Henry Hallam,¹ “was the first in which England produced a remarkable work in Physical Science; but this was one sufficient to raise a lasting reputation for its author. Gilbert, a physician, in his Latin treatise on the Magnet not only collected all the knowledge which others had possessed on the subject, but became at once the father of experimental philosophy in this island, and, by a singular felicity and acuteness of genius, the founder of theories which have been revived after a lapse of ages, and are almost universally received into the creed of science. . . . Gilbert was one of the earliest Copernicans, at least as to the rotation of the earth, and, with his usual sagacity, inferred, before the invention of the telescope, that there are a multitude of fixed stars beyond the reach of our vision.”

Gilbert’s book created a powerful impression at the time, especially among the learned in other parts of Europe. Galileo expressed the highest admiration of the work and of its author, and, it is said, pronounced Gilbert “great to a degree that is enviable.” It was, indeed, by the reading² of *De Magnete* that Galileo was induced to turn his mind to magnetism. In his own country, Gilbert was scarcely so highly appreciated; even Bacon, though he praises Gilbert as a philosopher, speaks with little respect of his theory. After a while his speculations came to be more esteemed, though perhaps not fully understood; but the great superiority of Gilbert over all who had previously treated of magnetism, and

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page continues the biographical memoir of William Gilbert, completing the sentence from the previous page concerning the historical recognition of Gilbert’s scientific foresight.</meta>

<page-num>xiii</page-num>

<header>BIOGRAPHICAL MEMOIR.</header>

"the extent to which he had anticipated by his conjectures much of our present knowledge" has only been perceived since the study of magnetism has assumed something like its present systematic and comprehensive character.¹

While Dr. Whewell observes² that "Gilbert's work contains all the fundamental facts of the science, so fully examined, indeed, that even at this day we have little to add to them," Dr. Thomas Thomson says³ that *De Magnete* "is one of the finest examples of inductive philosophy that has ever been presented to the world. It is the more remarkable because it preceded the *Novum Organum* of Bacon, in which the inductive method of philosophizing was first explained." How far Gilbert was ahead of his time is best proved by the works of those who wrote on magnetism during the first few decades after his death. They contributed in reality nothing to the extension of this branch of physical science. Poggendorff, from whose "Geschichte der Physik" (page 286) this is extracted, calls Gilbert "the Galileo of Magnetism." By Dr. Priestley he was named "the father of modern electricity."

In an article written not long ago, Mr. Conrad W. Cooke, of London, notes the high opinion of Gilbert's work held, more particularly, by Nathaniel Carpenter, William Barlowe, Francis Bacon, Galileo, and Humboldt, and he adds: "There is abundant testimony still existing that this '*De Magnete*' of Gilbert's produced a profound sensation, not only in this country but throughout the then-civilized world, and it is a singularly curious fact that the brilliance of a reputation so great and so original should have been allowed in subsequent generations to be lost sight of in the

<header>BIOGRAPHICAL MEMOIR.</header>

more blinding light of more recent knowledge and discoveries, and it is equally remarkable that a book so classic in its nature, so remarkable in its originality and prescience, and which was thought so much of during the periods which immediately followed its publication, should never have been translated into English, or indeed into any other language; and this is rendered still more curious by the fact that such a translation was actually called for at the time, and the want of it was considered remarkable as far back as the year 1618; and here it will be interesting to quote from the preface to a scarce old book, ‘*Magneticall Advertisements*,’ written at that date by the Ven. William Barlowe,¹ Archdeacon of Salisbury, and a very intimate friend of Dr. Gilbert. ‘*Many of our nation*,’ he says, ‘*both Gentlemen and others of excellent wits and lovers of these knowledges, not able to read Doctor Gilbert’s book in Latin have been (ever since the first publishing thereof) exceedingly desirous to have it translated into English, but hitherto no man has done it, neither (to my knowledge) as yet goes about any such matter, whereof one principal cause is that there are very few that understand his book, because they have not Load-stones of various forms, but especially round ones;*’ and the author gives a further supposition that ‘*a second cause may be for that there are various terms of art in the whole course of this book proper to this subject and fit for the explanation of his figures and diagrams*

which cannot be understood except by the help of mathematics and good experience in magnetic practice."

Dr. John Davy says^1 Gilbert's "work is worthy of being studied, and I am surprised that an English edition (translation) of it has never been published." He also alludes to the well-known reproach thrown upon Gilbert's philosophy by Francis Bacon, who, in his *De Augmentis Scientiarum*, remarks that "Gilbert has attempted to raise a general system upon the magnet, endeavoring to build a ship out of materials not sufficient to make the rowing-pins of a boat."

On the other hand, Digby and Barlowe place Gilbert on a level with Harvey, Galileo, Gassendi, and Descartes,^2 while the celebrated historian of the Council of Trent, Father Paul—Fra Paolo Sarpi—who will not be thought an incompetent judge, names Gilbert, with Francis Vieta (the greatest French mathematician of the sixteenth century), as the only original writer among his contemporaries.^3

It is worth noting that Gilbert was the first to use the terms "electric force," "electric emanations," and "electric attraction." It was also he who gave the name of "pole" to the extremities of the magnetic needle pointing to the poles of the earth, calling the *south pole* the extremity that pointed toward the north, and the *north pole* the extremity pointing toward the south. In the words of Sir David Brewster, Gilbert applies the term *magnetic* to all bodies which are acted upon by loadstones and magnets in the same manner as they act upon each other, and he finds that all such bodies contain iron in some state or other. He considers the phenomena of

To give here such an analysis as Gilbert's admirable work merits would be impracticable, but the short review of it made by Dr. John Robison<note>1</note> deserves full reproduction as follows :

> “In the introduction, he recounts all the knowledge of the ancients on the subject, and their passive inattention to what was so entirely in their hands, and the impossibility of ever adding to the stock of useful knowledge as long as men imagined themselves to be philosophizing while they were only repeating a few jargon words and the meaningless phrases of the Aristotelian school. It is curious to note the almost perfect similarity of Dr. Gilbert’s sentiments and language with those of Lord Bacon. They both command, in a decisive manner, all those who pretend to inform others to cease their dialectic labors—which are nothing but ringing changes on a few trite truths and many unfounded conjectures—and immediately turn to experimentation. He has pursued this method on the subject of magnetism with wonderful ardor, and with equal genius and success; for Dr. Gilbert possessed both great ingenuity and a mind suited for broad views of things. The work contains a prodigious number and variety of observations and experiments, sagaciously collected from the writings of others and conducted by himself with considerable expense and labor. It would indeed be a miracle if all Dr. Gilbert’s general inferences were correct, or all his experiments accurate. It was unexplored ground. But, on the whole, this work contains more real information than any writing of the age in

> “This work of Dr. Gilbert’s relates chiefly to the lodestone, and what we call magnets; that is, pieces of steel which have acquired properties similar to those of the lodestone. But he extends the term *magnetism* and the descriptive term *magnetic* to all bodies that are affected by lodestones and magnets in a manner similar to how they affect each other. In the course of his investigations, indeed, he finds that these bodies are only those that contain iron in some state or other; and in proving this limitation, he mentions a great variety of phenomena which have a considerable resemblance to those he considers magnetic—namely, those he called electrical, because they were produced in the same way that amber is made to attract and repel light bodies. He carefully notes the distinctions between these and the characteristic phenomena of magnets. He seems to have known that all bodies may be made electrical, while only <term>ferruginous</term> substances can be made magnetic. It is not saying too much of Dr. Gilbert’s work to affirm that it contains almost everything we know about magnetism. His tireless diligence in searching every writing on the subject, obtaining information from navigators, and his constant focus on experiments left very few facts unknown to him. We encounter many things in the writings of later researchers—some of high reputation and even from the present day—which are published and received as notable

The manner in which “this great man came to discover so much of magnetical philosophy” and “all the knowledge he gained on this subject,” we are told by Sir Kenelm Digby,¹ “was by forming a little lodestone into the shape of the earth. By this means he accomplished a wonderful design, which was to make the whole globe of the earth manageable; for he found the properties of the whole earth in that little body; which he therefore called a <term>terrella</term>, or little earth;² and which he could manage and conduct experiments upon at his will. And in like manner, anyone who aims to advance significantly in the natural sciences must endeavor to draw the matter he inquires about into some small model, or into some kind of manageable method; which he may turn and wind as he pleases. And then let him be sure, if he has a competent understanding, that he will not miss his mark.”

As described by Professor Sir William Thomson (Lord Kelvin), it is "in the form of a monument, ornamented with commemorative illustrations of Gilbert’s theory and experiments, and a fanciful representation of the earliest European mariner’s compass—a floating loadstone, but floating in a bowl on the sea and left behind by the ship sailing away from it! In the upper left-hand corner can be seen Gilbert’s <term>terrella</term> and <term>orbis virtutis</term>.<note>1</note> The <term>terrella</term> is a little globe of loadstone, which he made to illustrate his idea that the earth is a great globular magnet. . . . The <term>orbis virtutis</term> is simply Gilbert’s expression for what Faraday called the field of force—that is to say, the space around a magnet in which magnetic force is perceptibly exerted on another magnet, such as a small needle properly placed for the test. Gilbert’s word *virtue* expresses even more clearly than Faraday’s word *force* the idea argued so finely by Faraday, and proved so validly by his magneto-optic experiment, that there is a real physical action of a magnet through all the space around it, even though no other magnet is there to experience force and show its effects." The meaning of the little bars bordering the <term>terrella</term> is explained in Gilbert’s book (Book I, chapter iii, and Book V, chapter ii), where he alludes to the application of bits of fine iron wire as long as a barleycorn, etc.

After the death of Queen Elizabeth on March 24, 1603, Gilbert remained in his position as royal physician under King James I, but he survived his benefactress by only a few months. He died on November 30 of the same year; some say at Colchester, others at London. He was buried in the chancel of the Church of the Holy Trinity in Colchester, where a monu-

*Reserved, but not morose*, he never married, intentionally so that he might be more beneficial to his brothers. Besides Gilbert’s folio *De Magnete*, there appeared in Amsterdam, in 1651, a quarto volume of 316 pages entitled *De Mundo Nostro Sublunari Philosophia Nova*. This was edited—some say by his brother, William Gilbert Junior, while according to others, by the eminent English scholar and critic John Gruter—from two manuscripts found in the library of Sir William Boswell, Knight. According to Dr. John Davy, “this work of Gilbert’s, which is so little known, is a very remarkable one, both in style and matter; and there is a vigor and energy of expression belonging to it very suitable to its originality. Possessing a more detailed and practical knowledge of natural philosophy than Bacon, his opposition to the philosophy of the schools was more searching and specific, and at the same time probably no less efficient.”<note>1 “Memoirs of the Life of Sir Humphry Davy,” London 1836, Vol. I, page 311.</note> In the opinion of Prof. John Robison, *De Mundo* consists of an attempt to establish a new system of natural philosophy upon the ruins of the Aristotelian doctrine. We provide an extract from the work in a footnote to the present translation of Gilbert’s *De Magnete*, Book VI, Chapter VII, and are also able to provide a reproduction of the 1651 title-page, made through the courtesy of Dr. Park Benjamin.

I will make time for you, even if it were a month, to confer with you; you have shown me more—and brought more light—than any man has done. Sir, I will recommend you to my Lord of Effingham. There is here a wise, learned man, a Secretary of Venice; he was sent by that State and was honorably received by her Majesty. He brought me a Latin letter from a gentleman of Venice who is very well-learned, whose name is Johannes Franciscus Sagredus. He is a great man of magnetism and writes that he has conferred with various learned men of Venice and with the lecturers of Padua, and reports a wonderful liking for my book. You shall have a copy of the letter. Sir, I propose to add an appendix of six or eight sheets of paper to my book after a while; I am currently working on it regarding some new inventions, and I would like to have some of your experiments, in your name and as your invention, put into it if you please, so that you may be known as an improver of that art. So for this time, in haste, I take my leave, the 14th of February.
> ->Your very loving friend,<-
> ->W. GILBERT.<-

His intention to print the short appendix was never carried into effect.

<page-num>xxxvii</page-num>

->*To the most learned Mr. William Gilbert, the distinguished London physician and father of the magnetic philosophy: a laudatory address concerning these books on magnetism, by Edward Wright.*<-

Should there be anyone, most worthy sir, who disparages these books and researches of yours, and who deems these studies trifling and in no way worthy of a man dedicated to the more serious study of medicine, surely he will be considered no ordinary fool. For the uses of the <term>loadstone</term> are so significant, even remarkable, that they are too well known even among people of the lowest class to require many words or any praise from me at this time. Indeed, in my opinion, there is no subject of higher importance or greater utility to the human race to which you could have applied your philosophical talents. For by the God-given favor of this stone, it has come about that things which lay hidden for so many centuries—such vast continents of the globe, so infinite a number of countries, islands, nations, and peoples—have been easily discovered and often explored almost within our own memory. Furthermore, the entire globe has been circumnavigated more than once by our own Drake and Cavendish—a fact I wish to record for the eternal memory of those men. For, by the indication of the magnetized needle, the points North, South, East, and West, and the other points of the compass, are known to navigators, even while the sky is

<summary>Edward Wright praises William Gilbert's magnetic research, arguing that the study of the loadstone is of the highest importance because it enabled the discovery of new lands and the circumnavigation of the globe.</summary>
<keywords>William Gilbert, Edward Wright, magnetism, loadstone, navigation, Francis Drake, Thomas Cavendish, exploration, compass</keywords>

--- Page 42 ---
<meta>This page continues Edward Wright's address to William Gilbert, shifting from the general utility of the compass to the specific benefits of magnetic variation in navigation.</meta>

<page-num>xxxviii</page-num>
<header>ADDRESS BY EDWARD WRIGHT.</header>

murky and in the deepest night; by this means, seamen have understood toward which point they must steer their course, a thing that was quite impossible before the wondrous discovery of the north-pointing power of the <term>loadstone</term>. Consequently, sailors of old were often beset, as we learn from history, by incredible anxiety and great peril; for when storms raged and the sight of the sun and stars was cut off, they did not know where they were sailing, nor could they find out by any means or device. Therefore, how great must have been the gladness and joy of all mariners when this magnetic pointer first offered itself as a most certain guide on the route and as a god Mercury! But it was not enough for this magnetic Mercury simply to point out the way and, as it were, to show with a pointing finger where the course must be; it soon began even to indicate the distance of the place toward which the voyage is made. For since the magnetic pointer does not always point toward the same northern spot in every locality, but usually varies from it—either to the east or to the west—and yet nonetheless always has and holds the same variation in the same place, wherever that may be, it has come about that by means of this variation (as it is called), closely observed and noted in certain maritime regions along with an observation of the latitude, these same places can afterward be found by navigators when they approach and come near the same variation. In this, the Portuguese in their voyages to the East Indies have the surest signs of their approach to the Cape of Good Hope, as is shown in the accounts of Hugo *Lynschetensis*<note>Jan Hugo van Linscho(o)ten, Dutch voyager, 1563–1633.</note> and our very learned fellow-countryman Richard Hakluyt; by this means, too, many of our skilled British navigators, when voyaging from the Gulf of Mexico to the Azores,

# AUTHOR'S PREFACE.

## TO THE CANDID READER, DEDICATED TO THE MAGNETIC PHILOSOPHY.

SINCE in the discovery of secret things and in the investigation of hidden causes, stronger reasons are obtained from reliable experiments and demonstrated arguments than from probable conjectures and the opinions of ordinary philosophical speculators; therefore, so that the noble substance of that great <term>loadstone</term>, our common mother (the earth)—which is still quite unknown—and also the extraordinary and exalted forces of this globe may be better understood, we have decided first to begin with common stony and <term>ferruginous</term> matter, magnetic bodies, and the parts of the earth that we can handle and perceive with our senses; then to proceed with clear magnetic experiments and to penetrate to the inner parts of the earth. For after we had, in order to discover the true substance of the earth, seen and examined very many materials taken out of lofty mountains, the depths of the seas, deepest caverns, or hidden mines, we gave much atten-

Nor did we find our labor vain or fruitless, for every day in our experiments, novel, unheard-of properties came to light. Our Philosophy became so widened as a result of diligent research that we have attempted to set forth, according to magnetic principles, the inner constitution of the globe and its genuine substance; and through true demonstrations and experiments that appeal plainly to the senses—as though we were pointing with a finger—to exhibit Earth, mother of all, to mankind.

And even as geometry rises from certain slight and readily understood foundations to the highest and most difficult demonstrations, by which the ingenious mind ascends above the <term>aether</term>: so does our magnetic doctrine and science in due order first show certain facts of less rare occurrence. From these proceed facts of a more extraordinary kind; at length, in a sort of series, the most secret and private things in the earth are revealed, and the causes are recognized of things that were unnoticed or disregarded due to the ignorance of the ancients or the heedlessness of the moderns. There is no doubt that in the future these hypotheses will gain authority from the demonstrations themselves. Hence, the more advanced one is in the science of the <term>loadstone</term>, the more trust he will have in the hypotheses and the greater the progress he will make; nor will anyone reach anything like certainty in magnetic philosophy unless all, or at least most, of its principles are known to him.

This natural philosophy (*physiologia*) is almost a new thing, unheard of before; a very few writers have simply published some meager accounts of certain magnetic forces. Therefore, we do not cite the ancients and the Greeks as our supporters at all, for neither can petty Greek argumentation demonstrate the truth more subtly, nor can Greek terms do so more effectively; neither can explain it better. Our doctrine of the <term>loadstone</term> contradicts most of the principles and axioms of the Greeks. Nor have we included in this work any rhetorical flourishes or verbal ornamentation, but have aimed simply to treat difficult questions about which little is known in such a style and in such terms as are needed to make what is said clearly intelligible. Therefore, we sometimes employ new and unheard-of words—not (as <term>alchemists</term> are accustomed to do) in order to veil things with pedantic terminology and to make them dark and obscure, but so that hidden things which have no name and have never been noticed may be plainly and fully published.

After the magnetic experiments and the account of the <term>homogenic</term> parts of the earth, we proceed to a consideration of the general nature of the whole earth. Here we decided to philosophize freely—as freely as the Egyptians, Greeks, and Latins published their dogmas in the past. For very many of their errors have been handed down from author to author until our own time; and as our <term>sciolists</term> still take their stand on

<page-num>liii</page-num>

# EXPLANATION OF SOME TERMS USED IN THIS WORK.

*Terrella.* A spherical loadstone or natural magnet.<note>1</note>
*Verticity.*<note>2</note> Polar strength—activity (or what in Gilbert's day was understood as energy); not a spinning or dizzying motion, but a turning power. It is not polar rotation, but a directing quality, an innate turning force (*virtus convertens*). <note>3, 4</note>
*Electrics.* Bodies that attract in the same way as amber.
*Excited magnetic body.* One (such as iron or steel) that acquires magnetism from a loadstone or natural magnet.
*Magnetized versorium.* An iron bar or needle resting on a pivot (electroscope<note>5</note>) and set in motion—excited—by a loadstone or natural magnet.
*Non-magnetized versorium* (the electroscope itself). Made of any metal, for use in electrical experiments.
*Armed loadstone.* One that is equipped with an iron helmet or cap.<note>6</note>
*Meridionally.* In the direction of a meridian.
*Paralleletically.* In the direction of a parallel of latitude.
*Cuspis* (point). The end of a magnetized versorium.

---

<note>1. See Kenelm Digby's reference to the terrella in the Biographical Memoir, as well as *De Magnete*, Book I, Chapter III.</note>
<note>2. See *De Magnete*, Book I, Chapter X.</note>
<note>3. See *De Magnete*, Book II, Chapter VI, as well as Professor Sir William Thomson's reference to the *orbis virtutis* (sphere of influence) in the Biographical Memoir.</note>
<note>4. "Therefore it is true, and confirmed by every experiment, that steel and good iron, even when never excited by a loadstone, reveal a verticity within themselves; that is, a directing or polar faculty by which, when properly positioned, they point north at one end and south at the other" (Thomas Brown, *Pseudodoxia Epidemica*, 1658, Book II, Chapter II, page 63).</note>
<note>5. Humboldt says ("Cosmos," 1849, Vol. II, page 726) that Gilbert measured the strength of excited electricity by means of a small needle "not made of iron . . . ." *De Magnete* states that the *versorium* was made of any metal (*ex quouis metallo*) (Glossary, eighth line, and Book II, Chapter II, page 48), and refers (Book III, Chapter I, page 115) to the construction of a *versorium* made of two pieces of curved iron (*ex duobus curvis ferramentis*).</note>
<note>6. See *De Magnete*, Book II, Chapter XVII.</note>

<header>EXPLANATION OF SOME OF THE TERMS USED.</header>

*Crotch.* A name sometimes given to the end that is not touched or magnetized, although in some instruments both ends are commonly designated as such, depending on which is most convenient for magnetization by the loadstone.<note>1</note>

*Cork.* The bark of the cork tree.

*Radius (of a loadstone’s sphere).* A straight line drawn by the shortest path from the surface of a spherical loadstone to the surface of a body, which, when extended, passes through the center of the loadstone.

*Sphere of influence.* The entire space over which the force of a loadstone extends.<note>2</note>

*Sphere of coition.* The entire space over which even the smallest magnetic body moves toward a loadstone.

*Ostensio.* Physical demonstration (as opposed to mere theory).

*Magnetic coition.*<note>3</note> This phrase is used rather than *attraction* because magnetic movements do not result from the attraction of one body alone but from the coming together of two bodies harmoniously (not the drawing of one by the other)—‘Ομοδρομή [Homodromia]; the coition is always vigorous, even though heavy substances offer opposition.

*Declinatorium.* A bar or needle that moves vertically on its axis and is magnetized with a loadstone; it is used in the dip instrument.

---

<note>1. See *De Magnete*, Book II, Chap. XXXII.</note>
<note>2. See note 3, page xxxi.</note>
<note>3. See *De Magnete*, Book II, Chap. I, and following chapters.</note>

## BOOK FIRST.

### CHAPTER I.

#### WRITINGS OF ANCIENT AND MODERN AUTHORS CONCERNING THE LOADSTONE: VARIOUS OPINIONS AND DELUSIONS.

IN former times when philosophy, still rude and uncultured, was involved in the murkiness of errors and ignorance, a few of the virtues and properties of things were, it is true, known and understood: in the world of plants and herbs all was confusion, mining was undeveloped, and mineralogy was neglected. But when, through the genius and labors of many workers, certain things necessary for man’s use and welfare were brought to light and made known to others (reason and experience meanwhile providing a greater hope), then did mankind begin to search the forests, the plains, the mountains and precipices, the seas and the depths of the waters, and the innermost bowels of the earth, and to investigate all things. And by good luck at last the loadstone was found—as seems probable—by iron-smelters or by miners in veins of iron ore. On being treated by the metallurgists, it

# WILLIAM GILBERT.

quickly exhibited that strong, powerful attraction for iron—not a hidden or obscure property, but one easily seen by everyone; one observed and commended with much praise. After it had emerged, as if from darkness and deep dungeons, and was honored by men for its strong and marvelous attraction for iron, many ancient philosophers and physicians discussed it. They recorded it only briefly, however: for instance, Plato in the *Ion*, Aristotle only in his first book *De Anima*; likewise Theophrastus the Lesbian, Dioscorides, Gaius Plinius Secundus, and Julius Solinus. These authors record only that the loadstone attracts iron; its other properties were all hidden. But to prevent the story of the loadstone from being too meager and brief, certain fictions and falsehoods were added to this single known property. These were dealt out to be swallowed by mankind by superficial scholars and copyists, both in ancient times and today. For example, they asserted that a loadstone rubbed with garlic does not attract iron, nor does it do so in the presence of a diamond.<note>As for what some writers have reported—that a loadstone will not attract iron if there is a diamond nearby (Pliny, Book XXXVII, Chap. All of these writers are criticized by Cardan for being so careless and indifferent about such a remarkable subject—so broad a field of philosophy—and for failing to provide a more detailed account or a more developed philosophy. Yet Cardan himself, in his massive volumes, has left to posterity nothing worthy of a philosopher, aside from a few commonplaces, quotations from other writers, and false discoveries.¹ Among later authors, some speak only of its effectiveness in medicine, such as Antonio Musa Brassavola, Baptista Montanus, and Amatus Lusitanus, as did Oribasius before them in the 13th book of *De Facultate Metallicorum*, along with Avicenna, Serapio Mauritanus, Abohali (Hali Abbas), Santes de Ardoniis, Petrus Aponensis, Marcellus, and Arnaldus. # ANCIENT AND MODERN AUTHORS ON THE LOADSTONE.

Thomas Erastus, knowing nothing of the nature of the loadstone, draws from it weak arguments against Paracelsus. Georgius Agricola, like Encelius and other writers on metals, simply describes it. Alexander Aphrodiseus, in his *Problemata*, judges the question of the loadstone to be incapable of explanation. Lucretius Carus, the Epicurean poet, believes the attraction is due to this: that just as there is an outflow of the smallest bodies from all things, so there is an outflow of atoms from iron into the space between the iron and the loadstone—a space emptied of air by the loadstone's atoms (seeds). When these begin to return to the loadstone, the iron follows, as the corpuscles are entangled with each other. Joannes Costæus says something similar, following Plutarch. Thomas Aquinas, in Book 7 of his *Physica*, treating briefly of the loadstone, understands its nature fairly well; with his godlike and insightful mind, he would have developed many points had he been familiar with magnetic experiments. Plato considers the magnetic virtue to be divine. But when, some three or four hundred years ago, the magnetic movement toward the north and the south was discovered or recognized anew, many learned men—each according to his own gifts—strove to honor it with admiration and praise, or to explain with feeble reasoning a property so curious and so necessary for the use of mankind. Among more recent authors, very many have striven to discover the cause of this direction and movement to the north and south, and to understand this great miracle of nature and explain it to others. However, they wasted time and effort because they were not practical in researching natural objects; they were familiar only with books and were led astray by certain erroneous physical systems and

<meta>This page continues Gilbert’s critique of philosophers who relied on speculation rather than experiment, specifically discussing those who attributed magnetic properties to the stars before transitioning to the history and invention of the mariner's compass.</meta>

# WILLIAM GILBERT.

...having performed no magnetic experiments, they constructed certain reasonings based on mere opinions and, like superstitious old women, dreamed of things that did not exist. Marsilio Ficino ruminates on ancient opinions; to explain the reason for magnetic direction, he seeks its cause in the constellation Ursa. In the loadstone, he says, the power of Ursa prevails, and thus it is transferred into the iron. Paracelsus declares that there are stars which, gifted with the loadstone’s power, attract iron to themselves. Levinus Lemnius describes and praises the mariner’s compass and, on certain grounds, infers its antiquity; he does not reveal the hidden miracle which he claims to know. 

The people of Melfi <note>Likely referring to Amalfi</note>, in the kingdom of Naples, are said to have first constructed a mariner’s compass; and, as Flavio Biondo says, the townspeople boast, not without reason, that they were taught by one Joannes Goia, a fellow citizen, in the year 1300. This town is in the Kingdom of Naples, not far from Salerno, and near the promontory of Minerva. The sovereignty of the place was conferred by Charles V on Andrea Doria, the great naval commander, in recognition of his splendid achievements. It is certain that nothing has ever been devised by human art, nor has anything been of greater advantage to the human race, than the mariner’s compass; but many infer from ancient writings and from certain arguments and conjectures that the compass was discovered earlier and accepted among the arts of navigation. Knowledge of the mariner’s compass

For had it been used by them, the Greeks, the Italians, and all the "Barbarians" would undoubtedly have known of a thing so necessary and so celebrated through common use. Nor would things so famous, so easily understood, and of the highest necessity ever fall into oblivion; on the contrary, the knowledge would have been handed down to posterity, or some written memorial would survive.

Sebastian Cabot first discovered that the magnetized iron needle varied. Gonzales Oviedo first mentioned in his history that at the meridian of the Azores there is no variation. [Jean François] Fernel, in his book *De Abditis Rerum Causis*, says that in the <term>loadstone</term> is a hidden and abstruse cause; elsewhere he says this cause is celestial, and he merely explains the unknown by the even more unknown. Cardan places great importance on the star in the tail of Ursa Major; he attributes the cause of variation to its rising, thinking that variation is always certain when that star rises. But the difference of variation due to changes in location, and the shifts in many places—shifts that are irregular even in the southern regions—rule out this exclusive influence of one star at its northern rising. The College of Coimbra looks for the cause in some region of the sky near the pole. Scaliger, in the 131st of his *Exercitationes* on Cardan's work *De Subtilitate*, introduces a celestial cause unknown even to himself, and terrestrial loadstones that have never been discovered; he looks for the cause not in the "<term>siderite</term> <note>magnetic</note> mountains" but in the force that formed them—namely, in the part of the heavens that hangs over that northern point. This opinion the learned author presents with excessive wordiness and crowns with many subtle observations in the margin, but his reasons are not actually so subtle. Martinus Cortesius maintains that the source of the attraction lies beyond the poles, and that it is the moving heavens. A Frenchman named Bessard studies the pole of the Zodiac, but to just as little purpose. Jacobus Severtius of Paris, after quoting a few observations from others, invents new errors regarding how loadstones from different regions point in different directions, as well as errors concerning the eastern and western parts of a loadstone. <meta>This page continues the critique of Renaissance and early modern authors' theories on magnetism, specifically refuting those who rely on celestial or unproven geographical causes for magnetic behavior.</meta>

<header>ANCIENT AND MODERN AUTHORS ON THE LOADSTONE, II</header>

...a certain magnetic island mentioned by Olaus Magnus. Josephus Costa, knowing nothing whatever of the subject, nevertheless pours out empty words about the loadstone. Livio Sanuto, in his *Geography* (written in Italian), discourses at length on the prime magnetic meridian and the magnetic poles—whether they are terrestrial or celestial; he also treats an instrument for finding longitude. But as he does not understand the nature of the loadstone, he only adds errors and obscurities to his otherwise excellent treatise. Fortunius Affaitatus offers some rather silly philosophizing about the attraction of iron and its turning toward the poles. Very recently, Baptista Porta, a philosopher of no ordinary reputation, made the seventh book of his *Magia Naturalis* a virtual storehouse and collection of magnetic wonders; but he knows little about the movements of the loadstone and has never seen much of them. Much of what he has learned about its obvious properties—either from Messer Paolo the Venetian or through his own studies—is not very accurately noted or observed. The book is full of highly erroneous experiments, as will be shown in the appropriate place; still, I hold him worthy of praise because he attempted such a great task (just as he has attempted many other tasks, successfully and with significant results) and because he has provided the occasion for further research.

All these philosophers, our predecessors, discussing attraction on the basis of a few vague and indecisive experiments and reasoning from the hidden causes of things—and counting among the causes of the magnet's direction a region of the sky, celestial poles, stars, <term>asterisms</term> <note>constellations</note>; or mountains, cliffs, empty space, atoms, attractional or <term>collimational</term> <note>alignment-based</note> regions beyond the heavens, and other similar unproved paradoxes—are vastly astray from the truth and are wandering blindly. ...regarding the people of China, they were not ignorant of magnetic experiments in ancient times, for even in their country the most excellent magnets in the world are found. The Egyptians, as Manetho relates, give it the name ‘the bone of Horus,’ calling the power that presides over the revolution of the sun Horus, just as the Greeks called it Apollo. But later, as Plato declares, Euripides gave it the name *magnet*. It is mentioned and praised by Plato in the *Ion*, by Nicander of Colophon, Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Pliny, Solinus, Ptolemy, Galen, and other investigators of nature. But considering the great differences among loadstones—their variations in hardness, softness, weight, lightness, density, firmness, and brittleness; in color and in all other qualities—these writers have not handed down a sufficient account of it. The history of the magnet was overlooked by them, or, if recorded, was incomplete, because in ancient times many kinds of objects and foreign products never seen before were not brought in by traders and mariners as they usually are now, when all manner of commodities—stones, woods, spices, herbs, metals, and metallic wares—are eagerly sought throughout the world; nor was mining carried on everywhere in early times as it is today.

The difference between loadstones rests on their respective power: hence, one loadstone is male and another female; the ancients were accustomed to distinguish many objects of the same species in this way. Pliny quotes five kinds from Sotacus: namely, the loadstones of Ethiopia, Macedonia, Boeotia, Troas, and Asia, respectively, which were the main types known to the ancients.<note>Porta describes it this way: “The Ethiopian; the Magnesian from Magnesia near Macedonia, on the right hand as one travels toward Lake Boebeis; the third in Echium of Boeotia; the fourth near *Alexandria* at Troas; the fifth in Magnesia of Asia” (*Natural Magic*, Book VII, Chapter I).</note>

But we recognize as many kinds as there are regions in the whole world with differing soil; for in every climate, in every province, and in all kinds of land, the loadstone is either found or lies unknown because of its deep location or its inaccessible situation; or, because of its weaker and less potent virtues, it is not recognized by us even while we see it and touch it.¹

For the ancients, the differences were based on color: The magnets from Magnesia in Macedonia were red and black; those from Boeotia were red rather than black; those from the Troad were black without strength; and those from Asian Magnesia were white, without the power of attracting iron, and resembled pumice. A strong loadstone, and one that demonstrates its power under experiment, nowadays generally resembles unpolished iron and is usually found in iron mines; sometimes it is also found forming a continuous vein by itself. Such loadstones are imported from the East Indies, China, and Bengal, and they are the color of iron, or of a dark blood-red or liver color. These are the most excellent and are often of great size and weight, as if broken off a great rock; or again, they are as if complete in themselves. Some of these, though they may weigh only one pound, will lift four ounces, or half a pound, or even an entire pound of iron. In Arabia, red loadstones are found shaped like tiles; they are not as heavy as those imported from China, yet they are strong and good. Rather black loadstones are found in Ilva, an island of the Etrurian sea; with these also occur white loadstones like those from the mines of Caravaca in Spain, but they are of inferior strength. ...two natural poles of surpassing importance even in our terrestrial globe, constant points related to the movement of its daily revolution, namely, one pole pointing to Arctos (the Bear) and the north; the other looking toward the opposite part of the heavens. In like manner the loadstone has from nature its two poles, a northern and a southern; fixed, definite points in the stone, which are the primary endpoints of the movements and effects, and the limits and regulators of the several actions and properties. It is to be understood, however, that the force of the stone does not emanate from a mathematical point, but from the parts themselves; and all these parts in the whole—while they belong to the whole—the nearer they are to the poles of the stone, the stronger the powers they acquire and pour out on other bodies. These poles look toward the poles of the earth, and move toward them, and are subject to them. Magnetic poles may be found in every loadstone, whether strong and powerful (male, as the term was in antiquity) or faint, weak, and female; whether its shape is due to design or to chance, and whether it be long, or flat, or square, or three-cornered, or polished; whether it be rough, broken-off, or unpolished: the loadstone always has and always shows its poles. *

But because the spherical form, which is also the most perfect, agrees best with the earth, which is a globe, and also is the form best suited for experimental uses, we therefore intend to give our principal demonstrations with the aid of a globe-shaped loadstone, as being the best and the most fitting. Take then a strong loadstone, solid, of convenient size, uniform, hard, and without flaw; on a lathe, such as is used in turning crystals and some precious stones, or on any similar instrument (as the nature and toughness of the stone may require, for often it is worked only with difficulty), give the loadstone the form of a ball. The stone thus prepared is a true homogeneous off-

To find, then, poles corresponding to the earth’s poles, take the round stone in your hand and lay on it a needle or a piece of iron wire: the ends of the wire move around their middle point and suddenly come to a standstill. Now, with ochre or with chalk, mark where the wire lies still and stays. Then move the middle or center of the wire to another spot, and so to a third and a fourth, always marking the stone along the length of the wire where it stands still: the lines marked in this way will show meridian circles, or circles like meridians on the stone or *terrella*; and clearly they will all come together at the poles of the stone. The circles being continued in this way, the poles appear—both the north and the south—and between these, midway, we may draw a large circle for an equator, just as is done by the astronomer in the heavens and on his spheres and by the geographer on the terrestrial globe; for the line drawn this way on our *terrella* is also very useful in our demonstrations and our magnetic experiments. Poles are also found in the round stone by using a *versorium*—a piece of iron touched with a loadstone and resting on a needle or point (attached at its base to the *terrella*), so that it can freely revolve, as in the figure.

# CHAPTER IV.

## WHICH POLE IS THE NORTH: HOW THE NORTH POLE IS DISTINGUISHED FROM THE SOUTH POLE.

<margin>*</margin>One of the Earth’s poles is turned toward Cynosura <note>The constellation of the Little Bear, containing the North Star</note> and steadily points toward a fixed point in the heavens (except that it is unmoved by the precession of the fixed stars in longitude—a movement we recognize in the Earth, as we shall later show); the other pole is turned toward the opposite region of the heavens, a region unknown to the ancients, but which is decorated with a multitude of stars and is itself a striking sight for those who make long voyages. So, too, the loadstone possesses the quality and power of directing itself toward the North and the South (the Earth itself cooperating and giving it that power) according to the structure of nature, which adjusts the movements of the stone to its true locations. It is demonstrated in this manner: Place the magnetic stone (after you have found its poles) in a round wooden vessel—a bowl or a dish; then place the vessel holding the magnet (like a boat with a sailor in it) in a tub of water or a cistern where it may float freely in the middle without touching the rim, and where the air is not disturbed by winds or currents which might interfere with the natural movement of the stone. There the stone, as if in a boat floating in the middle of a calm surface of still water, will immediately set itself and the vessel containing it in motion, and will turn in a circle until its south pole faces North and its north pole faces South. For, from an opposite position, it returns to the poles; and although with its...

Whenever you move it out of its place, because of the extraordinary power with which nature has endowed it, it seeks its fixed and established points again. This does not only occur when the poles of the loadstone in the float are positioned evenly in the plane of the horizon; it also occurs even if one pole—whether north or south—is raised or lowered 10, 20, 30, 40, or 80 degrees from the plane of the horizon. You will see the north part of the stone seek the south, and the south part the north; so that even if the pole of the stone is only one degree from the zenith and the center of the heavens, the whole stone revolves until the pole finds its own place. And though the pole does not point exactly to its position, it will still incline toward it and will come to rest in the meridian of its true direction. It moves with the same force whether the north pole is directed toward the upper heavens or whether the south pole is raised above the horizon. Yet it must always be kept in mind that although there are many differences between stones, and one far surpasses another in strength and efficiency, all loadstones still have the same limits and turn toward the same points.

Furthermore, it should be remembered that everyone who has written about the poles of the loadstone until now—including all <margin>*</margin> instrument makers and navigators—is greatly mistaken in taking the part of the stone that points north for the north pole, and the part that looks south for the south pole. We will prove this to be an error later on. The entire philosophy of the magnet is still so poorly developed, even regarding its basic principles.

The causes of all these (nature's secrets being unlocked) will be demonstrated in their proper place with fitting words and the help of scientific equipment. It is a well-known and common fact that the loadstone attracts iron; in the same way, one loadstone also attracts another. Take the stone on which you have marked the poles, *N.* and *S.*, and place it in a vessel so that it may float. Similarly, if you present the north pole of the stone in your hand to the south pole of the floating one, they come together and follow each other. For opposite poles attract opposite poles. Nature will not tolerate an unjust and unfair peace, or an improper agreement, but makes war and employs force to make bodies settle fairly and justly. Therefore, when rightly arranged, the parts attract each other—that is, both stones, the weaker and the stronger, come together and with all their might strive for union. ## CHAPTER VI.

### THE LOADSTONE ATTRACTS IRON ORE AS WELL AS THE SMELTED METAL.

THE most powerful property of the loadstone, and the one valued most by the ancients, is its attraction for iron. Plato mentions that the magnet (so called by Euripides) draws iron to itself, and not only attracts iron rings but also endows them with the power to do as the stone itself does—that is, to attract other rings. The loadstone loses some of its attractive power and, as it were, enters the decline of old age if it is exposed too long to the open air and not kept in a case with a covering of iron filings or iron scales; therefore, it must be packed in such material. Nothing withstands this unbreakable power except what destroys the physical structure of the body or corrodes it; no, not even a thousand adamants joined into one. Iron is, by everyone, classified among metals; it is of a bluish color, very hard, grows red hot before melting, is very hard to melt, spreads under the hammer, and is resonant. Chemists say that if fixed earthy sulfur is combined with fixed earthy mercury and these two bodies present not a pure white but a bluish-white color, if the sulfur prevails, iron results. For those harsh masters of metals, who in many various processes put them to the torture—by crushing, calcining, smelting, subliming, and precipitating—distinguish this, on account of both the earthy sulfur and the earthy mercury, as more truly the child of earth than any other metal; for they do not consider gold, silver, lead, tin, or even copper to be so earthy. Therefore, it is treated only in the hottest furnaces with the help of bellows; and when thus smelted, if it becomes hard again, it cannot be smelted once more without great labor; and its slag can be melted only with the utmost difficulty. It is the hardest of metals, subduing and breaking them all because of the strong solidification of the more earthy substance. Hence, we shall better understand what iron is when we have explained, in a way different from those who have gone before us, the causes and the matter of metals. <term>Aristotle</term> supposes their matter to be an exhalation. The chemists in unison declare that <term>sulfur</term> and <term>quicksilver</term> are the primary elements. <term>Gilgil</term>, the Mauretanian, holds the primary element to be ash moistened with water; <term>Georgius Agricola</term> considers it a mixture of water with earth; and his opinion differs not at all from Gilgil's thesis. Oily bodies (*pinguia corpora*), fresh water void of properties, quicksilver, and sulfur: these are not the primary principles of metals. They are the results of another natural process; they do not have a place now, nor have they ever had a place, in the process of producing metals. The earth gives off various humors, which are produced neither from water nor from dry earth, nor from mixtures of these, but from the matter of the earth itself. These are not distinguished by opposite qualities or substances. Nor is the earth a simple substance, as the <term>Peripatetics</term> imagine. The humors come from sublimed vapors that have their origin deep within the earth. And all waters are, as it were, extractions and exudations from the earth. Therefore <term>Aristotle</term> is partly right when he says that the exhalation which condenses in the earth’s veins is the primary matter of metals; for exhalations are condensed in situations cooler than the place of their origin, and owing to the structure of lands and mountains, they are in due time condensed, as if in wombs, and changed into metals. But they do not by themselves alone constitute the veins of ore; they only flow into and merge with more solid matter and form metals. When, therefore, this hardened matter has settled in more temperate cavities, it takes shape in these moderately warm spaces, just as a seed or embryo grows in a warm uterus. Sometimes the exhalation merges only with matter that is homogeneous throughout, and hence some metals are occasionally—though not often—obtained pure and not needing to be smelted. But other exhalations, being mixed with foreign earths, must be smelted; this is how the ores of all metals are treated, which are freed from all their dross by the action of fire. But that there is gold, or silver, or copper, or that any other metals exist, does not happen from any *quantitas* <note>quantity</note> or proportion of matter, nor by any specific virtues of matter, as the chemists foolishly imagine; but it happens when, earth cavities and the shape of the ground coinciding with the appropriate matter, those metals take from universal nature the forms by which they are perfected, just as in the case of all other minerals, all plants, and all animals: otherwise the kinds of metals would be vague and undefined: in fact, the varieties are very few, hardly ten in number. But why nature should be so stingy in the number of metals, or why there should be even as many metals as are recognized by man, is not easy to explain, though simpletons and raving astrologers assign the respective metals to the various planets.¹ But neither do the planets agree with the metals nor the metals with the planets, either in number or in properties. For what is common between Mars and iron, except that, like many other implements, swords and artillery are made of iron? What has copper to do with Venus? Or how does tin, or zinc, relate to Jupiter? These would be better dedicated to Venus. But enough of such old wives' tales. Thus, exhalations are the remote cause of the generation of metals; the immediate cause is the fluid from the exhalations: like the blood and the semen in the generation of animals. ->WILLIAM GILBERT.<-

What the chemists (such as Geber and others) call the fixed earthy sulfur in iron is nothing else but the homogeneous matter of the globe held together by its own fluid and hardened by a second fluid; the metallic moisture is introduced with a minute quantity of earth-substance that is not lacking moisture. Hence, it is stated very incorrectly by many authors that pure earth exists in gold and impure earth in iron—as though natural earth and the globe itself had become impure in some incomprehensible sense. In iron, especially in the best iron, earth exists in its true and genuine nature. In other metals, there is not as much earth; instead of earth and precipitate, there are condensed and (so to speak) fixed salts, which are efflorescences of the Earth and which also differ in firmness and consistency. In mines, they rise in great volume with a double moisture from the exhalations; in the underground spaces, they are consolidated into metallic ores. So, too, they are produced together, and by virtue of their location and the surrounding bodies, they acquire their specific forms in natural matrices.

We have spoken before of the various bodily constitutions of loadstones, their different substances, colors, and properties; but now, after having explained the cause and origin of metals, the substance of iron—not in the smelted metal but in the ore from which it is obtained—must be examined. Iron that appears pure because of its color is found in the earth; yet it is not exactly metallic iron, nor is it quite suitable for the various uses of iron. Sometimes it is found covered with a white moss-like substance, or with a coating of other stones. Such ore is often seen in the sands of rivers; such is the ore from Noricum (the region south of the Danube, watered by the Inn [Aenus] and the Drave [Drau], mostly comprised of modern Austria). Nearly pure iron ore is often mined in Ireland; from this, the blacksmith forges iron implements in his shop without the labor of the smelting furnace.

From an ore the color of liver, a type of iron with bright scales <note>original: *bracteæ*</note> is very often obtained in France. In England, such iron is produced without these scales; carpenters there use it as a marking tool instead of chalk. In the English county of Sussex, there is a rich ore of a dark color, and another of a pale, ashy color. When both of these ores are heated until red-hot for some time, or kept in a moderate fire, they take on the color of liver. In Sussex, there is also a dark-colored ore found in square masses, which has a black outer rind made of a harder material.

The liver-colored ore is often mixed with other stones in various ways, as well as with pure loadstone <term>magnetite</term>, which yields the highest quality iron. There is also a rust-colored ore, a lead-colored ore mixed with black, a simple black ore, and a black ore mixed with cobalt. Additionally, there is an ore mixed with pyrites <term>iron disulfide, often called "fool's gold"</term> or "sterile" plumbago <term>likely a low-grade graphite or lead-like mineral that does not yield metal</term>.

One kind of ore resembles jet <note>a hard, black, coal-like gemstone</note>, while another resembles the precious stone hematite <note>original: *hæmatites*</note>. The stone emery <note>original: *smiris*; a form of corundum</note>—used by glassworkers for cutting glass and called "emery-stone" by the English and *schmergel* by the Germans—is actually a form of iron. Although iron is smelted from it with great difficulty, it is capable of attracting an unmagnetized needle. It is often found in deep silver and iron mines.

Thomas Erastus <note>a 16th-century Swiss physician and theologian</note> mentions being informed by a scholar about iron ores that look like metallic iron but are soft and greasy, capable of being molded with the fingers like butter. We have seen ores of nearly the same kind found in England; they resemble Spanish soap <note>a high-quality vegetable-oil soap, also known as Castile soap</note>. Besides these countless forms of stony ores, there is a substance similar to iron rust deposited from water containing iron <note>original: *ferriferous* water</note>; this is gathered from mud, loam, and ochre. ## CHAPTER VIII.

### IN WHAT COUNTRIES AND REGIONS IRON IS PRODUCED.

Iron mines are very numerous everywhere—both the ancient mines mentioned by the earliest writers and the new and modern ones. I believe the first and greatest were in Asia, for in the countries of Asia, which naturally abound in iron, government and the arts flourished most; and it was there that the things necessary for human use were first discovered and sought. It is recorded that iron existed in the neighborhood of Andria; in the land of the Chalybes, on the banks of the river Thermodon in Pontus; in the mountains of Palestine on the side toward Arabia; and in Carmania. In Africa, there was an iron mine on the island of Meroe. In Europe, iron was found in the hills of Britain, as Strabo writes; in Nearer Spain, in Cantabria; and among the Petrocorii and the Cubi Bituriges in Gaul, there were smithies in which iron was made. In Germany, there was a mine near Luna, mentioned by Ptolemy; the Gothinian iron is spoken of by Cornelius Tacitus; and the iron of Noricum is famous in poetry; there was also iron in Crete and in Euboea. Many other mines, neither meager nor small but of vast extent, were overlooked by writers or were unknown to them. Pliny calls Nearer Spain and the whole region of the Pyrenees

The earliest mines were iron mines, not mines of gold, silver, copper, or lead: for iron is more sought after for the needs of man; besides, iron mines are plainly visible in every country and in every soil, and they are shallower and less surrounded with difficulties than other mines. But if I were simply to list modern iron mines and those worked in our own time, a very large book would have to be written, and I would run out of paper before I ran out of iron: yet each one of these mines could supply 1,000 forges. For among minerals there is no other substance so plentiful: all metals and all stones distinct from iron ore are surpassed by <term>ferric</term> and <term>ferruginous</term> substances. For you cannot easily find a district—hardly even a township—throughout all Europe, if you search thoroughly, that does not have a rich and plentiful vein of iron, or that does not yield an earth either saturated with iron rust or at least slightly colored by it. That this is so is easily shown by anyone skilled in <term>metallurgy</term> and <term>chemistry</term>.

Besides iron and its ore, there is another ferric substance which, however, does not yield the metal, because its thin moisture is burned up by fierce fires and is converted into slag like that separated from the metal when first smelted. Such is the white clay and <term>argillaceous</term> earth which is seen to make up a great part of our British island; this, if treated with intense heat, either displays a ferric and metallic body or is transformed into a ferric <term>vitrification</term>. This fact can be verified in houses built of brick, for the bricks in the kiln that are laid nearest to the fires, and are burned there, show ferric vitrification at their other end, which turns black. Furthermore, all those earths, when prepared, are attracted by the magnet just like iron. The earth's supply of iron is both lasting and plentiful.

# IN WHAT COUNTRIES IRON IS PRODUCED.

Georgius Agricola says that nearly all mountainous regions are full of its ores; and we, ourselves, know that a rich iron ore is often dug in the lowlands and plains throughout England and Ireland, as Agricola tells of iron being dug in the meadows near the town of Saga¹ out of ditches not more than two feet deep. Nor is iron lacking, as some say, in the West Indies; but there, the Spaniards, intent on gold, avoid the toilsome manufacture of iron and do not search for rich iron ores and mines. It is probable that nature and the terrestrial globe cannot repress, but are ever sending forth into the light a great quantity of its own native substance, and that this action is not entirely impeded by the pressure of the mingled substances and efflorescences at the circumference.

But iron is produced not only in the common mother (the globe of Earth), but sometimes is also in the air, in the uppermost clouds from the earth's vapors. It rained iron in Lucania the year that Marcus Crassus met his death. They tell, too, of a mass of iron, resembling slag, having fallen out of the air in the Nethorian forest near Grina, which is said to have weighed several pounds; and that it could not be carried to that village because it was so heavy, and could not be taken on a wagon because there were no roads. This happened before the Civil War of the Saxons, waged by the Dukes. A similar occurrence is mentioned by Avicenna. In the Torinese, it once rained iron at several points, some three years before that province was conquered by the King. In the year 1510, as Cardan relates in

### CHAPTER X.

<margin>*</margin> MEN are deplorably ignorant regarding natural things; and modern philosophers, as if dreaming in the darkness, must be awakened and taught the uses of things and the practical handling of things. They must be made to abandon the kind of learning that comes only from books and rests only on vain arguments of probability and upon conjectures. Yet when treated artificially with fire, as described in the previous chapter, these acquire polar activity and strength (<term>verticity</term>, as we call it). And not only those ores that miners seek, but even earths simply impregnated with ferruginous matter, and many kinds of rock, do the same thing (provided they are skillfully placed). They tend and glide toward those positions of the heavens, or rather of the earth, until they reach the point they seek; there they rest eagerly.

## CHAPTER XI.

### WROUGHT-IRON, NOT MAGNETIZED BY THE LODESTONE, ATTRACTS IRON.

<margin>*</margin> IRON is extracted from the ore in the first furnace. This ore is converted or separated partly into metal and partly into dross by the action of very intense heat continued for eight, ten, or twelve hours. The metal flows out, leaving behind the dross and useless substances, and forms a large, long mass, which is cut into pieces under the blows of a heavy hammer. From these pieces—after being refined in another furnace and placed again on the anvil—the workmen form cubical masses, or more usually bars, which are sold to merchants and blacksmiths. From these blocks or bars, various implements are made everywhere in blacksmiths' shops.

This we call wrought iron, and, as everyone knows, it is attracted by the lodestone. But we, steadily trying all sorts of experiments, have discovered that mere iron itself, magnetized by no lodestone nor impregnated with any outside force, attracts other iron, though it does not seize the other iron as eagerly nor pull it to itself as suddenly as a strong lodestone would. You may learn that this is so from the following experiment: A small, round piece of cork the size of a hazelnut has an iron wire passed through its middle. Float this in still water and bring the end of another wire near (without touching) one end of the floating wire. Wire attracts wire, and when one is slowly withdrawn, the other follows; yet this action takes place only within proper limits. In the figure, *A* is the cork holding the wire, *B* is one end of the

# CHAPTER XII.

## A LONG PIECE OF IRON, EVEN NOT MAGNETIZED, ASSUMES A NORTH AND SOUTH DIRECTION.

<margin>*</margin> All good and perfect iron, if it is drawn out long, acts like a lodestone or like iron rubbed with a lodestone: it takes a north and south direction—something not at all understood by our great philosophers, who have labored in vain to demonstrate the properties of the lodestone and the causes of the attraction of iron to the lodestone. Experiments can be conducted with either large or small iron objects, in either air or water. A straight rod of iron six feet long and as thick as a finger is (as described in the previous chapter) suspended in exact equilibrium with a fine but strong silk thread. The thread, however, should be composed of several silk filaments twisted in different ways, not all in one direction. Let the experiment be performed in a small room with all doors and windows closed to prevent air currents in the room; therefore, it is not advisable to experiment on windy days or when a storm is brewing. The iron rod acts freely according to its properties and moves slowly until, at last coming to a stop at its targets, it points north and south, like magnetized iron in a sundial, a common magnetic compass, or a mariner's compass. If you are curious about such experiments, you may suspend several iron rods, wires, or knitting needles from slender threads at once: you will find them all in agreement unless there is some flaw in the conduct of this interesting experiment; for unless you make all preparations precisely and exactly, your labor will be in vain.
