<header>FIXED NORTH AND SOUTH PARTS OF IRON.</header>

Test this in water as well; there, the result is more certain and more easily obtained. Push an iron wire—two or three fingers long, more or less—through a round cork so that it just floats in the water. The moment you place it in the water, it turns on its center; one end of the wire moves toward the north and the other toward the south. You will find the cause of this later when we discuss the reasons for the lodestone's directions. <margin>*</margin> It is also useful to know and remember well that just as a strong lodestone—and iron magnetized by it—does not always point toward the true pole but exactly toward the point of variation, so too will a weaker lodestone and iron that directs itself by its own force (rather than by force derived from the impression of a magnet). Similarly, all iron ores and all substances filled with any iron matter and properly prepared will turn to the same point on the horizon—to the place of variation for that specific location (if variation exists there)—and there they remain and rest.

### CHAPTER XIII.

### SMELTED IRON HAS IN ITSELF FIXED NORTH AND SOUTH PARTS, MAGNETIC ACTIVITY, VERTICITY, AND FIXED VERTICES OR POLES.

**IRON** takes a direction toward the north and south, but not <margin>*</margin> with the same end directed toward either pole; for one end of a piece of iron ore or of an iron wire steadily and constantly points to the north, and the other to the south, whether it is suspended in the air or floating in water, and whether the specimens are iron bars or thin wires. Thus, if you divide the rod or wire into several pieces, you will know the poles even before testing them by floating the pieces in water. In all these fragments, a northern end attracts a southern one and repels another northern one, and *vice versa*, according to magnetic law. 

But in this regard, manufactured iron differs from lodestone and iron ore: in an iron ball of any size—for example, bombs, cannonballs, culverin balls, or falcon balls—polarity (verticity) is less easily acquired and less clearly shown than in the lodestone itself, in ore, or in a spherical lodestone. However, in iron instruments of any length, the force is immediately apparent. Thus, pretenders to science foolishly and absurdly seek remedies, ignorant of the true causes of things. Headaches, despite the opinion of many, are no more cured by the application of a <term>loadstone</term> than by putting an iron helmet or a steel hat on the head. Administering <term>loadstone</term> to <term>dropsical</term> persons is either an error of the ancients or a clumsy quotation by their transcribers, although a <term>loadstone</term> may be found capable of purging the bowels, in the manner of various metallic substances; however, the effect would be due to some impurity of the stone, not to its magnetic force. ## CHAPTER XV.

### THE MEDICINAL POWER OF IRON.

It will not be irrelevant to our purpose to treat briefly the medicinal power of iron; for it is beneficial in many diseases of the human system, and by its virtues—both natural and acquired through appropriate and skillful preparation—it brings about wonderful changes in the human body. We may more clearly describe its nature through its medicinal power and by means of a few well-known experiments, to the end that even those apprentices of medicine who abuse this most excellent medicinal agent may learn to prescribe it more judiciously for the curing of patients, and not, as is too often the case, to their destruction. The best iron, that is, *<term>stomoma</term>*, *<term>chalybs</term>*, *<term>acies</term>*, or *<term>aciarium</term>* (steel), is reduced by filing to a fine powder; strong vinegar is poured on this powder, which is then dried in the sun, treated again with vinegar, and once more dried. Then it is washed in spring water or other available water and dried. It is again pulverized and pounded fine on porphyry, sifted through a fine sieve, and kept for use. It is given chiefly in cases of a lax and overly humid liver, and in cases of a swollen spleen after suitable evacuations; hence young women of pale, muddy, and blotchy complexions are restored by it to health and beauty, for it is highly drying and harmlessly astringent. But some, who always identify obstructions of the liver and spleen in every internal disorder, think it beneficial in such cases as a means of removing obstructions; and in this, they chiefly follow the opinions of certain Arabic writers. ## CHAPTER XVI.

### THAT LOADSTONE AND IRON ORE ARE THE SAME, AND THAT IRON IS OBTAINED FROM BOTH, LIKE OTHER METALS FROM THEIR ORES; AND THAT ALL MAGNETIC PROPERTIES EXIST, ALTHOUGH WEAKER, BOTH IN SMELTED IRON AND IN IRON ORE.

So far we have described the nature and properties of the loadstone, as well as the properties and nature of iron; it now remains for us to point out their mutual affinities—their kinship, so to speak—and to show that the two substances are very closely related. In the uppermost part of the terrestrial globe or its surface of debris—its rind, as it were—these two bodies come into being and are generated in the same matrix, in one bed, like twins. Strong loadstones are mined from separate deposits, and weaker loadstones also have their own beds. Both occur in iron mines. Iron ore usually occurs by itself, unaccompanied by strong loadstone (for more perfect loadstones occur more rarely). A strong loadstone looks like iron: from it the best iron is often made, which the Greeks call *stomoma*, the Latins *acies*, and others, not inappropriately, *aciare* or *aciarium*. This stone attracts and repels other loadstones and governs their directions; it points to the earth's poles, attracts molten iron, and does many other wonderful things, some of which we have already mentioned, while many more remain to be pointed out. A weak loadstone will do the same, but less forcefully; and iron ore, as well as smelted iron (if they are prepared), show their virtues

He notes that high-quality steel can be produced directly from loadstone, further proving their shared nature.</summary>

Sometimes ironstone or iron ore exerts an attractive action the moment it comes from the mine, without being prepared in any way; native iron, also, or ore of iron color, attracts iron and makes it point to the poles. Thus the form, appearance, and essence are one. For to me there seems to be a greater difference and unlikeness between a very strong loadstone and a weak one that is hardly able to attract a single particle of iron filings; between a hard, firm, and metallic loadstone and one that is soft, crumbly, and clay-like, with so great a difference between them in color, substance, qualities, and weight; than between the best ore, rich in iron, or iron that from the start is metallic, on the one hand, and the best loadstone on the other. Indeed, the two are usually not to be distinguished by any signs, nor can miners tell one from the other, for they agree in all respects. Further, we see both the finest magnet and iron ore affected, as it were, by the same ills and diseases, aging in the same way and with the same indications, and preserved by the same remedies and protective measures, thereby retaining their properties. So, too, the one adds to the other’s power and intensifies and increases it when the two are artificially connected. For they are both impaired by the action of acidic liquids as though by poisons; the *aqua fortis* <note>nitric acid</note> of the chemists does equal injury to both; exposed for a long time to the action of the atmosphere, they both, in equal degree, age, as it were, and decline; each is saved from impairment by being kept in the *debris* and scrapings of the other, and when a suitable piece of steel or iron is applied to its pole, the magnetic power is intensified by the steadfast union. For just as in their native sites and mines, similar bodies surrounded by other bodies of the same kind—for example, the smaller internal parts of some great mass—endure for ages whole and undecayed; so loadstone and iron ore, when buried in a similar material, do not lose their native moisture and do not become weak, but retain their original properties. A loadstone packed in iron filings, as well as iron ore in scrapings of loadstone, and manufactured iron in the same or in iron filings, lasts longer. Thus, these two related bodies possess the true, precise form of a single species, though, because of their different outward appearance and the inequality of the very same innate power, they have until now been held by everyone to be different, and by pretenders to knowledge to be specifically different; for these pretenders have not understood that exactly the same powers reside in both substances, differing only in strength. They are, in fact, true and essential parts of the globe, retaining nature's primary powers of mutual attraction, of mobility, and of aligning themselves according to the position of the globe itself. They impart these powers to each other, enhancing, confirming, receiving, and holding each other's powers. One is activated by the other without any loss of power. For if one were to drive a number of iron nails weighing a total of 1,000 pounds into a wall, and were to apply to them an equal number of other nails properly magnetized by contact with a loadstone, the nails would clearly hang suspended in the air through the power of that single stone. Hence, this is not the action, work, or expenditure of the loadstone alone; for iron—which is something extracted from loadstone, a transformation of loadstone into metal—gains force from the loadstone. Whatever ore it may have been derived from, by its proximity it strengthens the loadstone's magnetic power; at the same time, it enhances its own native force by the proximity of the loadstone and by contact with it, even though solid bodies may stand between them. Iron touched by a loadstone activates other iron by contact and gives it magnetic direction; and that piece does the same for a third piece of iron. But if you rub any other metal, wood, bone, or glass with a loadstone, they will not move toward a fixed and specific quarter of the heavens, nor will they be attracted by a magnetized body; likewise, they cannot impart any magnetic property to other bodies or to iron itself through rubbing or transmission. Loadstone differs from iron ore, as well as from some weak loadstones, in that when reduced in the furnace to a ferric and metallic molten mass, it does not always easily become fluid and change into metal, but is sometimes burnt to ash in large furnaces. Hence, they are farther removed from the common mother and are degenerate; in the furnace, they are more easily melted and produce a softer sort of iron and no good steel. Most loadstones, if they are not excessively burnt, yield the best iron in the furnace. But in all these primary qualities, iron ore agrees with loadstone; for both, being more akin to the earth and more closely associated with it than any other bodies around us, possess within themselves the magnetic, genuine, homogeneous, and true substance of the terrestrial globe. They are less tainted and impaired by foreign impurities, and less mixed with the efflorescences on the earth's surface and the *débris* of generations of organisms. On this ground, Aristotle seems, in the fourth book of his *Meteora*, to distinguish iron from all other metals. Gold, he says, along with silver, copper, tin, and lead, belong to water; but iron is earthy. Galen, in the fourth book of *De Facultatibus Simplicium Medicamentorum*, says that iron is an earthy and dense body. So, according to our reasoning, loadstone is primarily earthy; next after it comes iron ore or weak loadstone. Thus, loadstone is by origin and nature <term>ferruginous</term>, and iron is magnetic, and the two are one in species. Iron ore in the furnace yields iron; loadstone in the furnace also yields iron, but of far finer quality, which is called steel. The better sort of iron ore is weak loadstone, just as the best loadstone is the most excellent iron ore, in which we will show that grand and noble primary properties reside. It is only in weaker loadstone, or iron ore, that these properties are obscure, faint, or scarcely perceptible to the senses.

## CHAPTER XVII.

### THAT THE TERRESTRIAL GLOBE IS MAGNETIC AND IS A LOADSTONE; AND JUST AS IN OUR HANDS THE LOADSTONE POSSESSES ALL THE PRIMARY POWERS (FORCES) OF THE EARTH, SO THE EARTH BY REASON OF THE SAME POTENCIES LIES EVER IN THE SAME DIRECTION IN THE UNIVERSE.

BEFORE we explain the causes of magnetic movements and bring forward our demonstrations and experiments regarding matters that for so many ages have remained hidden—the real foundations of terrestrial philosophy—we must formulate our new and, until now, unheard-of view of the earth, and submit it to the judgment of scholars. When it has been supported by a few arguments of *prima facie* cogency, and these have been confirmed by subsequent experiments and demonstrations, it will stand as firm as anything that was ever proposed in philosophy, backed by ingenious argumentation or supported by mathematical demonstrations. The terrestrial mass which, together with the world of waters, produces the spherical figure and our globe—insofar as it consists of firm, durable matter—is not easily altered. It does not wander or fluctuate with indeterminate movements like the seas and the flowing streams; but in certain hollows, within certain bounds, and in many veins and arteries, as it were, it holds the entire volume of liquid matter, nor does it allow it to spread abroad and be dissipated. ## CHAPTER I.
### OF MAGNETIC MOVEMENTS.

We have briefly discussed the opinions concerning the <term>loadstone</term> and its varieties; its poles and its recognized powers (*facultatibus*); iron and its properties; and the magnetic substance common to the <term>loadstone</term>, iron, and the earth itself in the preceding book. There now remain the magnetic movements and their broader philosophy, as developed through experiments and demonstrations. These movements are the impulses of <term>homogeneous</term> parts toward one another or toward the primary structure of the whole earth. Aristotle admits only two simple movements for his elements—away from the center and toward the center; light objects moving upward, and heavy objects moving downward. Thus, in the earth, there is but one motion of all its parts toward the center of the world—a wild, headlong falling. We, however, will consider elsewhere what this "lightness" might be, and will show how erroneously it is inferred by the Peri-

The second, of 77 degrees to the pole, is no movement, but a direction or a variation toward the earth’s pole. The third and the fourth are magnetic and are but one movement. ## CHAPTER II.

### ON MAGNETIC COITION; AND, FIRST, ON THE ATTRACTION EXERTED BY AMBER, OR MORE PROPERLY THE ATTACHMENT OF BODIES TO AMBER.

GREAT has always been the fame of the loadstone and of amber in the writings of the learned: many philosophers cite the loadstone and also amber whenever, in explaining mysteries, their minds become clouded and reason can go no further.<note>1. Dr. William Whewell remarks that the manner in which Gilbert expresses himself shows us how mysterious the fact of attraction appeared then, so that, as he says, “the magnet and amber were called upon for help by philosophers as illustrations, when our senses are in the dark in complex inquiries; and when our reason can go no further” (*History of Inductive Sciences*, 1859, Vol. II, page 192).</note> Over-inquisitive theologians, too, seek to illuminate God’s mysteries and things beyond man’s understanding by means of the loadstone and amber: just as light-headed metaphysicians, when they utter and teach their vain imaginings, employ the loadstone as a sort of Delphic sword and as an illustration of all sorts of things. Medical men also (at the bidding of Galen), in proving that purgative medicines exercise attraction through likeness of substance and kinship of juices (a silly and baseless error!), bring in the loadstone as a witness—a substance

But it seems to be produced in the earth and at a considerable depth below its surface, like the rest of the bitumens; then to be washed out by the sea-waves, and to gain consistency under the action of the sea and the saltness of its waters. For at first it was a soft and viscous matter, and hence contains, buried in its mass forevermore (*æternis sepulchris relucentes*—shining in eternal tombs), but still visible, flies, grubs, midges, and ants. The ancients as well as moderns tell (and their report is confirmed by experience) that amber attracts straws and chaff. The same is done by jet, a stone taken out of the earth in Britain, Germany, and many other regions: it is a hard mass of black bitumen—a kind of transformation of bitumen into stone.

Many modern authors have written about amber and jet attracting chaff and about other facts unknown to the general public, or have copied from other writers; the results of their labors cram the booksellers’ shops. Our generation has produced many volumes about hidden, obscure, and occult causes and wonders, and in all of them amber and jet are represented as attracting chaff; but you will find in them no proof from experiments, nor any demonstration.¹ The writers deal only in words that shroud the subject matter in thicker darkness; they treat the subject esoterically, like miracle-mongers, obscurely, hiddenly, and mystically. Consequently, such philosophy bears no fruit; for it rests simply on a few Greek or unusual terms—just as our barbers toss off a few Latin words within earshot of the ignorant crowd as a sign of their learning and thus gain a reputation—it bears no fruit because few of the philosophers themselves are investigators or have any first-hand acquaintance with things; most of them are lazy and untrained, add nothing to knowledge through their writings, and are blind to the things that might shed light on their reasoning. For not only do amber and (<term>gagates</term> or) jet,² as they suppose, attract light particles (substances): the same is done by diamond, sapphire, carbuncle, <term>iris stone</term>,* opal, amethyst, <term>vincentina</term>, English gem (Bristol stone, <term>bristola</term>), beryl, and rock crystal.³ Like powers of attracting are

Galen recognizes in total three kinds of attraction in nature: first, the attraction exercised by those bodies which attract by an elemental quality—namely, heat; secondly, by those which attract by the rush into a vacuum; thirdly, by those which attract through a property pertaining to their entire mass: and these three kinds are enumerated by Avicenna and others. This division cannot satisfy us at all, nor does it define the causes (*causas*) of the forces possessed by amber, jet, diamond, and other similar substances, which owe their power to the same virtue; nor of the loadstone or of other magnetic bodies, which possess a force altogether different from that of those other bodies, both in its effectiveness and in the sources from which it is derived. Fracastorio thinks that all bodies that mutually attract are alike, or of the same species, and that this similarity exists either in their action or in their proper *subjectum* <note>The underlying matter or substance.</note>: "now the proper *subjectum*," says he, "is that from which is emitted that emanational something which attracts, and, in mixed substances, this is not perceptible on account of deformation, whereby they are one thing *actu* (in actuality), another *potentiâ* (in potentiality). So much for Fracastorio. But had he noted through experiment that all bodies are attracted by electrics save those which are afire or flaming, or extremely rarefied, he never would have entertained such views. Men of acute intelligence, without actual knowledge of facts, and in the absence of experiment, easily slip and err. In greater error are they who hold amber, diamond, etc., and the objects attracted by them, to be like one another, but not the same, near to one another in kind, and that therefore like moves toward like, and is by it perfected. But that is reckless speculation; for all bodies are drawn to all electrics, save bodies aflame or too rarefied, as the air which is the universal effluvium of the globe. Plants draw moisture, and thus our crops thrive and grow; but from this analogy Hippocrates in his book *De Natura Hominis*, I., illogically infers that morbid humor <note>Diseased or unbalanced bodily fluids in ancient medicine.</note> is purged by the specific virtue of a drug. <meta>This page continues Gilbert’s discussion of attraction, transitioning from a critique of earlier theories to an empirical distinction between electric attraction, magnetic coition, and other physical phenomena like absorption and evaporation.</meta>

When a bottle of water is covered by a heap of wheat, its liquid is drawn out; for in fact, the liquid is reduced to vapor by the spirit of the fermenting wheat, and the wheat absorbs that vapor. Nor do elephants' tusks suck up moisture; instead, they transform it into vapor and absorb it. Thus, many bodies are said to attract, whereas the basis of their action should be sought elsewhere. A large polished lump of amber attracts;* a smaller piece, or a piece of impure amber, does not seem to attract without friction. However, many electric bodies (such as precious stones, etc.) do not attract at all unless they are first rubbed; while various other bodies, including some gems, have no power of attraction and cannot be made to attract even by friction. Such bodies [anelectrics—non-electrics] are emerald, agate, carnelian,¹ pearls, jasper, chalcedony, alabaster, porphyry, coral, various marbles, lapis lydius (touchstone, basanite), flint, bloodstone, emery or corundum (*mugris*), bone, ivory; the hardest woods, such as ebony; other woods, such as cedar, juniper, and cypress; and metals, such as silver, gold, copper, and iron. The loadstone, though it is susceptible of a very high polish, does not have electric attraction. On the other hand, many bodies (already mentioned) that can be polished do attract when rubbed. All this we shall understand when we have more closely studied the primary origin of bodies. As is plain to all, the Earth's mass—or rather the Earth's framework and its crust—consists of a twofold matter: namely, a matter that is fluid and humid, and a matter that is firm and dry. From this twofold matter, or from the simple solidification of one of these matters, come all the bodies around us; these consist in major proportion sometimes of earthy matter, and sometimes of watery matter. If they possess sufficient firmness, and are rubbed after being polished until they shine, such substances attract all bodies presented to them in the air, unless those bodies are too heavy. For amber and jet are solidifications of water; so too are all shining gems, such as rock crystal, which is a product of clear water—not always of such water at an extremely low temperature, as some have thought, but sometimes at a more moderate degree of cold, with the nature of the ground shaping them, and the fluids or juices being trapped in specific cavities, just as fluorites are generated in mines. Similarly, clear glass is produced from sand and other substances that have their origin in moist juices. But those <margin>*</margin>substances that contain a quantity of metallic impurities, or metals themselves, stones, rocks, wood, or earth, or are largely mixed with earth, do not attract. Rock crystal, mica, glass, and other electric bodies do not attract if they are burned or highly heated, for their original fluid is destroyed by the heat, altered, and expelled as vapor. Hence, all bodies that derive their origin principally from fluids, are firmly solidified, and retain the appearance and properties of a fluid in a firm, solid mass, attract all substances, whether moist or dry. Those that are parts of the true substance of the earth, or differ but little from it, appear to attract also, but in a very different way—magnetically, so to speak; we shall discuss these later. ...form a solid mass <note>original: "concretion"</note> by itself, but mingles with earthy matter—such bodies are powerless to attract anything to themselves unless they are in actual contact with it, nor can they repel it. <margin>*</margin> For this reason, neither metals, marbles, flints, woods, grasses, flesh, nor various other substances can attract or move a body, whether magnetically or electrically. (We choose to call "electric force" that force which originates in fluids <note>original: "humors"</note>). However, bodies consisting mostly of fluid and not firmly compacted by nature—which therefore cannot withstand friction but either crumble, soften, or become sticky—do not attract particles <note>original: "corpuscles"</note>. Such substances include pitch, soft resin, camphor, galbanum <note>a bitter aromatic gum resin</note>, ammoniacum <note>a medicinal gum resin</note>, storax <note>a fragrant resin</note>, asafoetida <note>original: "asa"</note>, benzoin <note>original: "gum benjamin"</note>, and asphalt (especially in a warm atmosphere). For without friction, few bodies give off their true natural electric *emanation* and discharge <note>original: "effluvium"</note>. Turpentine resin in its liquid state does not attract because it cannot be rubbed; but when it hardens into a gum <note>original: "mastic"</note>, it does attract.

And now, at last, we must see why particles are drawn toward substances that originate from water, and by what kind of force—by what "hands," so to speak—these substances grasp the objects near them.

<margin>*</margin>
In every body, two causes or principles are present by which the bodies are produced: namely, matter <note>original: "*materia*"</note> and form <note>original: "*forma*"</note>. Electrical movements come from the *matter*, but magnetic movements come from the primary *form*. These two differ widely from each other and are quite distinct. One is ennobled by many powers and is dominant; the other is lowly, less powerful, and confined as if in prison. Therefore, its force must be awakened by friction until the substance reaches a moderate heat, gives off a discharge <note>original: "effluvium"</note>, and its surface begins to shine. Moist air blown upon it from the mouth, or a current of humid air from the atmosphere...

A loadstone <margin>*</margin> attracts only magnetic bodies; electrics attract everything. A loadstone lifts great weights; a strong one weighing two ounces lifts half an ounce or one ounce. Electrics attract only light weights; for example, a piece of amber weighing three ounces lifts only one-fourth of a barleycorn's weight.

But this attraction of amber and of electric bodies must be investigated further; and since it is an acquired state (*affectio*), the question arises why amber is rubbed, and what state is brought about by rubbing; also, what causes are evoked that seize all sorts of substances. Through friction, it is made moderately hot and also smooth; and these conditions must in most cases occur together. Besides, the exhalation produced in the amber by a foreign heat is feeble, for the amber must not have any heat except that produced by friction: its own heat, so to speak—not heat contributed by other bodies.

And now, what is it that produces the movement? Is it the body itself, bounded by its own outline? Or is it something imperceptible to us, flowing out of the substance into the surrounding air? (This seems to have been, in a sense, the opinion of Plutarch, who, in the *Platonic Questions*, says that there is something flame-like or of the nature of breath in amber, and that this—when the paths are cleared by friction of the surface—is emitted and attracts bodies.) And if it is an effluvium, does that effluvium set the air in motion, and is that current then followed by the bodies? Or are the bodies themselves directly drawn up? But if the amber attracts the body itself, then assuming its surface is clean and free from any stuck particles, why is friction needed? Nor does the force come from the luster produced by the rubbed and polished electric; for the <term>vincentina</term> <note>A type of transparent quartz or "St. Vincent's rock."</note>, the diamond, and pure glass attract even when they are rough, though not as strongly.

According to Pythagoras, the principle through participation in which a thing is said to be one. Since no action can be performed by matter except by contact, these electric bodies do not appear to touch; yet, of necessity, something is given out from the one to the other to come into close contact with it and be a cause of incitement to it.

All bodies are united and, as it were, cemented together by moisture; hence, a wet body attracts another body upon touching it if the other body is small, and wet bodies on the surface of water attract other wet bodies. But the unique <term>effluvia</term> of electrics, being the most subtle matter of dissolved moisture, attract <term>corpuscles</term>.<note>1</note> Air, too (the earth’s universal <term>effluvium</term>), unites parts that are separated, and the earth, by means of the air, brings back bodies to itself; otherwise, bodies would not so eagerly seek the earth from great heights. The electric <term>effluvia</term> differ much from air, and just as air is the earth’s <term>effluvium</term>, so electric bodies have their own distinctive <term>effluvia</term>. Each unique <term>effluvium</term> has its own individual power of leading to union, its own movement toward its origin, toward its source, and toward the body that emits the <term>effluvium</term>. However, bodies that give out a thick, vaporous, or airy <term>effluvium</term> when rubbed have no effect; for either such <term>effluvia</term> are different from <term>humor</term> (the unifier of all things), or, being very similar to common air, they become blended with the air and one with it. Therefore, they have no effect in the air and do not produce any movements different from those of that universal and common element.

material rods—hold and take up straws, chaff, and twigs, until their force is spent or vanishes; and then these small bodies, being set free again, are attracted by the earth itself and fall to the ground. The difference (distinction) between electric and magnetic bodies is this: all magnetic bodies come together by their joint forces (mutual strength); electric bodies attract the electric only, and the body attracted undergoes no modification through its own native force, but is drawn freely under impulsion in proportion to its matter (composition). Bodies are * attracted to electrics in a straight line toward the center of electricity: a loadstone approaches another loadstone on a line perpendicular to the circumference only at the poles, elsewhere obliquely and transversely, and it adheres at those same angles. The electric motion is the motion of the massing (coacervation) of matter; the magnetic is that of arrangement and order. The matter of the earth's globe is brought together and held together by itself electrically. The earth's globe is directed and revolves magnetically; it both coheres and, so that it may be solid, is firmly joined in its interior.<sup>5</sup>

Therefore, if we have at any time spoken of magnetic attraction, what we meant was magnetic <term>coition</term> and primary confluence.¹ But here it will not be useless to first set forth briefly the views of others, both among the ancients and the moderns. Orpheus, in his hymns, tells that iron is drawn by the loadstone like a bride to the embraces of her spouse. Epicurus holds that iron is drawn by the loadstone as straws are by amber; and adds a reason: “Atoms,” he says, “and indivisible bodies that flow from stone and from iron, match one another in their shapes, so that they readily embrace each other; hence, when they strike the solid masses of both iron and stone, they rebound into the middle space, joined together along the way, and carry the iron with them.” This, surely, cannot be; for even though solid and very dense bodies, or blocks of marble, stand between them, they do not hinder the passage of this power, even though they can separate atoms from atoms; besides, according to this hypothesis, the stone and iron would quickly be broken down into atoms, so profuse and constant would be the atomic outflow. And as the mode of attraction is quite different in amber, the Epicurean atoms there cannot match in their shapes. Thales, as we are told by Aristotle in Book I of *De Anima*, believed the loadstone was endowed with a sort of life, because it possesses the power of moving and attracting iron. Anaxagoras was of the same opinion. The opinion of Plato in the *Timaeus*, regarding the effect of the Herculean stone, is baseless. He says: “With respect to all the motions of water, the falling of thunder, and

A similar explanation is offered by Plutarch in the *Platonic Questions*. He says that the loadstone emits heavy exhalations, by which the neighboring air, being pushed, makes the air in front of it dense, and that air, driven around in a circle and returning to the part from which the air was displaced, forcibly carries the iron with it. The following theory of the powers of the loadstone and amber is proposed by Joannes Costæus of Lodi: Costæus holds that “there is work on both sides, a result on both sides, and therefore the motion is produced in part by the loadstone’s attraction, and in part by the iron’s spontaneous movement; for, just as we say that the vapors given out by the loadstone naturally hurry to attract the iron, so, too, do we say that the air pushed by the vapors, while seeking a place for itself, is turned back, and when turned back pushes and transfers the iron, which is picked up, as it were, by it, and which, besides, moves on its own account. In this way, a certain composite movement is found, resulting from attraction, spontaneous motion, and impulsion; this composite motion, however, is rightly to be referred to as attraction, because the beginning of this motion is invariably from one point, and its end is there too; and that is precisely the distinguishing character of attraction.” There is, it is true, mutual action, but not mutual work; the loadstone does not attract in this way, and there is no impulsion; neither is the principle of the motion found in vapors

# CHAPTER IV.

## OF THE STRENGTH OF A LOADSTONE AND ITS FORM: THE CAUSE OF COITION.

<margin>¹ Whewell, “History of the Inductive Sciences,” 1859, Vol. II, Chap. II, page 220.</margin>

Leaving behind the opinions of others regarding the attraction of the <term>loadstone</term>, we will now show the reason for its <term>coition</term> and the nature of its motion. There are two kinds of bodies that are seen to attract other bodies by motions perceptible to our senses—electric bodies and magnetic bodies. Electrical bodies do this by means of natural <term>effluvia</term> from moisture; magnetic bodies by formal powers, or rather by primary native strength (*vigor*). This form is unique and peculiar: it is not what the Peripatetics call *causa formalis* and *causa specifica in mixtis* and *secunda forma*; nor is it *causa propagatrix generantium corporum*; but it is the form of the primary and chief globes; and it belongs to the homogeneous and unaltered parts of those globes, being their proper entity and existence, which we may call the primary, radical, and <term>astral form</term>;¹ not Aristotle’s prime form, but that unique form which preserves and organizes its own globe. Such a form exists in each globe—the sun, the moon, the stars—as one; in the earth also it is one, and it is that true <term>magnetic potency</term> which we call the primary energy. Hence, the magnetic nature is specific to the earth and is implanted in all its real parts according to a primary and remarkable proportion. It is not derived from the heavens as a whole, nor is it generated by them through sympathy, or influence, or other <term>occult qualities</term>; neither is it derived from any special star; for there is in the earth a magnetic strength or energy (*vigor*) of its own,

A body that is attracted by a magnetic body is not altered by it, but remains unimpaired and unchanged as it was before, nor does it now possess greater power. A loadstone draws magnetic bodies, and from its energy they eagerly draw forces not only in their extremities, but in their innermost parts. For an iron rod held in the hand is magnetized at the end where it is grasped, and the magnetic force travels to the other extremity, not along the surface only, but through the inside, through the middle. Electrical bodies have material, physical <term>effluvia</term>. Is any magnetic effluvium emitted, whether physical or non-physical? Or is nothing that exists emitted at all? Is it like what is exhaled from lead when quicksilver—which is liquid and fluid—is solidified by the mere odor and vapor of lead, and remains a strongly coherent metal? Gold, too, which is very solid and dense, is reduced to a powder by the thin vapor of lead. -> ## WILLIAM GILBERT. <-

Even the loadstone itself loses its native and inborn powers of attraction, and all other magnetic properties, if left for a long time in fire. And although some magnetic ores, when roasted, exhale a deep-blue or sulfurous and foul-smelling vapor, nevertheless such a vapor is not the soul of the loadstone; nor is it the cause of the attraction of iron, as Porta supposes.<note>Porta’s “Natural Magick,” 1658, Book VII, Chapter II.</note> Nor do all loadstones smell of sulfur or give off sulfur fumes when roasted or burned: that property is something added, a sort of congenital defect that comes from the foul bed or matrix in which the loadstone is produced. Nor does the material physical cause introduce anything of that same sort into the iron; for iron derives from the loadstone the power of attracting and the property of <term>verticity</term>, even if glass or gold or another sort of stone stands in between, as we shall clearly prove later when treating of magnetic direction.

But fire destroys the magnetic qualities in the loadstone, not because it plucks any particular attracting particles out of it, but because the quick, penetrating force of the flame deforms it by breaking up its matter; just as in the human body, the soul’s primary powers are not burned, yet the burned body remains without its faculties. But although the iron remains after complete ignition, and is not converted into either ash or slag, still—as Cardan quite wisely remarks—red-hot iron is not iron, but something existing outside its own nature until it returns to itself. For just as water is changed from its own nature into ice by the cold of the surrounding air, so iron made white-hot by fire has a confused, disordered form. Therefore, it is not attracted by a loadstone and even loses its power of attracting, however it was acquired; it also acquires a different <term>verticity</term> when, as though born anew, it is impregnated by a loadstone

Thales attributed a soul to the loadstone, because it is stimulated, directed, and moved in a circle by a force that is present in its entirety within the whole and in every part (as will be shown later), and because it seems to resemble a soul very closely. ## CHAPTER V.

### IN WHAT MANNER THE ENERGY INHERES IN THE LOADSTONE.

That the loadstone draws loadstone, iron, and other magnetic bodies was shown in Book I, as were the forces by which magnetic <term>coition</term> <note>Gilbert uses "coition" to describe the mutual attraction and coming together of magnetic bodies, rather than a simple one-way pull.</note> is regulated; we must now inquire how this energy is ordered within magnetic bodies. Here we must apply the analogy of a large loadstone. A magnetic body unites forcibly with a loadstone if the loadstone is powerful—feebly if it is defective or if it has become impaired by some fault. A loadstone does not attract iron with equal force at every point; in other words, a magnetic body does not move with the same force toward every point of the loadstone. This is because the loadstone has points (that is, true poles) at which its exceptional energy is most conspicuous. The regions nearest the poles are stronger, and those farthest away are weaker; yet, in all of them, the energy is in some sense equal. In the figure of a <term>terrella</term> <note>A "little earth"; a spherical loadstone used by Gilbert to model the Earth's magnetic properties.</note>, *A* and *B* are the poles, and *CD* is the equinoctial line; the greatest attractive force is seen at *A* and *B*. ### DIAGRAM OF THE MAGNETIC ENERGY DIFFUSED FROM THE PLANE OF THE EQUATOR TO THE PERIPHERY OF A TERRELLA OR OF THE EARTH.

Let *HEQ* be a <term>terrella</term>, *E* a pole, *M* the center, and *HMQ* the plane of the <term>equinoctial circle</term> <note>The magnetic equator.</note>. From every point of the equinoctial plane, the energy reaches out to the periphery, but differently from each point: for from *A*, the <term>formal energy</term> <note>The organizing or essential magnetic force.</note> goes toward *CFNE* and to every point between *C* and *E* (the pole), and not toward *B*; nor does it go from *G* toward *C*. The attractive force in the region *FGH* is not strengthened by the force residing in the region *GMFE*; instead, *FGH* increases the energy in the rising curve *FE*. Thus, energy never proceeds from the lines parallel to the axis to points above those parallels, but always internally from the parallels to the pole. From every point of the plane of the equator, the energy goes to the pole *E*; the point *F* derives its forces only from *GH*, and the point *N* from *OH*; but the pole *E* is strengthened by the whole plane *HO*. Therefore, this mighty power has its chief excellence here; here is its throne, so to speak. But in the intervals—at *F*, for example—there resides only as much attractional energy as can be provided by the section *HG* of the plane.

MAGNETIZED IRON AND SMALLER LOADSTONES.

## CHAPTER VI.

### HOW MAGNETIZED IRON AND SMALLER LOADSTONES CONFORM TO THE TERRELLA AND TO THE EARTH ITSELF, AND ARE GOVERNED BY THEM.

The <term>coition</term> <note>The mutual attraction or coming together of magnetic bodies.</note> of bodies that are separate from one another, and that cohere naturally, takes place by another sort of movement if they are free to move. The <term>terrella</term> <note>A "little earth"; a spherical loadstone used for experiments.</note> sends its force out in all directions, according to its energy and its quality. But whenever iron or another <term>magnetic body</term> of suitable size occurs within its sphere of influence, it is attracted; yet the nearer it is to the <term>loadstone</term>, the greater the force with which it is carried toward it. Such bodies tend toward the loadstone *not as if toward a center nor toward its center*: they do that only at its poles—that is, when the attracted object and the pole of the loadstone, as well as its center, are in a straight line. But in the intervals between the poles, they tend toward it in an oblique line, as seen in the figure below, which shows how the force extends to the associated magnetic bodies within the sphere. At the poles, the line is straight. The nearer the parts are to the <term>equinoctial circle</term> <note>The magnetic equator.</note>, the more obliquely magnetic bodies are attracted, but the parts nearer the poles attract more directly; at the poles themselves, attraction is in a straight line. All loadstones alike, whether spherical or oblong, have the same way of turning to the poles of the world; but it is easiest to experiment with oblong ones. For whatever the shape, <term>verticity</term> <note>The property of having magnetic poles and aligning with the Earth's magnetic field.</note> is present, and there are poles; but owing to imperfect and irregular shapes, loadstones are often subject to limitations.

<summary>Gilbert explains that magnetic bodies align with a terrella or the Earth in straight lines at the poles and oblique lines elsewhere. He notes that while all loadstones possess polarity (verticity), their physical shape can influence their magnetic behavior.</summary>

POTENCY OF THE MAGNETIC FORCE.

## CHAPTER VII.

### OF THE POTENCY OF THE MAGNETIC FORCE, AND OF ITS SPHERICAL EXTENSION.¹

THE magnetic force is emitted in all directions around the body; around the <term>terrella</term> it is emitted spherically; around <term>loadstones</term> of other shapes, it is emitted unevenly and less regularly. But the sphere of influence does not persist, nor is the force that is diffused through the air permanent or essential; the <term>loadstone</term> simply excites magnetic bodies situated at a convenient distance. And as light—so <term>opticians</term> tell us—arrives instantly, in the same way, and with far greater instantaneousness, the magnetic energy is present within the limits of its field of force; and because its action is far more subtle than light, and it does not interact with non-magnetic bodies, it has no relationship with air, water, or other non-magnetic bodies. Neither does it act on magnetic bodies by means of forces that rush upon them with any motion whatever, but by being present, it draws bodies that have a natural affinity for itself. And as light strikes whatever confronts it, so does the <term>loadstone</term> strike a magnetic body and excite it. And as light does not remain in the atmosphere above the vapors and <term>effluvia</term>, nor is it reflected back by those spaces, so the magnetic ray is caught neither in air nor in water. The forms of things are in an instant taken in by the eye or by lenses; so does the magnetic force seize magnetic bodies. In the absence of light

In a different sense we accept those bounds and circles, for we have discovered many such, both in the <term>terrella</term> and in the earth; but these are determined by nature itself, and are not merely imaginary lines. Geographers make a division of the earth chiefly by defining the <term>equator</term> and the <term>poles</term>; and these bounds are set and defined by nature. <term>Meridians</term>, too, indicate tracks from pole to pole, passing through fixed points in the equator; along such lines the <term>magnetic force</term> proceeds and gives direction. But the tropics and the arctic circles, as also the parallels of <term>latitude</term>, are not natural bounds described on the earth; yet all these parallel circles indicate that a certain conformity exists among regions of the earth situated in the same latitude or diametrically opposite to them. All these are of service to mathematicians in constructing globes and maps. Thus such circles are of use in the <term>terrella</term>, but they need not be drawn as geographers draw them—on the surface—for the <term>loadstone</term> may be perfectly even and uniform all over. Nor are there any “upper” or “lower” parts in the terrestrial globe, just as there are also none in the <term>terrella</term>, except perhaps that one may choose to call those parts “upper” which are at the periphery and those “lower” which are closer to the center.

## CHAPTER IX.

### OF THE EQUINOCTIAL CIRCLE OF THE EARTH AND THE TERRELLA.

**THE** equinoctial circle conceived by astronomers, which is equidistant from both poles and divides the earth in the middle, measures the movements of their *primum mobile* or tenth sphere,¹ and is called the zone of the *primum mobile*; it is called “equinoctial” because when the sun is in this circle—which must happen twice a year—the days are of equal length to the nights. This circle is also designated *æquidialis*; hence the Greeks give it the name ἰσημερινὸς (which means the same: “equal day”). It is also appropriately called the “equator,” for it divides the whole globe of the earth from pole to pole into two equal parts. To the <term>terrella</term> also is rightly assigned an equator by which its power is distributed between two parts. By the plane of this equator, as it passes through the center, the whole <term>terrella</term> is divided into two parts equal in mass and in verticity, and imbued with equal energy, as though a wall stood between the two verticities.

<header>PARALLELS.</header>

Magnetic meridians are infinite in number, and, just like the earth's geographical meridians, they pass through fixed and opposite points on the equator and through the poles. Magnetic latitude is also measured along them. Through them, we understand declinations; and along them, there is a fixed direction toward the poles, unless the magnetic body varies for some reason and is pushed off its proper course. The meridian commonly called "magnetic" is not truly magnetic, nor is it a meridian, but is instead supposed to pass through the limits of variation on the horizon. Variation is, in fact, a faulty deviation from the meridian; in various places, it is not fixed or constant on any meridian.¹

## CHAPTER XI.

### PARALLELS.

**In** parallel circles, the same energy and equal potency are observed throughout when different magnetic bodies are placed on the same parallel, whether of the earth or of the <term>terrella</term>. This is because the bodies are at equal distances from the poles, have equal changes of declination, and are attracted, held, and brought together by the action of similar forces; just as regions of the earth on the same parallel—though they may differ in longitude—are said to have the same amount of daylight and the same climate.

WILLIAM GILBERT.

# CHAPTER XII.

## THE MAGNETIC HORIZON.

A horizon is a great circle separating the things seen from those that are out of sight, just as one half of the heavens is always plainly visible while the other half is always hidden. So it seems to us because of the great distance of the starry sphere; yet the difference is in the ratio of the earth's semi-diameter to the semi-diameter of the starry heavens—a difference not perceived by the senses. But we take the magnetic horizon to be a plane perfectly level throughout, tangent to the earth or to the <term>terrella</term> at the place of the region; with this plane, the semi-diameter (whether of the earth or of the <term>terrella</term>), when extended, makes right angles on all sides. Such a plane is to be imagined for the earth, and for the <term>terrella</term> likewise, for the sake of magnetic proofs and demonstrations. For we are considering the bodies themselves, and not the general aspects of the world. Therefore, not with reference to sight—for that varies according to the elevation of regions—we assume a sensible horizon in magnetic demonstrations, not what is called by astronomers the rational horizon.

---

## CHAPTER XVII.

### OF THE IRON HELMET (CAP) OF THE <term>LOADSTONE</term>, WITH WHICH IT IS ARMED AT THE POLE TO INCREASE ITS ENERGY; AND THE EFFICIENCY OF THE SAME.¹

A concave hemisphere of thin iron, a finger's width in diameter, is applied to the convex polar surface of a <term>loadstone</term> and properly fastened; or an iron acorn-shaped ball rising from the base into an obtuse cone, hollowed out a little and fitted to the surface of the stone, is made fast to the <term>pole</term>. 

The iron must be of the best quality (steel), smooth, polished, and even. Fitted with this contrivance, a <term>loadstone</term> that before lifted only 4 ounces of iron will now lift 12 ounces. 

But the greatest force of the cooperating or rather unified matter is seen when two <term>loadstones</term> fitted with these projections are so joined* as to mutually attract and lift each other: in this way, a weight of 20 ounces may be lifted, though either stone unarmed would lift only 4 ounces. 

Iron is held more firmly by an armed <term>loadstone</term> than by one that is not armed, and hence it lifts greater weights because iron clings more strongly to the armed stone. For, by the contiguous presence of the <term>loadstone</term>, the iron of the <term>armature</term> and the iron being attracted are bound fast together; and when the <term>armature</term> has absorbed the <term>magnetic energy</term> by reason of the presence of the <term>loadstone</term>, and another piece of iron adjoining it at the same time derives force from the presence of a <term>loadstone</term>, the two unite energetically. # CHAPTER XVIII.

->AN ARMED LOADSTONE DOES NOT ENDOW MAGNETIZED IRON WITH GREATER FORCE THAN AN UNARMED ONE DOES.<-

TAKE two pieces of iron, one <term>magnetized</term> with an armed and the other with an unarmed <term>loadstone</term>, and apply to one of them a weight of iron proportioned to its strength: the other <term>loadstone</term> will lift the same weight, and no more. Two needles also turn with the same velocity and constancy toward the <term>poles</term> of the earth, even though one needle may have been touched by an armed magnet and the other by one unarmed.

## CHAPTER XIX.

## CHAPTER XX.

### THAT AN ARMED MAGNET LIFTS ANOTHER, AND THAT ONE A THIRD: THIS HOLDS GOOD THOUGH THERE BE LESS ENERGY IN THE FIRST.

ARMED <term>loadstones</term> duly joined together cohere firmly and form one; and though the first be weak, the second nevertheless clings to it, not alone with the force of the first, but of the second, the stones thus helping each other: to the second a third will often cling, and with strong <term>loadstones</term> a fourth to the third.

### CHAPTER XXI.

<margin>*</margin>
#### THAT WHEN PAPER OR ANOTHER MEDIUM IS INTERPOSED, AN ARMED LOADSTONE DOES NOT LIFT MORE THAN AN UNARMED ONE.

It has been shown above that an armed <term>loadstone</term> does not attract at a greater distance than an unarmed one, but that it lifts a greater quantity of iron if it is in contact with the iron and continuous with it. But put a leaf of paper between them, and this close connection is hindered; iron objects are then no longer held together by the action of the loadstone.

---

### CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>*</margin>
#### THAT AN ARMED LOADSTONE DOES NOT ATTRACT IRON MORE THAN AN UNARMED ONE; AND THAT THE ARMED STONE IS MORE STRONGLY UNITED TO THE IRON, IS SHOWN BY MEANS OF AN ARMED LOADSTONE AND A CYLINDER OF POLISHED IRON.

On a flat surface, place a cylinder too heavy for an unarmed <term>loadstone</term> to lift; then, with paper in between, apply the pole of an armed <term>loadstone</term> to the middle of the cylinder. If the cylinder is pulled by the loadstone, it follows it with a rolling motion; but when there is no paper in between, the cylinder, joined to the loadstone, is pulled by it and does not roll.

## CHAPTER XXIII.

### THE MAGNETIC FORCE MAKES MOTION TOWARD UNION, AND WHEN UNITED CONNECTS FIRMLY.

<margin>*</margin>
<margin>*</margin>

<margin>*</margin>
<term>Magnetized</term> objects cohere well and properly to one another according to their forces. Pieces of iron in the presence of a <term>loadstone</term>, even if not in contact with it, come together, eagerly seek and seize one another, and when joined are, as it were, glued together. Iron dust or iron reduced to a powder, packed in paper tubes and placed on the meridian of a <term>loadstone</term> or merely brought near it, coalesces into one mass; in an instant, the many particles come together and combine. This multitude of united grains acts on a piece of iron and attracts it as though they formed but one continuous rod of iron, and they take the north and south direction when laid on the <term>loadstone</term>. But if they are taken any distance away from the stone, the particles return to their original condition and separate, each standing alone. In this way, the foundations of the earth are joined, connected, and held together magnetically. So, let not Ptolemy of Alexandria, his followers, and our philosophers maintain that the earth will fall apart, nor should they be alarmed if the earth spins in a circle.

Fracastorio, in his Chapter VIII, *De Sympathia*, says that a piece of iron will be suspended in the air so that it cannot move either up or down if a <term>loadstone</term> be placed above it that has an attractive force on the iron equal to the force by which the iron pulls downward: thus the iron will stand fixed in mid-air. Baptista Porta suspends a piece of iron in the air (with a <term>loadstone</term> fixed above) and holds back the iron by means of a thin thread fastened to it from below, so that it shall not rise to the stone—hardly a very brilliant idea. The piece <margin>*</margin> of iron is pulled in a perpendicular line by the <term>loadstone</term>, though the two are not in contact but only near each other; but as, on account of the greater proximity, the iron mass is moved by the force that was lifting it, it immediately speeds to the <term>loadstone</term> and clings to it. For the nearer the iron comes to the <term>loadstone</term>, the more it is excited and the stronger the attraction is.

### CHAPTER XXV.

#### INTENSIFYING THE LOADSTONE'S FORCES.

ONE <term>loadstone</term> far surpasses another in energy, for one will snatch up almost its own weight of iron, while another is hardly able to move the smallest particle. All animals and plants that possess life have need of food of some sort, so that their powers may last and become firmer and stronger. But iron is not attracted by the <term>loadstone</term>, as Cardan and Alexander Aphrodiseus supposed, so that it may be nourished with pieces of it; neither does the <term>loadstone</term> gain strength from iron filings as from a nutritious food. Baptista Porta, doubting this view and wishing to perform an experiment, took a <term>loadstone</term> of a specific weight and buried it in iron filings of a known weight; and, after he had left it there many months, he found the stone heavier and the filings lighter. But the difference was so minute that Porta was uncertain of the truth. This experiment of Porta's does not prove that the stone devours anything, nor does it show any process of nutrition, for small quantities of filings are easily lost by handling. So, too, a very small amount of iron dust may adhere to some small part of the <term>loadstone</term> and go unnoticed, thus adding somewhat to the weight of the stone; but that is a superficial accretion and can be brushed off without much difficulty. Many think that when weak and sluggish, the stone can bring itself back to a better condition, and that a very strong stone can endow a weaker one with the highest degree of force. Surely nothing can do such a thing except what possesses magnetic properties. Magnetic bodies can restore health (when not totally lost) to other magnetic bodies, and can give some of them powers greater than they originally had; but it is not possible to give further strength to those that are by their nature already perfect in the highest degree. Hence, the charlatanry of <term>Paracelsus</term> becomes all the more infamous; he declares that the loadstone's force and energy may be increased and transformed to tenfold what it is naturally. But a loadstone dipped in this way not only acquires no force but suffers some loss of what it already has.

A loadstone rubbed and smoothed with steel is made better. When covered with filings of the best iron or pure steel, if not rusty, it retains its properties. Sometimes, too, a good strong loadstone gains some strength when rubbed on its opposite pole with the pole of another loadstone: it takes in force. ## CHAPTER XXVI.

### WHY THE ATTRACTION BETWEEN IRON AND LOADSTONE APPEARS GREATER THAN THAT BETWEEN TWO LOADSTONES, OR TWO PIECES OF IRON WHEN NEAR A LOADSTONE AND WITHIN ITS FIELD.

One loadstone does not attract another on all its sides as it does iron, but only at one fixed point: hence the poles of the two must be properly arranged, otherwise they do not join properly and powerfully. But this arrangement is not easy, nor is it the work of an instant; therefore, one loadstone will seem to be resistant toward another, even though they may be in perfect harmony. Iron, suddenly influenced by a loadstone, is not only attracted by it, but is transformed and its powers enhanced, by which it pursues and attracts the loadstone with a force no less than its own, and also captures other iron objects. Suppose a small iron bar is firmly attached to a loadstone: if you bring an iron rod near this piece of iron, without touching the loadstone, you shall see the iron bar instantly follow the rod, leaving the loadstone and leaning toward the rod. Upon contact, it will stick firmly to it; for iron, when joined and in contact, pulls another piece of iron within the magnetic field of a loadstone more vigorously than the loadstone itself does. The natural magnetic force, which in iron lies confined and dormant, is awakened by a loadstone, associates itself with it, and comes

<summary>William Gilbert explains that while loadstones require precise polar alignment to attract each other, iron is easily magnetized by a loadstone's field and can even exert a stronger pull on other iron than the loadstone itself.</summary>
<keywords>William Gilbert, loadstone, iron, magnetic field, magnetic force, poles, cohesion, attraction, magnetism</keywords>

--- Page 207 ---
<meta>This page continues the explanation of how iron interacts with a loadstone's magnetic field, detailing why iron-to-iron attraction within that field can be stronger than the attraction between loadstones.</meta>

into sympathy with it by virtue of its primary form:¹ hence comes the perfect magnetized iron, which is as strong as the loadstone itself; for as the one imparts and awakens, so the other receives, and, being awakened, persists, and by its very action returns the force again. But since iron is more like iron than a loadstone is, and when two pieces of iron are within the field of a loadstone, the proximity of the stone enhances the powers of both: then, their forces being equal, the similarity of substance becomes the deciding factor, and iron gives itself up to iron. The two pieces are united by their nearly identical and homogeneous forces. This is achieved not only by <term>coition</term>, but by a firmer union; and a steel cap or snout (*glans vel nasus*) properly fitted to the pole of a loadstone lifts greater weights than the stone can by itself. When steel or iron is made from loadstone or from iron ore, the slag and impurities are separated from the substance through a more effective smelting process: thus, such iron usually contains the matter of the earth cleansed of foreign mixtures and dross, and is more homogeneous and perfect (than before smelting), although its shape is altered by the melting. And this matter, when acted upon by a loadstone, receives the magnetic virtue, and within the magnetic field, it is endowed with a force surpassing that of a lower-quality loadstone, which is rarely without some mixture of impurities.

## CHAPTER XXVII.

### *THAT THE CENTER OF THE MAGNETIC FORCES IN THE EARTH IS THE CENTER OF THE EARTH; AND IN THE TERRELLA THE TERRELLA’S CENTER.*

The rays of magnetic force are dispersed in a circle in all directions; and the center of this sphere is not in the pole (as <term>Baptista Porta</term> believes, Chapter XXII), but in the center of the stone and of the <term>terrella</term>. So, too, the earth’s center is the center of the earth’s magnetic movements, though magnetic bodies are not carried directly toward the center in magnetic movement except when they are attracted by the pole. For as the formal power of loadstone and earth promotes simple unity and conformity between separate things, it follows that everywhere at an equal distance from the center or from the convex circum-

### CHAPTER XXVIII.

#### THAT A LOADSTONE DOES NOT ATTRACT TO A FIXED POINT OR POLE ONLY, BUT TO EVERY PART OF A <term>TERRELLA</term>, EXCEPT THE EQUINOCTIAL CIRCLE.

<term>COITION</term> is always strongest when pole touches pole, for at the poles the force is greatest by the combined action of the whole; hence, one pole seizes the other with the greatest force. Points at distances from the poles also possess attraction power, but it is somewhat weaker and more sluggish in proportion to the distance, so that finally, at the equinoctial line, they are utterly weak and faint. The poles, too, do not attract as mathematical points, nor does magnetized iron unite at its poles only with the poles of a <term>loadstone</term>. On the contrary, the <term>coition</term> takes place all over the periphery, north and south, with the force emanating from the whole mass. Magnetic bodies, however, are attracted feebly in the parts near the equator, but quickly in the parts near the poles. Therefore, it is not the poles alone, nor the parts near the poles alone, that attract and draw magnetic bodies; instead, magnetic bodies are controlled, rotated, and united with other magnetic bodies according to how the neighboring and adjoining parts contribute their forces. These forces are always of the same potency along the same parallel, except when they are otherwise distributed by causes producing variation.

## CHAPTER XXIX.

### ON THE DIFFERENCE OF FORCES DEPENDENT ON QUANTITY OR MASS.

Loadstones coming from the same mine, and not mixed with neighboring metals or ores, have the same potency; yet the stone that is largest exhibits the greatest force, as it carries the greatest weight and has a wider sphere of influence. A loadstone weighing an ounce does not lift an iron spike as one that weighs a pound does, nor does its control reach as far, nor does its force extend to such a distance. And if you take a part away from a one-pound stone, some of its power will be seen to leave as well; for when a part is taken <margin>*</margin> away, some of the energy is lost. But when such a part is properly applied and united to the stone—even if it is not cemented there or perfectly fitted by mere placement—the original strength is recovered, and the force returns. Sometimes, <margin>*</margin> however, the energy is increased by the removal of a part because of the malformation of the stone, such as when the force is spread out through awkward corners.

In stones of different sorts, the ratio of power is different: one weighing a <term>drachm</term> may have more force than another weighing 20 pounds. Many a loadstone is so weak that the force can scarcely be noticed, and such faint magnets are often surpassed by masses prepared from potter's earth. But we may ask: Supposing that a stone of a given kind and of definite quality, weighing a <term>drachm</term>, carries one <term>drachm</term>, will one weighing an ounce carry an ounce, a pound carry a pound, and <margin>*</margin> so on? It is so, for in proportion to its size, such a loadstone has greater or less strength: so that a loadstone of proportionate

<summary>This chapter explains that while the quality of a loadstone depends on its source, its total magnetic strength and range are directly proportional to its mass. It also notes that removing parts of a stone usually decreases its power, unless the stone was poorly shaped.</summary>

# CHAPTER XXXI.

## CONCERNING OBLONG AND ROUND STONES.

**IRON** bodies are more forcibly attracted by an oblong stone
than by a round one, provided only the pole of the stone is at
the extreme end of its length. The reason is that in the
oblong stone the magnetic body at the extremity is directed
straight toward a body wherein the force proceeds in straight
lines and through a longer diameter. But the oblong stone
has only little force on the side; for, plainly, the attraction at
*a* and *B* is stronger in a round loadstone at an equal distance
<margin>*</margin> from the pole, than in *c* and *D*.

## CHAPTER XXXII.

### SOME PROBLEMS AND MAGNETIC EXPERIMENTS ON THE <term>COITION</term> <note>attraction or mutual coming-together</note>, AND REPULSION, AND REGULAR MOVEMENT, OF MAGNETIC BODIES.

<margin>*</margin>
<term>LOADSTONES</term> that are equal come together with equal mutual <term>incitation</term> <note>speed or impulse of movement</note>.

<margin>*</margin>
Magnetized iron bodies that are equal in all respects also come together with equal mutual <term>incitation</term>.

<margin>*</margin>
Iron bodies that are not magnetized, if they are equal and not hindered by their size, also come together with equal movement.

<margin>*</margin>
Two <term>loadstones</term> placed apart on suitable floats on the surface of water attract each other if they are properly arranged within their <term>magnetic field</term>. Similarly, a proportionate piece of iron on one float hastens toward a <term>loadstone</term> with the same speed as the magnet itself, afloat, strives to reach the iron. For both are impelled from their respective positions on either side to meet in the middle and join together. Two magnetized iron wires, floated in water by suitable corks, move forward until they touch and, with the correct ends facing, strike and are joined.

<margin>*</margin>
With magnetic bodies that are equal, <term>coition</term> is more vigorous and quicker than <term>repulsion</term> and separation. That magnetic bodies are more sluggish in repelling than in attracting is seen in every magnetic experiment, such as when <term>loadstones</term> are carried on suitable floats on water, or when magnetized iron wires or small bars are pushed through cork and set afloat in water, as well as in experiments with a needle. # PROBLEMS AND MAGNETIC EXPERIMENTS.

South parts of a stone repel other south parts, and north parts repel other north parts. Nevertheless, if you bring the south end of a piece of iron near to the south part of the stone, the iron is seized and the two are held in a friendly embrace; this is because the <term>verticity</term> <note>magnetic orientation or polarity</note> fixed in the iron is reversed and changed by the presence of the more powerful <term>loadstone</term>, which is more constant in its forces than the iron. For they come together in accordance with nature if, either by reversal or change, there is produced true conformity and orderly <term>coition</term> <note>attraction or mutual coming-together</note> as well as regular direction. <term>Loadstones</term> of identical shape, size, and strength attract each other with equal force, and when placed in the wrong position, they repel with the same energy.

Little rods of unmagnetized iron, though similar and equal,<margin>*</margin> yet often act on one another with different force; for just as there are different grounds for the acquisition of <term>verticity</term> and also of strength and vigor, so the particles that are most strongly excited by the <term>loadstones</term> themselves act in turn with the most force.

Pieces of iron that have been magnetized at the same pole<margin>*</margin> of a <term>loadstone</term> repel one another at the magnetized ends; and their other extremities are also mutually hostile.

In rotating needles, when the points are magnetized but<margin>*</margin> not the crotches <note>the central part of the needle near the pivot</note>, the latter repel one another, but only feebly and in proportion to their length.

In similar rotating needles, when the points are magnetized by<margin>*</margin> the same pole of a <term>loadstone</term>, the crotches attract each other with equal force.

In a long rotating needle, the crotch is attracted feebly by<margin>*</margin> the point of a short needle; the crotch of a short one is attracted strongly by the point of a long one, because the crotch of a long needle has feeble <term>verticity</term>, but the point of a long needle has strong <term>verticity</term>.

The laws of rotation and attraction are the same as between <term>loadstone</term> and <term>loadstone</term>, <term>loadstone</term> and iron, and iron and iron.

When the parts of a magnetic body that has been broken up by force and cut into pieces are put together again and properly joined, they form one body and their joint force is one; nor do they have separate poles.

<margin>*</margin> The separated parts, if the division has not been made along the parallels, assume new poles, north and south; if the division is along a parallel, they may retain one pole in the same place as before.

<margin>*</margin> Two <term>loadstones</term>, or two magnetized pieces of iron that are properly joined together, fly apart upon the approach of a stronger <term>loadstone</term> or a stronger magnetized mass of iron. This is because the newcomer, by presenting the opposite pole, drives one away and overpowers it, and the mutual action of the two that were previously joined ceases. Thus, the forces of one of the bodies are reduced and fail; if it were possible, it would shake off its partner and, turning around, would roll over to the stronger one. For this reason, magnetic bodies held hanging in the air drop to the ground when the opposite pole of a <term>loadstone</term> is presented to them. This does not happen because of any weakening or numbing of the forces in both of the previously joined bodies, as <term>Baptista Porta</term> maintains; for a pole cannot be hostile to both ends that are joined, but only to one. The newcomer—the stronger <term>loadstone</term>—drives this end away from itself by presenting its opposite pole, and thus one of the smaller bodies is forced to end its friendly association with the other.

<summary>Gilbert explains that magnetic bodies act together to increase attraction when aligned naturally but repel each other when aligned unnaturally. He also refutes Baptista Porta's explanation for why magnets drop joined iron, attributing it to polar repulsion rather than a loss of magnetic strength.</summary>

STRENGTH AND MOVEMENT OF COITION.

# CHAPTER XXXIII.

## OF THE DIFFERENCE IN THE RATIO OF STRENGTH AND MOVEMENT OF <term>COITION</term> WITHIN THE SPHERE OF INFLUENCE.

If the greatest weight that is attracted to a <term>loadstone</term> at the nearest distance be divided into a given number of parts, and the radius of the sphere of magnetic attraction into the same number of parts, the parts of the weight will correspond to the intermediate parts of the radius.

The sphere of influence extends farther than the sphere of movement of any magnetic body, for a magnetic body is affected at the outermost edge though it may not move with local motion: that is done when the <term>loadstone</term> is brought nearer. A needle, even a very small one, turns around while remote from a <term>loadstone</term>, though, at the same distance and free to move and in no wise hindered, it does not come to the <term>loadstone</term>.

The velocity of the movement of a magnetic body to a <term>loadstone</term> is in proportion to the strength of the <term>loadstone</term>, or its mass, or its shape, or the nature of the medium, or the distance within the magnetic sphere of action.

A magnetic body approaches a powerful <term>loadstone</term> with greater velocity than a weak one, in the ratio of the respective energies of the two <term>loadstones</term>. A smaller mass of iron, as also one rather oblong in shape, is attracted with the greater velocity. The velocity of the movement of a magnetic body to a <term>loadstone</term> varies according to the medium, for

### CHAPTER XXXV.

### ON A PERPETUAL-MOTION ENGINE POWERED BY THE ATTRACTION OF A LOADSTONE, AS MENTIONED BY VARIOUS AUTHORS.

CARDAN writes that a perpetual-motion engine can be constructed from iron and a loadstone—not that he ever saw such a machine himself; he merely offers the idea as an opinion and quotes the report of Antonius de Fantis of Treviso. He describes such a machine in Book IX of *De Rerum Varietate* (*On the Variety of Things*). However, the inventors of such machines have very little practical experience in magnetic experiments. For no magnetic attraction can be greater (regardless of the skill or the form of instrument you use) than the force of retention; and objects that are already joined and nearby are held with greater force than objects drawn and set in motion are made to move. Furthermore, as we have already shown, this motion is a <term>coition</term> <note>a coming together</note> of both parts, not merely the attraction of one. *Petrus Peregrinus* either devised or sketched such an engine centuries ago after he had obtained the idea from others; and *Joannes Taysner* published this, illustrating it with poor diagrams and copying the theory word for word. May the gods damn all such fraudulent, plagiarized, and distorted works, which do nothing but confuse the minds of students! ¹

<header>HOW A STRONG LOADSTONE MAY BE RECOGNIZED.</header>

## CHAPTER XXXVI.

### HOW A STRONG LOADSTONE MAY BE RECOGNIZED.

A strong <term>loadstone</term> sometimes lifts in the air a mass of iron weighing as much as itself; a weak <term>loadstone</term> hardly attracts a bit of fine wire. Therefore, those are the stronger <term>loadstones</term> which attract and hold the larger bodies, unless there is some defect of shape, or unless the pole of the stone is not properly applied. Besides, the stronger <term>loadstone</term>, when afloat, more readily turns its poles toward the poles of the earth or the points of variation on the horizon. But the stone that acts sluggishly betrays some flaw in itself and shows that its force is exhausted. <term>Loadstones</term> are all to be prepared in the same way, shaped alike, and made of the same size; for when they are unlike and unequal, experiments are doubtful. All <term>loadstones</term> are tested for strength in the same way—namely, with a <term>versorium</term> (rotating needle) held at some distance; the stone that is able to make the needle rotate from the greatest distance is the best and strongest. Baptista Porta also correctly determines the power of a <term>loadstone</term> by weighing it in a
