balance. A piece of loadstone is placed in one scale and an equal weight of another substance in the other, so that the scales are balanced. Then some iron lying on a board is brought near, so that it shall cling to the loadstone in the scale, and the two bodies cohere perfectly at their points of attraction; into the opposite scale, sand is poured gradually until the scale containing the loadstone separates from the iron. By weighing the sand, the force of the loadstone is determined. In the same way, we can conduct an experiment to find the stronger stone by weighing sand if we place loadstones that balance each other in a pair of scales. Such is an experiment given by Cardinal Cusanus in his *Statica*, and it seems that Porta learned the one he cites from him. The stronger loadstones turn readily toward the poles or the points of variation; they also propel their floats and cause them and other burdens, such as wood, to turn around. In an inclination or dip instrument, the greater power of a loadstone is shown, and in that case, greater power is required. Therefore, loadstones are stronger the more quickly they perform their work, the more rapidly they move from side to side and back again, and the sooner they come to a standstill. Weak, exhausted loadstones move more sluggishly, come to a rest more slowly, settle at the pole less decisively, and are easily displaced from it.

<header>USES OF THE LOADSTONE AS IT AFFECTS IRON.</header>

## CHAPTER XXXVII.

### USES OF THE LOADSTONE AS IT AFFECTS IRON.

By means of <term>magnetic coition</term> we test an iron ore. The ore is roasted in a furnace, is crushed, washed, dried, and so is freed from foreign humors <note>impurities or moisture</note>. The <term>loadstone</term> being thrust among the particles collected from the bath attracts the iron dust, which, being removed by a feather brush, is caught in a crucible; again and again the <term>loadstone</term> is dipped in and the iron dust brushed into the crucible, until nothing remains that it will attract. Then the powdered iron is heated together with <term>halinitro</term> <note>a salt-based flux used in smelting</note> until it is melted and becomes a mass of iron. Now, if the <term>loadstone</term> picks up the iron dust readily and easily, we deem the ore to be rich; if slowly, the ore is poor; if the <term>loadstone</term> seems to reject it entirely, the ore is judged to have little or no iron. By the same method, iron particles may be separated from particles of any other metal. And many tricks are played by secretly attracting bits of iron to light bodies, or causing a concealed <term>loadstone</term> to attract the iron; to persons who do not know the cause, the movements of the objects seem amazing. Any ingenious workman may exhibit a great number of such tricks for sport, with the air of one dealing in incantations and magic.

# CHAPTER XXXVIII.

## OF THE ATTRACTIONS OF OTHER BODIES.

Philosophers of the common sort and mere copyists often repeat, from the memoirs of others on natural philosophy, opinions and errors regarding the attractive force of various bodies. They say, for example, that diamond attracts iron and pulls it away from a loadstone; that loadstones differ, some attracting gold, others silver, copper, lead—even flesh, water, or fish. The flame of sulfur is said to seek iron and stones; similarly, white naphtha is said to draw fire to itself. I have already stated that inanimate natural bodies attract or are attracted on this terrestrial globe in no other way except either magnetically or electrically. Therefore, it is not true that there are loadstones that attract gold or other metals; for a magnetic body attracts only another magnetic body. Fracastorio claims to have seen a loadstone attracting silver. If that were true, it must have been because some iron had been artificially mixed with the silver and lay hidden within it, or because nature had mixed iron with the silver (as she sometimes does, though very rarely); for iron is occasionally mixed with silver by nature, but silver is rarely or never mixed with iron. Counterfeiters and greedy princes mix iron with silver when money is coined; we have an example of this in Anthony’s denarius, if what Pliny declares is true. Likewise, Cardan (perhaps led into error by others) says there is a certain kind of loadstone that attracts silver; he adds a very foolish test of the matter: “If,” he says, “a thin rod of silver be

But what does attraction have to do with the numbing of the senses, or what is there in common between stupefaction and the mind of a philosopher while he discusses attraction?

Many are the stones, both of natural origin and artificially compounded, that possess the power of dulling the senses.

The flame of sulfur is said by some to attract because it consumes certain metals by reason of its penetrating force.

Similarly, naphtha attracts flame because it emits and exhales inflammable vapor, and therefore is set aflame at some distance; just as the smoke of a candle that has just been extinguished catches fire again from another flame; for fire creeps to fire through an inflammable medium.

Endorsing the absurdities of the ancients, they published the most blunderous theories and ridiculous theses—for example, that there are rocks having the power of attraction and that the remora dwells there; and they postulate the necessity of some sort of vacuum, or how it is produced. Pliny and Julius Solinus tell of the stone *cathochites* and affirm that it attracts flesh and holds one's hand, just as a loadstone holds iron and amber holds chaff. But that is due solely to its viscosity and its natural glutinousness, for it adheres most readily to a warm hand. The *sagda*, or *sagdo*, is a gem of leek-green color mentioned by Pliny, Solinus, Albertus Magnus, and Euace, who themselves make up or copy from others the story that this stone has the peculiarity of attracting wood. And there are others who utter the nonsense that the wood attracted cannot be pulled off, but has to be cut away; while some tell of a stone of this kind that clings as firmly to ships' bottoms as do the barnacles gathered on a long voyage. But though a stone may cling to a surface, it does not therefore attract; and if it did attract, surely it would draw to itself chips and shavings electrically. A stone of this sort was seen by Encelius in the hands of a certain sailor; it was a weak stone, hardly able to attract the smallest twigs; and its color was not a true leek-green. Diamond, carbuncle, rock-crystal, and other stones attract in that way. I say nothing of other fabulous stones, of *pantarbes*, of which Philostratus affirms that it attracts other stones to itself; of *amphitane*, said to also attract gold. Pliny, in telling of the discovery of glass, makes the loadstone attract glass as it does iron; for when in speaking of the method of making glass he describes its nature, he adds this concerning the loadstone: "In time the skill of the workmen, clear-sighted and resourceful, was no longer content with mixing in natron; loadstone began to be added because it is believed to

But sometimes it happens that because of the magnetic stone, or magnesia, or iron ore, or pyrites, the glass has a dusky tinge, as these substances are too resistant to fire and thus are not burnt up, or have been introduced in too great a quantity. For this reason, glassmakers obtain the right kind of stone and carefully attend to the proportion of ingredients in the mixture. Thus, then, Georgius Agricola and later writers are badly led astray by Pliny’s foolish philosophy when they declare that loadstone is needed by glassmakers for its magnetic virtues and attractive force. And Scaliger (*De Subtil, ad Cardanum*) strays far from the truth when, in treating of magnetic bodies, he speaks of diamond attracting iron; unless he means only that diamond electrically attracts iron just as it does bits of wood, straws, and other small bodies of all kinds. Fallopius thinks that quicksilver attracts metals by virtue of an occult property, just as the loadstone does iron, or as amber attracts chaff. But there is no attraction, properly so called, when quicksilver enters into metals. For metals absorb quicksilver as clay does water, but only when the substances are in contact; for quicksilver does not draw gold or lead to itself from a distance, but remains fixed in its place.

<summary>Gilbert argues that the use of "magnesia" or loadstone in glassmaking is for chemical purification through heat rather than magnetic attraction. He also refutes the claims of Scaliger and Fallopius regarding the supposed attractive powers of diamonds and quicksilver.</summary>

MUTUALLY REPELLANT BODIES.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.

### OF MUTUALLY REPELLANT BODIES.

Authors who have treated the forces of attracting bodies have also discussed the powers of repellant bodies, particularly those who have classified natural objects according to sympathy and antipathy. Therefore, it seems we must say something about the conflict between bodies, lest widespread errors—accepted by everyone to the ruin of true philosophy—should spread further. They tell us that just as similar things attract for the sake of preservation, so unlike things and opposites repel and drive each other away, as is seen in the *antiperistasis* (counteraction) of many bodies; but this is said to be most powerful in plants and animals, which, as they attract things related and similar to them, so they reject things that are extreme and disadvantageous to themselves.

But in other bodies, the same reason does not exist for their coming together through mutual attraction when they are separated. Animals take in food (as do all living things), bring it into their internal parts, and absorb their nourishment by means of certain organs (the vital principle acting and operating). They only benefit from things set before them and nearby through a natural instinct, not things placed far away; in this, there is no exercise of force and no movement on the part of those other things. Therefore, animals neither attract nor repel bodies. Water does not repel oil, as some think, for oil floats on water; nor does water repel mud, because when it is mixed with water, the mud eventually settles. This is a separation of unlike bodies

<summary>Gilbert refutes the traditional theories of sympathy and antipathy, arguing that what appears to be repulsion in nature is actually due to biological instincts or mechanical separation rather than a specific repellant force. He specifically dismisses the idea that animals or substances like water and oil exert attractive or repellant forces over a distance.</summary>

<keywords>repellant bodies, sympathy, antipathy, antiperistasis, vital principle, biological instinct, natural philosophy, oil and water separation</keywords>

WILLIAM GILBERT.

or not perfectly mixed because of their nature; but after they have been separated, they still remain together without any natural conflict. Thus, at the bottom of a vessel, muddy sediment rests quietly, and oil remains on top of the water; it is not driven away. A drop of water remains whole on a dry surface and is not chased away by the dryness. Therefore, those who discuss these things wrongly attribute an antipathy—*antipathia* (that is, a power of repulsion through opposite passions); for there is no repellant force in them, and repulsion comes from action, not from passion. But these people dearly love their Greek terms. The question for us is whether there is any body that drives another away to a distance without physical impact, just as the <term>loadstone</term> <note>a naturally magnetized piece of the mineral magnetite</note> attracts. Now, a loadstone does repel another loadstone; for the pole of one is repelled by the pole of another that does not naturally agree with it; by driving it away, it causes it to turn around so that they may come together perfectly according to their nature. But if a weak loadstone floating freely in water cannot easily turn around because of obstacles, then it is repelled and driven further away by the other. All <term>electrics</term> <note>substances that can be electrified by friction, like amber</note> attract objects of every kind; they never repel or push them away. What is said of some plants (for example, the cucumber, which is said to move away when oil is placed beneath it) is a physical change caused by proximity, not a hidden sympathy. But when they show you a candle’s flame turning to one side when it touches a cold solid (such as iron), and claim that this is antipathy, they talk nonsense. They will see the reason for this more clearly than light when we come to discuss heat and what it is. As for *Fracastorio’s* belief that a loadstone may be found that can repel iron because of some hidden principle within it that is opposed to iron, it is without any foundation.

<summary>Gilbert argues that apparent repulsion in nature, such as oil floating on water or plants reacting to substances, is due to physical properties rather than "antipathy." He explains that magnetic repulsion is merely a mechanism to force proper alignment between two magnets.</summary>

## CHAPTER I.

### OF DIRECTION.

IN the preceding books it has been shown that a <term>loadstone</term> <note>a naturally magnetized piece of the mineral magnetite</note> has its poles, and that iron also has poles, rotation, and a fixed <term>verticity</term> <note>the tendency of a magnetic body to point in a specific direction</note>; and finally, that loadstone and iron direct their poles toward the poles of the earth. But now we must set forth the causes of these things and their wonderful powers, which were known in the past but not demonstrated. Regarding these rotations, all the writers who preceded us have given their opinions with such brevity and vagueness that, it would seem, no one could be persuaded by them, while the authors themselves could hardly be satisfied with them. By intelligent men, all their petty reasonings—being useless, questionable, and absurd, and based on no proofs or premises—are rejected, with the result that magnetic science, neglected more and more and understood by no one, has been exiled. This direction would be the same all over the earth—toward the true poles and along the true meridian—if hindrances and disturbing causes were not present to prevent it. ## CHAPTER II.

### DIRECTIVE (OR VERSORIAL) FORCE, WHICH WE CALL <term>VERTICITY</term>: WHAT IT IS; HOW IT RESIDES IN THE LOADSTONE; AND HOW IT IS ACQUIRED WHEN NOT NATURALLY PRODUCED.

THE directive force, which we also call <term>verticity</term>, is a force distributed by the innate energy from the equator in both directions to the poles. That energy, proceeding north and south to the poles, produces the movement of direction, and also produces a constant and permanent position in the system of nature—and that not in the earth alone, but in all magnetic bodies also. Loadstone occurs either in a special vein or in iron mines; for, being a homogeneous earth-substance possessing and conceiving a primary form, it becomes converted into or solidified with a stony body which, in addition to the

# CHAPTER III.

### HOW IRON ACQUIRES <term>VERTICITY</term> FROM THE LOADSTONE, AND HOW THIS <term>VERTICITY</term> IS LOST OR ALTERED.

An oblong piece of iron, on being stroked with a loadstone, receives magnetic forces—not physical, nor inherent in or consisting of any material body, as has been shown in the chapters on <term>coition</term>. Clearly, a body vigorously rubbed on one end with a loadstone, and left for a long time in contact with the stone, receives no physical property of the stone and gains nothing in weight; for if you weigh a piece of iron in a goldsmith's smallest and most accurate scales before it is touched by the loadstone, you will find that after the rubbing it has the same precise weight, neither less nor more. And if you wipe the magnetized iron * with cloths, or if you rub it with sand or with a whetstone, it loses nothing at all of its acquired properties. For the force is diffused through the entire body and through its innermost parts, and can in no way be washed or wiped away. Test it, therefore, in fire—that fiercest tyrant of nature. Take a piece of iron the length of your hand and as thick as a goose-quill; pass it through a suitable round piece of cork and lay it on the surface of water, and note the end of the bar that faces north. Rub that end with the true smooth end of a loadstone; thus the magnetized iron is made to turn to the north. Take off the cork and put that magnetized end of the iron in the fire * until it just begins to glow; on becoming cool again it will retain the virtues of the loadstone and will show <term>verticity</term>, though not so promptly as before, either because the action of the fire

<summary>Gilbert demonstrates that iron acquires magnetic properties when rubbed with a loadstone without gaining weight or physical matter. He also explores how these properties reside deep within the iron and can partially survive the intense heat of fire.</summary>

Remove the cork again, drop the entire piece of iron into the fire, and fan the fire with bellows so that it becomes glowing hot, and let the glowing iron remain for a little while. After it has cooled again (but while cooling it must not remain in one position), put the iron and * cork once more in water, and you shall see that it has lost its acquired <term>verticity</term>. All this shows how difficult it is to remove the <term>polar property</term> bestowed by the loadstone. And if a small loadstone were to remain for just as long in the same fire, it too would lose its force. Iron, because it is not as easily destroyed or burned as many loadstones are, retains its powers better, and after they are lost, it may regain them from a loadstone; but a burned loadstone cannot be restored.

Now this iron, stripped of its <term>magnetic form</term>, moves differently from any other iron, for it has lost the <term>polar property</term>; and though before contact with the loadstone it may have had a movement toward the north, and after contact toward * the south, now it turns to no fixed and specific point. However, afterward—very slowly and after a long time—it turns unsteadily toward the poles, having received some measure of force from the earth. As I have said, there is a twofold cause of direction: one inherent in the loadstone and in iron, and the other in the earth, derived from the energy that organizes things. For this reason, after iron has lost the ability to distinguish the poles and its <term>verticity</term>, a slow and weak power of direction is acquired anew from the <term>earth's verticity</term>. From this we see how difficult it is—and how it is only possible through the action of intense heat and by prolonged firing of the iron until it becomes soft—to remove the magnetic force impressed upon it. But we must inquire further into how it is that iron remains possessed of <term>verticity</term>. Rub one end of a piece of iron wire with a <term>loadstone</term> so as * to magnetize it and make it turn toward the north; then cut off part of it, and you shall see it move to the north as before, though weakly. But when the iron is removed from contact, it becomes much weaker, especially at the end not touched by the <term>loadstone</term>. And just as a long rod, with one end thrust into a fire and made red-hot, is very hot at that end, less hot in the adjoining and middle parts, and can be held by the hand at the farther end because that end is only warm—so the magnetic force diminishes from the energized end to the other. However, the force is there in an instant; it is not introduced over an interval of time or successively, as when heat enters iron, for the moment the iron is touched by the <term>loadstone</term>, it is energized throughout. It has already been shown that the north part of a <term>loadstone</term> does not attract the north part of another stone, but rather the south part, and that it repels the north end of another stone applied to its north end. That general <term>loadstone</term>, the terrestrial globe, with its inborn force, disposes magnetized iron, and the <term>magnetic iron</term> also does the same with its inborn force, producing movement and determining the direction. For whether we compare together and experiment on two <term>loadstones</term>, or a <term>loadstone</term> and a piece of iron, or iron and iron, or * *earth and loadstone, or earth and iron shaped by the earth or deriving force from the energy of a loadstone, of necessity the forces and movements of each and all agree and harmonize in the same way.*

# WHY MAGNETIZED IRON TAKES OPPOSITE VERTICITY.

But the question arises: Why does iron touched by a <term>loadstone</term> take a direction of movement toward the Earth's opposite pole, and not toward that pole of the Earth toward which the pole of the loadstone (used for magnetizing it) was facing? Iron and the <term>loadstone</term>, as we have said, are of the same primary nature; when iron is joined to a <term>loadstone</term>, it becomes, as it were, one body with it, and not only is one extremity of the iron altered, but the rest of its parts are also affected. Let *A* be the north pole of a <term>loadstone</term> to which the tip of an iron pointer is attached: the tip is now the south part of the iron because it is adjacent to the north part of the stone; the crotch of the pointer becomes north.

### CHAPTER X.

#### ON THE MUTATION OF VERTICITY AND MAGNETIC PROPERTIES, OR THE ALTERATION OF THE FORCE AWAKENED BY THE LOADSTONE.

<margin>* Which end of the wire?</margin>
IRON excited by the magnetic influx has a <term>verticity</term> <note>the magnetic power of turning toward the poles</note> that is quite strong, yet it is not so stable that the opposite parts cannot be altered by friction—not only from a stronger <term>loadstone</term>, but even from the same one. It may lose all of its first verticity and take on the opposite direction. Obtain a piece of iron wire and rub each end equally with the very same pole of a loadstone; pass the wire through a suitable cork float and place it in the water. Then one end of the wire will face toward a pole of the earth that the end of the loadstone used for rubbing does not face. But which * end of the wire? It will be specifically the one that was rubbed last. Now rub the other end again with the same pole, and immediately that end will turn in the opposite direction. Again, rub the end that first pointed to the pole of the loadstone, and at once that end—having, as it were, received its orders (*imperium nactus*)—will go in the direction opposite to the one it took last. In this way, you will be able to alter the direction again and again

The loadstone itself, however, is not robbed of its property and <term>verticity</term> by friction with another larger or stronger stone; nor is it turned, when on a float, toward the opposite direction or toward another pole different from that toward which, by its own nature and <term>verticity</term>, it tends. ## CHAPTER XII.

### HOW <term>VERTICITY</term> EXISTS IN ALL SMELTED IRON NOT MAGNETIZED BY THE LOADSTONE.

SO FAR we have explained the natural and inherent causes and the powers acquired through the loadstone; but now we are to investigate the causes of the magnetic power existing in manufactured iron not magnetized by the loadstone. The loadstone and iron present and show us wonderful, subtle properties. It has already often been shown that iron not magnetized by the loadstone turns toward the north and south; furthermore, that it possesses <term>verticity</term> <note>magnetic polarity</note>, that is, distinct poles proper and specific to itself, just like the loadstone or iron rubbed with a loadstone. This seemed to us at first strange and unbelievable: the metal, iron, is smelted from the ore in the furnace, flows out of the furnace, and hardens into a large mass; the mass is cut up in large workshops and drawn into iron bars, and from these again the smith shapes all sorts of necessary tools and objects of iron. Thus the same mass is worked in various ways and transformed into many shapes. What, then, preserves the <term>verticity</term>, or where is it derived from? But when inferior iron ore, in which no magnetic properties are apparent, is put in the fire <margin>*</margin> (its position with reference to the world’s poles being noted) and heated there for eight or ten hours, then cooled away from the fire and in the same position with regard to the poles, it acquires <term>verticity</term> according to its position during heating and cooling.

Let a bar of iron be brought to a white heat in a strong <margin>*</margin> fire, in which it lies <term>meridionally</term>, that is, along the track of a meridian circle; then take it out of the fire and let it cool and return to its original temperature, lying the while in the same position as before. It will happen that, because the same ends were directed toward the same poles of the earth, it will acquire <term>verticity</term>; and that the end that faced north when the bar, before the heating, was floated in water by means of a cork, will now point to the south if that same end during the heating and the cooling faced southward. If perhaps the turning toward the pole should at any time be weak and uncertain, put the bar in the fire again, take it out when it has reached a white heat, cool it perfectly while it lies pointing in the direction of the pole from which you wish it to take <term>verticity</term>, and the <term>verticity</term> will be acquired. Let it be heated again, lying in the opposite direction, and while it is still <margin>*</margin> white-hot, lay it down until it cools; for, from its position during cooling (the earth's <term>verticity</term> acting upon it), <term>verticity</term> is infused into the iron and it turns toward points opposite to the former <term>verticity</term>. So the end that before faced north now turns to the south. For these reasons and in these ways, the north pole of the earth gives to that end of the <margin>*</margin> iron which is turned toward it a south <term>verticity</term>; hence, too, that

<header>ONLY MAGNETIC BODIES IMBUED WITH <term>VERTICITY</term>.</header>

### CHAPTER XIII.

#### WHY NO OTHER BODIES EXCEPT THE MAGNETIC ARE ENDOWED WITH <term>VERTICITY</term> BY FRICTION WITH A LOADSTONE; AND WHY NO BODY THAT IS NOT MAGNETIC CAN IMPART AND AWAKEN THAT FORCE.

WOOD floating on water never turns by its own power toward the poles of the world except by chance: likewise, threads of gold, silver, copper, zinc, lead, or glass, when passed through cork and floated, never have a reliable direction; and, therefore, when rubbed with a loadstone they show neither poles nor points of variation. For bodies that do not of their own accord turn toward the poles and are not obedient to the earth are in no way governed by the loadstone's touch; neither has the energy of the loadstone entrance into their interior, nor are their forms excited magnetically. Nor, if the energy did enter in, could it accomplish anything, for the reason that there are no primary qualities in such bodies, mixed as they are with a variety of efflorescent humors <note>Discharge or waste products in the material's composition</note> and degenerate from the primal property of the globe. On the other hand, the properties of iron which are primal are awakened by the approach of a loadstone: like brute animals and men when awakened out of sleep, the properties of iron now move and put forth their strength.

Here we must express wonder at a manifest error of Baptista Porta, who, though he properly refuses to agree with the long-standing falsehood about a force opposite to the magnetic, imparts an even falser opinion: namely, that iron rubbed

Indeed—and this is noteworthy—the opposite part, like the lodestone itself at its south end, repels iron, and when we experimented with a multitude of small iron rods in water, they all stood at equal distances apart and pointed north.” Now this is contrary to our magnetic rules; and therefore we conducted the experiment ourselves with seventy-five * diamonds in the presence of many witnesses, using a number of iron bars and pieces of wire, handling them with the utmost care while they floated in water, supported by corks; yet I was never able to see the effect mentioned by Porta. He was led astray by the <term>verticity</term> of the iron in the bars or wires obtained from the earth (as shown above); the iron naturally tended toward its specific pole, and Porta, being unaware of this, supposed the effect was caused by the diamond. But let researchers of nature beware lest they be further deluded by their own poorly observed experiments, and lest, through errors and blunders, they throw the republic of letters into confusion. Diamond (*adamas*) is sometimes called siderite (*siderites*), not because it is ferruginous or because it attracts iron (*σίδηρος*, *sideros*), but because of its luster, like that of shining iron; the finest diamonds possess this brilliance. Due to this confusion of names, many effects are credited to the diamond that actually belong to the lodestone siderite.¹

<header>POSITION DOES NOT AFFECT <term>VERTICITY</term>.</header>

## CHAPTER XIV.

### THE POSITION OF A LODSTONE, NOW ABOVE, THEN BENEATH, A MAGNETIC BODY SUSPENDED IN EQUILIBRIUM, ALTERS NEITHER THE FORCE NOR THE <term>VERTICITY</term> OF THE MAGNETIC BODY.

WE cannot rightfully pass over this point, because we must correct an error that has recently arisen from a faulty observation by Baptista Porta; out of this erroneous judgment, Porta, through pointless repetition, creates three chapters—namely, the eighth, the thirty-first, and the sixty-second. Now, if a lodestone or a piece of iron suspended in equilibrium or floating in water is attracted or controlled by another piece of iron or another lodestone held above it, the stone or iron does not turn in the opposite direction when you apply the second iron or stone beneath it; on the contrary, the ends of the floating lodestone or floating iron will always turn to the same points of the stone, regardless of how the lodestone or iron is suspended in equilibrium or whether they are mounted on a pivot so that they may revolve freely. Porta was led into error by the uneven shape of some lodestone or by the fact that he did not conduct the experiment correctly. Thus, he is badly mistaken, thinking it fair to conclude that just as the lodestone has a north and a south pole, it also has an east and a west pole, and a top and a bottom pole. In this way, many foolish imaginings arise from mistakes committed and accepted as true judgments.

### CHAPTER XVI.

->IF A PART IS BROKEN OFF FROM THE SOUTH PART OF A LOADSTONE,<-
->SOME POWER IS ALSO TAKEN AWAY FROM THE<-
->NORTH PART.<-

FOR although the south part of magnetic iron is attracted by the north part of the <term>loadstone</term>, the south part of the stone does not reduce but actually increases the power of the north part. Therefore, if a <term>loadstone</term> is cut and divided at the Arctic circle, or at the tropic of Cancer, or at the equator, the south part does not attract at its pole as powerfully as before; for a new whole arises, and the equator leaves its former place and moves toward the pole because of the division of the stone. In its previous state, because the opposite part of the stone beyond the plane of the equator increased the mass, it also strengthened the <term>verticity</term>, the force, and the movement toward union.

# CHAPTER XVII.

## ON THE USE OF ROTARY NEEDLES AND THEIR ADVANTAGES; HOW THE DIRECTIVE IRON ROTARY NEEDLES OF SUN-DIALS AND THE NEEDLES OF THE MARINER'S COMPASS ARE TO BE RUBBED WITH <term>LOADSTONE</term> IN ORDER TO ACQUIRE STRONGER <term>VERTICITY</term>.

Magnetized <term>versoriums</term> (or magnetized rotary needles) serve so many purposes in human life that it will not be out of place to show the best process for rubbing and magnetically exciting them, as well as the proper method of applying that process. With the help of a small bar of iron, magnetically prepared and balanced in equilibrium, rich iron ores and those containing the most metal are identified; magnetic stones, clays, and earths—whether raw or processed—are also distinguished. A little iron bar—that soul of the mariner’s compass, that wonderful director in sea voyages, that finger of God, so to speak—points the way and has made known the whole circle of the earth, which was unknown for so many ages. Spaniards (and Englishmen too) have repeatedly circumnavigated the entire globe on a great circle with the help of the mariner’s compass. Those who travel by land or stay at home use sun-dial horologes. The magnetic needle seeks out and searches for veins of iron in mines; with its help, tunnels are driven when cities are besieged, and cannons and military engines are aimed at night in the desired directions. The needle is useful for topography, for determining the area and position of buildings, and for constructing underground aqueducts. On it depend

Sometimes, also, the stone has an artificial cap or snout of steel at the top, right above the pole, to provide more strength; iron <term>versoria</term> are rubbed on this cap, and afterward they turn to that same pole just as if they had been magnetized at that spot without the cap.

The stone should be of a good size and strong; the <term>versorium</term>, even if it is long, must be fairly thick and not too thin, with a moderate-sized point that is not too sharp, though the energy is not in the point itself but in the entire needle. Any powerful, large loadstone works well for rubbing <term>versoria</term>, though sometimes, due to its power, it causes some dip and disturbance when the needle is long; as a result, the needle—which was balanced horizontally before being rubbed—now dips at one end as low as its support allows after being rubbed and magnetized. Therefore, in the case of a long <term>versorium</term>, the end intended to point north should be slightly lighter than the other end before being rubbed, so that it may remain perfectly balanced afterward. However, a <term>versorium</term> prepared this way performs its function poorly at any significant distance from the equinoctial circle <note>the equator</note>.

Porta wrongly seeks a ratio between the loadstone and iron: a small mass of iron, he says, cannot hold a great measure of power, for it is wasted by the mighty energy of the loadstone. Clearly, the iron takes its own virtue to the full, even if it weighs only one scruple <note>a very small unit of weight</note> and the mass of the loadstone is more than 100 lbs. It is also pointless to make the <term>versorium</term> rather flat at the end that is rubbed so that it may become a better and stronger magnetic body, or so that it may better seize and hold certain magnetic particles, few of which can adhere to a sharp point. For it was Porta’s belief that the energy is transmitted and retained by the adhesion of particles from the loadstone, like hairs, whereas these particles are simply scrapings detached by the iron from the softer stone; besides, the magnetized iron points steadily north and south even if, after friction, it is scoured with sand or emery or other material, and even though its outer parts are ground down and worn away by long-continued friction. In stroking the loadstone with a <term>versorium</term>, each stroke should terminate at one end of the <term>versorium</term>; otherwise, if the stroke is made toward the middle, a lesser degree of <term>verticity</term>, or none at all, or very little, is excited in the iron. For where the contact ends, there is the pole and the point of <term>verticity</term>. To produce stronger <term>verticity</term> in iron by friction

<margin>*</margin> with a loadstone, it is necessary in northern latitudes to turn the loadstone’s true north pole toward the zenith <note>the point in the sky directly overhead</note>; on that pole, that end of the <term>versorium</term> is to be rubbed which afterward will

## CHAPTER I.

### OF VARIATION.

So far, we have treated direction as if there were no such thing as variation; for we chose to have variation left out and disregarded in the preceding natural history, just as if variation could not exist in a perfectly and absolutely spherical terrestrial globe. But since the magnetic direction of the earth, through some fault or flaw, departs from the correct track and the meridian, the occult and hidden cause of variance—which has troubled and tormented the minds of many to no effect—must be brought to light and demonstrated by us. Those who have written until now about magnetic movements have recognized no distinction between direction and variation, but maintain that there is only one movement of the magnetized needle. But true direction is a movement of the magnetic body toward the true meridian, and continu-

He distinguishes between true magnetic direction and the "variance" caused by the Earth's physical imperfections.</summary>

Yet it happens very often, both at sea and on land, that a magnetic needle does not point toward the true pole, but is drawn to a point on the horizon near the meridian. There is a deflection not only of the needle and magnetized iron in general and of the mariner’s compass, but also of a terrella on its
<margin>*</margin> float, of iron ore and ironstone, and of magnetic clays artificially treated; for they often point with their poles toward directions other than the meridian. The variation, then, as observed with the aid of instruments or of the mariner’s compass, is an arc of the horizon between the intersection of the horizon by the meridian and the point of deflection on the horizon, or the range of deviation of the magnetized body. This arc varies and is different according to locality.<note>Gilbert defines variation to be the arc intersected between the point where the meridian of the place cuts the horizon and that point to which the magnetic needle looks; the length of this arc varies with the place of observation (“*Nature*” for April 27, 1876, page 523). The variation is now known by scientific writers as the declination. As expressed by Commander A. W. Greely, “declination is the variation of the magnetic meridian from the geographical meridian. It is measured by the angle between the two meridians, and is expressed in degrees of azimuth from zero either to the east or to the west of the true north. When the magnetic north is west of the true north it is west declination, and east when the reverse occurs.”</note> Thus the limit of the variation is commonly assigned to a great circle—the circle of variation, as it is called—and a magnetic meridian passing through the zenith and the point of variation on the horizon.

In northern terrestrial latitudes this variation takes place either in the direction from north toward east, or from north toward west; in southern latitudes, in like manner, it is from south toward east, or south toward west. Hence in northern
<margin>*</margin> latitudes we must heed the end of the needle that tends north, and in southern latitudes the end looking south: this naviga-

...tors and sciolists <note>Those with superficial knowledge</note> seldom understand, for on both sides of the equator they note only the north point terminal of the compass, or the one that looks north. As we have already said, every movement of the loadstone and needle—every turn and dip, and their coming to rest—are effects of the magnetic bodies themselves and of the Earth, mother of all, which is the fount, source, and producer of all these forces and properties. Thus, then, the Earth is the cause of this <term>variation</term> and its tendency toward a different point on the horizon; but we have to inquire further how and by what powers it acts.

    Here we must first reject the common opinion of modern writers concerning magnetic mountains, or a certain magnetic rock, or a distant phantom pole of the world controlling the movement of the compass or of the *<term>versorium</term>*. This opinion *Fracastorio* adopted and developed after it had been introduced by others; but it does not agree with experiments at all. For, if it were correct, in different places on land and sea, the <term>variation</term> point would change toward the east or west in a geometrical ratio, and the *<term>versorium</term>* would always point toward the magnetic pole; but experience teaches that there is no specific pole, no fixed endpoint of <term>variation</term> on the globe. For the arc of <term>variation</term> changes erratically in different ways, so that in different meridians—and even in the same meridian—where, according to the opinion of recent writers, the magnetized needle would deviate toward the east, it suddenly shifts from north toward the west upon a slight change of location, as in the northern regions near *Nova Zemlya (Nova Zembla)*.¹ In southern latitudes also, and at sea far away from the equator and toward the Antarctic—and not only in northern latitudes near those magnetic mountains—is <term>variation</term> frequent and great.

But even more vain and foolish are the fantasies of other writers—*Cortesius*, for example, who speaks of a moving force beyond the farthest heavens; *Marsilio Ficino*, who finds the cause of variation in a star in Ursa; *Petrus Peregrinus*, who finds it in the pole of the world; *Cardan*, referring it to the rising of a star in the tail of Ursa; the Frenchman *Bessard*, to the pole of the zodiac; *Livius Sanutus*, to a certain magnetic meridian; *Franciscus Maurolycus*, to a magnetic island; *Scaliger*, to the heavens and to mountains; the Englishman *Robert Norman*, to the “respective point.”¹

Leaving behind, therefore, those opinions that are at odds with everyday experience, or that at least are by no means proven, let us look for the true cause of variation. The Great Loadstone, or the terrestrial globe, gives, as I have said, to iron a north and south direction; magnetized iron readily conforms itself to those points. But as the globe of Earth is at its surface broken and uneven, marred by materials of diverse nature, and has elevated and convex parts that rise to the height of some miles and that are uniform neither in matter nor in constitution but opposite and different, it comes about that this entire earth-energy turns magnetic bodies at its periphery toward stronger massive magnetic parts that are more powerful and that stand above the general level. Therefore, at the outermost surfaces of the Earth, magnetic bodies are turned a little away from the true meridian. And since the Earth’s surface is diversified by elevations of land and depths of seas, great continental lands, oceans, and seas differing in every way—while the force that produces all magnetic movements comes from the constant magnetic earth-substance, which is strongest in the most massive continent and not where the

For this reason a magnetic body under the action of the whole earth is attracted toward a great elevated mass of land as toward a stronger body, so far as the disturbed <term>verticity</term> permits or gives up its right. Yet the variation takes place not so much because of these elevated but less perfect parts of the earth and these continental lands, as because of the inequality of the magnetic globe and of the true earth-substance which projects farther in continents than beneath sea-depths. We have therefore to inquire how the demonstration of this new natural philosophy may be drawn from unquestionable experiments.

## CHAPTER III.

### VARIATION IS CONSTANT AT A GIVEN PLACE.<note>Henry Gellibrand, an English mathematician and professor of geometry at Gresham College, discovered the *secular variation* of the <term>declination</term> between 1633 and 1635. In the words of Dr. Whewell (*History of the Inductive Sciences*, 1859, Vol. II, page 219): “Gellibrand discovered that the variation is not constant, as Gilbert imagined, but that in London it had diminished from eleven degrees east in 1580 to four degrees in 1633. Since that time the variation has become more and more westerly; it is now about twenty-five degrees west, and the needle is supposed to have begun to travel eastward again. It may be added that the *diurnal variation* was subsequently found by George Graham during the year 1722, while the *annual variation* was made known by Jean Jacques Dominique Cassini between 1782 and 1791.”</note>

### CHAPTER IV.

#### THE ARC OF VARIATION DOES NOT VARY IN PROPORTION TO THE DISTANCE BETWEEN PLACES.

On the open ocean, while a ship is carried by a favorable wind along the same parallel, if the variation is reduced by exactly one degree in a voyage of 100 miles, it does not follow that the next 100 miles will reduce it by another degree. For the needle varies according to the position and shape of the land and the magnetic force; it also varies according to distance. For example, when a ship from the Scilly Islands bound for Newfoundland has traveled so far that the compass points to the true magnetic pole, then, as she sails on, the <term>borrholybic</term> <note>north-northwestern</note> variation begins, but faintly and with a small divergence. But after a while, the arc increases at a higher rate as equal distances are traversed, until the ship comes near the continent, when the variation is very great. Yet before she quite reaches land or enters port, while still some distance away, the arc is slightly lessened again. But if the ship in her course departs significantly \*from that parallel, either to the north or south, the needle will vary more or less according to the position of the land and the latitude of the region; for, all other things being equal, the higher the latitude, the greater the variation.

## CHAPTER V.

### AN ISLAND IN THE OCEAN DOES NOT ALTER THE VARIATION; NEITHER DO MINES OF LOADSTONE.

ISLANDS, although they are more magnetic than the seas, still do not alter magnetic direction or variation. For direction is a movement produced by the energy of the entire earth, and is not due to the attractive force of any particular prominence but to the controlling power and <term>verticity</term> of the whole mass; therefore, variation (which is a disturbance of the directive force) is a straying from the true verticity and arises out of the great inequalities of the earth. Because of these, the earth itself, even when very large and powerful magnetic bodies are present, has little power to turn away magnetic bodies that revolve freely. As for the wonders that some report about the island of Elba: loadstones abound there, but, nevertheless, the <term>versorium</term> (or the mariner’s compass) makes no special inclination toward it when ships sail by in the Tyrrhenian Sea.¹ The reasons already given sufficiently account for this; furthermore, a reason may be found in the fact that the energy of minor loadstones reaches but little beyond their own location; for variation is not produced by a "pulling to," as those who have imagined magnetic poles would suggest. Besides, mines of loadstone are only agnate <note>added or attached to the surface</note>, not innate <note>inherent or essential to the core</note>, in the true substance of the earth, and, therefore, the globe as a whole does not heed them; neither are magnetic bodies drawn toward them, as is proved in the diagram of prominences.

## CHAPTER VI.

### THAT VARIATION AND DIRECTION ARE PRODUCED BY THE CONTROLLING FORCE OF THE EARTH AND THE ROTATORY MAGNETIC NATURE, NOT BY AN ATTRACTION OR A <term>COITION</term>, OR BY OTHER OCCULT CAUSE.

SINCE the lodestone is thought by ordinary philosophers to seize and snatch objects away, as it were, and since pretenders to science have, in fact, noticed no other properties except this much-praised force of attraction, they have therefore supposed that the entire movement to the north and south is produced by some natural force urging bodies along. But the Englishman Robert Norman first strove to show that this is not done by attraction; he, therefore, originated the idea of the "respective point," looking, as it were, toward hidden principles, and held that the magnetized needle always turns toward this, and not toward any point of attraction; but he was greatly in error, although he refuted the ancient false opinion about attraction. Norman proves his theory as follows: Take a round vessel full of water; on the middle of the water's surface, float a small bit of iron wire supported by just enough cork to keep it afloat while the water is in equilibrium; the wire must have first been magnetized so as to clearly show the variation point *D*. Let it remain in the water for a while. Clearly, the wire and its cork do not move toward the rim *D* of the vessel, as they would if attraction were acting on the iron from *D*, in which case the cork would move from its place. This assertion by the Englishman Robert Norman is demonstrable, and

## CHAPTER IX.

### WHETHER TERRESTRIAL LONGITUDE CAN BE FOUND FROM VARIATION.

THAT would be a welcome service to mariners and would greatly advance geography. But Porta (Book VII, Chap. 38) is deluded by a vain hope and by a baseless theory. For he thinks that, in moving along a meridian, the needle observes order and proportion, so that the closer it is to the east, the more it will deviate eastward, and, as you advance west, the needle takes a westerly direction: all of which is as false as can be. This is incorrect, for the needle’s departure from the geographic meridian (called its variation or declination) is marked for different points of the sea on the atlas of Andrea Bianco, which was made in the year 1436; but what Columbus really did discover was a line of no variation 2½° east of the island of Corvo on September 13, 1492” (A. M. Mayer, “The Earth a Great Magnet,” 1872, page 253).

See Thomas Browne, *Pseudodoxia Epidemica*, 1658, Book II, pages 68, 69.

# CAN LONGITUDE BE FOUND FROM VARIATION?

Then the <term>anatolism</term> (easting) begins to grow less as far as Helmshud, which place is not far from North Cape in Finmark: there the needle points to the north again. There are 60 degrees of longitude between Corvo and Helmshud, but the variation is greatest at Plymouth, whose longitude is 30 degrees." But although these statements are in part true, the compass does not point due north along the entire meridian of the island of Corvo. Neither is the variation 13 degrees 24 minutes at other places on the whole meridian of Plymouth, nor does the needle point to the true pole in other parts of the meridian of Helmshud. For, on the meridian passing through Plymouth at 60 degrees latitude, the north-by-east variation is greater; in 40 degrees latitude it is much less; and in 20 degrees latitude it is very small indeed. On the meridian of Corvo, although the variation near the island is zero, yet in 55 degrees latitude the variation north-by-west is about 1/2 <note>likely half a point of the compass</note>; in 20 degrees latitude the variation is 1/4 of a point toward the east. Hence the boundaries of variation are not properly defined by great meridian circles, and far less are the ratios of increase or decrease toward a given region of the heavens investigated by that method. Therefore the rules of <term>elattumen</term> (decreasing) or <term>auxanomen</term> (increasing), <term>anatolism</term> (easting) or <term>dysism</term> (westing), cannot possibly be found by that device. The grounds of variation in the southern regions of the earth, which Stevinus thereafter searches into in the same way, are utterly vain and absurd; they have been put forth by some Portuguese mariners, but they do not agree with investigations: equally absurd are various observations wrongly accepted as correct. ## CHAPTER X.

### WHY IN VARIOUS PLACES NEAR THE POLE THE VARIATIONS ARE MUCH GREATER THAN IN LOWER LATITUDES.

On the equator or near it, the variation of a needle is often trifling, and not unusually it is zero. In higher latitudes, such as 60, 70, or 80 degrees, the variations are not infrequently very great. The reason for this is found partly in the nature of the earth, and partly in the position of the <term>versorium</term>. The earth causes magnetic bodies to rotate and directs them strongly toward the poles at the equator; at the poles there is no direction, but only a fast <term>coition</term> of terminals that agree. Hence, directional force is weaker at the poles because the <term>versorium</term>, by reason of its tendency to turn toward the pole, dips greatly and is but feebly directed; however, the force of the lands and eminences is strong, with an energy proceeding from the entire earth, and, besides, the causes of variation are nearer: therefore the <term>versorium</term> deflects more toward those eminences. It must be known also that the direction of a <term>versorium</term> poised on a needle toward the plane of the horizon is much stronger at the equator than anywhere else by reason of the orientation of the <term>versorium</term>; and in proportion as latitude increases, the direction is less strong. For at the equator the <term>versorium</term> is directed naturally toward the plane of the horizon, but in other places it is forced to be in equilibrium

<summary>Gilbert explains that magnetic variation is minimal near the equator but becomes much larger at higher latitudes because the horizontal directional force of the needle weakens as it begins to dip toward the pole.</summary>
<keywords>magnetic variation, latitude, equator, versorium, coition, Stevinus, Grotius, magnetic dip</keywords>

--- Page 313 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on why magnetic variation is stronger near the poles, concluding Chapter X and beginning Chapter XI, which critiques Girolamo Cardan’s theories on the earth's center.</meta>

rium and remains in equilibrium because of an external force: by its nature it dips under the horizon as the latitude increases, as will be shown in the Book on Inclination or <term>Dip</term>. Therefore, direction becomes weaker and at the pole itself is zero. For this reason, a weak direction is easily overcome by powerful causes of variation, and near the pole the needle deflects more from the meridian. This is demonstrated with a <term>terrella</term>, on which is put an iron wire two finger-breadths long: the wire is quickly and strongly directed toward the poles on a meridian, but in the intervals between the equator and the pole it is directed weakly; herein we may see the great tendency toward variation near the poles.

### CHAPTER XI.

#### CARDAN’S ERROR IN SEEKING TO DETERMINE THE DISTANCE OF THE EARTH’S CENTRE FROM THE CENTRE OF THE WORLD BY MEANS OF THE LOADSTONE (IN HIS *De Proportionibus*, V).

How very easy it is to make mistakes and errors in the absence of trustworthy experiments, while investigating the hidden causes of things, is well shown by a gross blunder of Cardan. He thinks he has discovered the distances of the centers of the earth and the world through the variation of the magnetic needle over nine degrees; for he believed that the variation point on the horizon is everywhere distant eastward nine degrees from due north: on this basis he establishes a mathematical ratio of the different centers.

When the plank is placed accurately level with the horizon by using the leveling instrument and its plumb line (*instrumento plano cum suo perpendiculo*), turn the end of the pointer toward the north so that the <term>versorium</term> rests exactly on the centerline of its case, which aligns with the point of variation on the horizon. Afterward, at a convenient hour in the morning—8 or 9 o'clock—observe the tip of the shadow cast by the <term>stilus</term> when it reaches the nearest semicircle, and mark the position of the shadow's tip with chalk or ink. Now, move the pointer to 그 mark and record the number of the degree on the horizon indicated by the pointer. In the afternoon, watch for when the end of the shadow again reaches the edge of the same semicircle; then, move the pointer to the tip of the shadow and find the degree on the other side of the <term>lily</term>. From the difference in degrees, you find the variation: by subtracting the smaller number from the larger, half of the remainder is the arc of variation.

Many people attempt to determine the amount of variation with many other instruments and in many other ways, in conjunction with the mariner's compass—by using a globe, calculation, and the ratio of triangles and sines, provided the latitude is known and a single observation of the sun's altitude is made. However, these methods and means are of little advantage, for it is useless to seek through roundabout ways and intricate paths what you can find more quickly and surely by taking a shorter route. The whole secret consists in the proper use of the instruments by which the sun's position is determined easily and quickly (since the sun does not stand still but continues to move), for either the hand shakes, the eyesight is failing, or the instrument does not function correctly. Furthermore, observing the sun's altitude on both sides of the meridian is as easy as observing it on one side only while simultaneously determining the elevation of the

Nevertheless, these exercises of mathematical minds are praiseworthy. It is easy for anyone standing on land, by means of accurate observations and the use of suitable instruments, to determine the variation, especially in a relatively right sphere <note>a region where the celestial equator is at a right angle to the horizon, such as near the equator</note>; but at sea, due to the motion and the turning of the waters, experiments cannot be made with precision regarding degrees and minutes. As for us, we have devised a method of finding the variation by means of a convenient, handy instrument, based on the rising of certain stars, the rising or setting of the sun, or, in northern regions, from the pole-star. For at sea, when the ship is tossed by the waves, even the skilled observer determines the variation more surely with the help of a simple instrument that does not require extreme precision. Such an instrument is constructed as follows:

# FINDING THE AMOUNT OF THE VARIATION.

### *An instrument for finding the ortive amplitude on the horizon.*

Draw the circumference of a circle and divide it into quarters by two diameters intersecting at right angles. One of the diameters indicates the equinoctial circle, and the other the axis of the world. Divide the four quarters in the usual way, each into 90 degrees, and for every fifth or every tenth degree from each end of the two diameters in both directions, assign numbers on the two margins (outside of this circumference) provided for the purpose. Then, from each degree, draw a straight line parallel to the equator. Next, make a rule, or alidade, of the same length as the diameter of the circle and divided into exactly the same parts as the diameter which represents the axis of the world. In the middle of this rule, let a small projecting piece be left attached so that the middle of the *linea fiducialis* $^1$ of the rule may be connected with the center of the circle; and to each fifth or tenth part of the rule, give a number, beginning in the middle and numbering right and left. The circle represents the plane of the meridian; its center represents the exact point of rising or setting—that is, the intersection of the horizon and equator. All these lines equidistant from the equator represent the parallels of the sun and stars; the *linea fiducialis* of the rule or alidade represents the horizon, and its parts represent degrees of the horizon, beginning at the point of rising or setting. Therefore, if to the given latitude of the place, as numbered at each end of the diameter that represents the

In physics, the term fiducial denotes a fixed position or character, and is therefore used as a basis of reference or comparison ("Century Dictionary," 1889, Vol. II, page 2202, and Vol. III, page 3463. See also Noah Webster's "International Dictionary," 1891, page 556; L. N. Bescherelle, "Nouv. Dict. Nat.," 1887, Vol. II, page 1576; Larousse, "Dict. Universel," 1872, Vol. VIII, page 336; M. P. E. ## CHAPTER XIII.

### OBSERVATIONS MADE BY SEAMEN COMMONLY VARY AND ARE UNRELIABLE, PARTLY THROUGH MISTAKES AND LACK OF KNOWLEDGE AND THE IMPERFECTION OF THE INSTRUMENTS, AND PARTLY BECAUSE THE SEA IS SELDOM SO CALM THAT SHADOWS OR LIGHTS CAN REMAIN STEADY ON THE INSTRUMENTS.

FROM the time when the variation of the needle was first noticed, many alert navigators have in various ways strived to investigate the difference in the direction of the mariner’s compass; but this has not been done with the exactness that was necessary, much to the disadvantage of the art of navigation. For, either being uneducated, they knew of no sure method, or they used poorly constructed and unsuitable instruments, or they adopted some conjecture based merely on the false hypothesis of some prime meridian or magnetic pole; while many copy the writings of others and pass off the observations of earlier writers as their own. And these early authors—however foolish the writings in which they recorded their observations—are held in high respect simply because of their antiquity, and their successors consider it unsafe to differ from them. Hence on long voyages, especially to the East Indies, the inexact records of variation of the compass kept by the Portu-

## CHAPTER XIV.

### ABOUT THE VARIATION AT THE EQUATOR AND NEARBY.

In northern regions, the compass varies because of the northern landmasses; in southern regions, because of the southern landmasses. On the equator, if the landmasses on both sides were equal, there would be no variation. But because this seldom happens, variation is often observed even under the equator; and even at a distance of three or four degrees from the equator, variation may be produced by southern landmasses, if extensive and powerful southern continents lie nearby on one side.

---

## CHAPTER XVI.

### OF THE VARIATION IN NOVA ZEMBLA.

The variations are greatest in regions near the poles, as has been proved, and there, too, the changes of variation are sudden, as Dutch observers noted some years ago, though their observations were not exact; yet the inaccuracy can be excused, for, with ordinary instruments, it is hard to get at the truth in such high latitudes—about 80 degrees. But now the variation of the compass gives clear evidence of the existence of an open passage eastward through the North Sea—the Arctic Ocean (*Mare Scythicum*); for, since the compass has so great an arc of variation to the west, it is evident that no continent stretches for any great distance along that whole route eastward. Therefore, we can strive and explore more hopefully for a passage to the Moluccas by the northeast than by the northwest.

## CHAPTER XVII.

### VARIATION IN THE SOUTH SEA.

After passing through the Strait of Magellan, the variation off the Peruvian coast is toward the southeast; and a similar deflection continues all along the coast of Peru to the equator. In higher latitudes, up to 45 degrees, the variation is greater than near the equator; and, just as on the eastern coast of South America the deflection was from south toward west, so now it is toward the southeast. From the equator northward, the variation is very small or nonexistent until you reach New Galicia; from there, along the whole coast as far as Quivira, the inclination is from the north to the east.

### CHAPTER XIX.

### THE VARIATION IN THE INTERIOR OF THE GREAT CONTINENTS.

GREAT seas usually have great variations; in some parts, however, there is no variation, but a true direction toward the pole. On the continents, too, the needle often deflects from the meridian, such as on the coastlines and borders, but the arc of variation is usually small: in the middle regions of great continents there is no variation. Hence, in the heart of northern Europe and of Asia, in the interior of Africa, Peru, and of North or Mexican America, the <term>versorium</term> rests on the meridian.

# CHAPTER XX.

## THE VARIATION IN THE EASTERN OCEAN.

The variation in the Eastern Ocean, all the way to Goa and the Moluccas, is noted by the Portuguese, but they are mistaken in very many points; for they follow the first observers who recorded the variations for various places, determined by the use of unfit instruments, by inaccurate observations, or by conjecture. Thus in the island of Brandö¹ they claim the compass varies 22 degrees to the northwest. Now, in no region, in no place on earth that does not have a higher latitude than that, is the variation as much as 22 degrees: in fact the deviation on that island is trifling. So, when they say that in Mozambique the compass varies to the northwest one point, they are in error even though the compass they use is that of Portugal; for, without a doubt, the needle varies in Mozambique to the southwest one quarter of a point or more. Again, they are all wrong in holding that beyond the equator, on the route toward Goa, the compass varies westward one point and one half; it would have been better if they had said that in the first part of the route the Portuguese compass inclines one point, but that a <term>meridional compass</term> varies only one-half point. Yet to determine the amount of the variation in the Eastern Ocean according to our rules, we need a more exact and correct reconnaissance of the <term>austral continent</term>, which stretches farther from the south toward the <term>equinoctial</term> than it is described in current charts and globes.

---

¹ <note>The island of Brandö lies in the Gulf of Bothnia, close by the east coast of Sweden.</note>

# CHAPTER XXI.

## HOW THE DEVIATION OF THE NEEDLE IS GREATER OR LESS ACCORDING TO THE DISTANCES OF PLACES.

In the heart of great continents there is no variation; similarly, there is none in the middle of great oceans. On the edges of such lands and seas, the variation is often large, though not as great as it is a short distance out at sea. For instance, off Cape Sao Agostino there is variation, but 50 miles to the east the variation is larger; it is larger still 80 miles away and 100 miles away. However, starting from a distance of 100 miles, the reduction of the deviation is slower as you approach the continent than it is from 80 miles away, and slower from 80 miles than from 50; for the deviation changes and reduces somewhat more quickly as you approach the shore from nearby than from afar. Thus, for mariners approaching Newfoundland, the variation changes more quickly (that is, a degree of variation is lost over a smaller arc of the route along a parallel) when they are near land than when they are 100 miles away; but when they travel inland, the changes are slower at first than when they penetrate further into the interior.

The figure shows the ratio of the arcs on a parallel circle as a <term>versorium</term> is brought toward a continent that reaches to the pole; the ratio corresponds to the degrees of variation. At *D*, the variation is greatest because there the needle is attracted—or is caused by the whole earth to turn—toward the projecting land *B*. There, the needle is neither hindered, nor checked, nor led toward

You sail more miles on the parallel circle *CD* as long as you are near *C* to record one degree of variation than you sail when near *D*; so, too, in traveling from *D* toward *E*, you must cover a greater number of miles when near *D* than when near *E*. Thus, there are equal deviations for unequal distances sailed, both for increasing and decreasing variation; yet it decreases within a smaller space than it increases. There are, however, several other incidental factors that complicate this ratio.

## CHAPTER I.

### OF THE DIP OF THE MAGNETIC NEEDLE.

We come at last to that excellent experiment, that wonderful movement of magnetic bodies as they dip beneath the horizon by virtue of their natural <term>verticity</term>; after we have mastered this, the wondrous combination, harmony, and concordant interaction of the earth and the loadstone (or magnetized iron), being made manifest by our theory, stand revealed. This motion we have so illustrated and demonstrated with many experiments, and intend in what follows to point out the causes and reasons so clearly, that no one endowed with reason and intelligence may justly scorn, refute, or dispute our fundamental magnetic principles. Direction, as well as variation, is demonstrated on the plane of the horizon whenever a magnetic needle, balanced in equilibrium, comes to a rest at any fixed point on it. But inclination (dip) is seen to be the motion of the iron bar—first balanced on its axis and then excited by a loadstone—from that point in the

Obtain a smooth, circular board with a diameter of at least six finger-lengths, which is to be fastened to one face of an upright square post and rested on a wooden base. In the center of the instrument, drive a brass nail, and in the center of its head, drill a small hole that is well-reamed and smoothed. Attach to the instrument a circle or ring of brass about two finger-breadths wide, with a transverse plate or flat bar of the same metal fastened across the middle of the ring to serve as the <term>horizon</term>. In the middle of this horizon bar, drill another hole that is exactly opposite the center of the instrument where the first hole was drilled. Next, get a steel wire such as is used for compass needles. At its exact middle and at right angles to it, pass a very thin iron axis through it so that the middle of the axis and the middle of the needle meet exactly. # DIP OF THE MAGNETIC NEEDLE.

Just as with the lodestone in our demonstration, so in this inclination (dip) the agreement between the globe of the Earth and the lodestone is positive and manifest. The true and definite cause of this great and previously unknown effect is as follows: The lodestone moves and rotates until one of its poles, being drawn toward the north, comes to rest at its fixed point on the horizon; the pole that comes to a stop facing north is (as shown in the previous rules and demonstrations) southern, not northern, although until now everyone has assumed it to be northern because it turns toward the north. An iron wire or <term>versorium</term> touched by this pole of the stone turns south, and is made northern because it was rubbed at the south end of the stone; likewise, when the point of a <term>versorium</term> is magnetized in that way, it will be directed toward the Earth’s south pole and turn toward it, while the other end (the crotch) will be southern and will turn toward the northern regions of the Earth (the Earth itself causing the motion). For in this way, direction results from the orientation of the stone and the needle, and from the Earth’s <term>verticity</term>. But inclination (dip) occurs when the needle turns toward the body of the Earth, with its south end pointed toward the north, in any latitude away from the equator. For it is a fixed and unchanging law that exactly beneath the celestial equator, or rather on the equator of the terrestrial globe, the magnetic inclination or dip of the needle is *zero*; and in whatever way it may have been energized or rubbed, it rests exactly on the horizontal plane in the inclination instrument, provided it is first properly balanced. The reason for this is that the needle, being at an equal distance from the two poles, does not dip toward either during its rotation, but remains balanced, pointing toward the level of the equator, just as it does when mounted on a sharp point or floating freely and unhindered on water.

But when the needle is at any latitude away from the equator, or

The rim of the cavity in the block represents a meridian circle, and some meridian circle of the <term>terrella</term> corresponds to it, for the poles on both sides are upon the inner circumference of the rim. This is precisely what takes place on the earth itself where there is no variation; but when there is variation either of direction or of dip—that is, a disruption of the proper magnetic rotation for causes to be explained later—then there is some difference. ## CHAPTER IV.

### ON A SUITABLE LENGTH OF NEEDLE ON THE TERRELLA FOR SHOWING THE DIP.

When one seeks to define the dip by means of a dip-indicating instrument on the earth itself, we may use either a short <term>versorium</term> or one of any length, provided only that the magnetic property of the <term>loadstone</term> with which it has been rubbed is able to pervade its whole substance and length. For the greatest length of a <term>versorium</term>, as compared with the earth’s diameter, is insignificant and has no ratio perceptible by the senses. But on a <term>terrella</term>, or on a plane near a meridian of a <term>terrella</term>, a short needle is required—one barleycorn’s length; for longer <term>versoria</term> (because they reach farther) descend suddenly and irregularly in the first degrees of dip and turn toward the body of the <term>terrella</term>. For example, as soon as the long <term>versorium</term> in the figure is moved onward from the equator *A* to *C*, it lays hold of the stone with its point *C* as if with a long outspread wing, when the point reaches the parts around *B*, which give it a greater rotation than those at *C*. # CHAPTER V.

## THAT DIP IS NOT CAUSED BY THE ATTRACTION OF A LOADSTONE, BUT BY ITS POWER OF GIVING DIRECTION AND ROTATION.

Throughout nature we must recognize that wondrous work of the Creator whereby the principal bodies are restricted within particular localities and, as it were, hedged around with fences, as nature ordains. Hence it is that heavenly bodies do not get confused in their motions and in their progressions

beyond each other. Similarly, magnetic revolutions are produced by the force of a greater and dominant body as well as by that of a lesser and subject body, even though the latter may be of very small volume. For the work is not done by attraction but by incitation on the part of both, and that with a proportionate movement toward fixed points beyond which there is no further motion. For if the <term>versorium</term> dipped under the action of an attractive force, then a <term>terrella</term> fashioned out of a very powerful loadstone would pull it toward itself more than one made of an ordinary loadstone would, and iron stroked by a strong loadstone would have a greater dip; but that is never the case. Further, a piece of iron attached to and projecting from the <term>terrella</term> at any latitude does not cause a small iron bar to rise more toward the perpendicular than the unarmed stone does, even though the stone, when so armed <note>An "armed" loadstone is one fitted with iron caps, or an armature, to increase its lifting power.</note>, seizes and lifts far heavier weights. But if a loadstone is fashioned somewhat into a point at one end and is rather blunt at the other, the sharp end or pole draws magnetized iron with greater force, while the blunt, thick end makes the iron turn toward itself more powerfully. However, a spherical stone makes it * turn to itself powerfully and in a true direction according to magnetic laws and the form of spheres; while a loadstone of some length from pole to pole stirs the <term>versorium</term> unequally, for in such a stone the pole of the <term>versorium</term> is always pointed toward the pole of the loadstone itself. So, too, if the loadstone takes a disk shape, with the poles in the circumference but with a flat and not spherical body: when the flat surface is brought near to the <term>versorium</term>, the <term>versorium</term> does not move with the regular magnetic movement as it does with a <term>terrella</term>, but turns around, always pointing toward the pole of the loadstone situated on the circumference of the disk. Besides, if the stone caused the <term>versorium</term> to revolve by attraction, then in the first degrees of latitude it would attract it toward the mass

For here the point of a <term>versorium</term> at a low latitude neither touches the stone nor comes into <term>coition</term> with it, but only inclines toward it. Furthermore, when the <term>versorium</term> rotates as it dips, the pole of the <term>versorium</term> is not stayed or held by the pole of the earth or the <term>terrella</term>, but revolves regularly. It does not remain at any fixed point or boundary, nor does it look straight toward the pole toward which the center of the <term>versorium</term> moves, except at the pole itself, and that only once between the pole and the equator; instead, the inclination continues as the change in the position of the center produces a dip in conformity with magnetic laws. The dip of the needle in water, demonstrated later, is also constant: the needle does not dip toward the bottom of the vessel, but stands poised on its center in a middle direction according to its proper dip; yet this would not be the case if the earth or its poles caused the end of the needle to dip by means of attraction.

<summary>Gilbert argues that magnetic dip is not caused by a simple attractive pull toward the poles, but by a rotational alignment according to magnetic laws. He supports this by observing that a magnetized needle in water remains poised in its dip rather than being pulled toward the bottom of the container.</summary>

## CHAPTER VI.

### OF THE RATIO OF DIP TO LATITUDE AND THE CAUSES THEREOF.

WE have spoken of the construction of the instrument for determining the dip, of the causes and modes of the dip, and of the different inclinations of the needle for different localities; of the inclination of the loadstone, too, and of an instrument for showing the power of the stone at any latitude, as well as of the demonstrated rotation (by standing upright) of pieces of iron on a meridian of the stone, according to latitude. We have now to treat more at length of the causes of this proportionate inclination. A loadstone and a piece of iron wire, when moved along a meridian from the equator to the pole, turn toward a spherical loadstone—and toward the earth also—with a circular motion. In a right horizon (as also upon the equinoctial circle of the stone) the axis of the iron, which is its middle, is a line parallel with the earth's axis. When that axis reaches the pole, which is its center, it stands still in the same straight line with the earth's axis. The same end of the iron that at the equator points south turns to the north; for it is not a movement of center to center, but of one magnetic body to another, and a natural turning of the axis of the body to the axis of the <term>terrella</term>, not caused by the pole's attraction in a way that the iron should look toward the earth's polar point. On the equator the magnetic iron stands in horizontal equilibrium, but toward the pole on either side of the equator, at every latitude from the
