# CHAPTER VII.

## EXPLANATION OF THE DIAGRAM OF THE ROTATION OF MAGNETIZED IRON.

LET *ACDL* be the body of the earth or of a <term>terrella</term>, *M* the center, *AD* the equator, *CL* the axis, and *AB* the horizon, which changes according to the locality. From point *F* in the horizon, at a distance from the equator *A* equal to the semi-diameter *CM* of the earth or <term>terrella</term>, an arc is described to *H* as the endpoint of the quadrants of dip: for all quadrants of dip that serve the regions between *A* and *C* begin at that arc and terminate in the earth’s center, *M*. The semi-diameter of this arc is a chord drawn from the equator *A* to the pole *C*. And a line equal to that chord, drawn in the horizon to *B*, gives the starting point of the arc of the endpoints of the arcs of revolution and rotation, which arc is continued on to *G*. For just as the quadrant of a circle around the earth’s center (the starting point of it being in the horizon, at a distance from the equator equal to the earth’s semi-diameter) is the endpoint of all the quadrants of dip produced from every horizon to the center, so a circle around the center from the starting point of the first arc of rotation *B* to *G* is the endpoint of the arcs of rotation. Between the arc of rotation *BL* and *BG* are intermediate arcs of revolution and rotation of the magnetic needle. The center of the arc is the region or place where the observation is obtained; the beginning of the arc is taken from the circle that is the endpoint of the revolutions, and it ends at the opposite pole, as from *O* to *L*,

It defines the specific arcs, points, and measurements—such as the semi-diameter and horizon—that dictate how magnetized iron aligns with the earth's magnetic field.</summary>

in 45 degrees latitude. Divide any arc of revolution into 90 equal parts from the endpoint of the arcs of revolution to the pole. Whatever the degree of latitude of the place, that part of the arc of revolution is considered to correspond to it, which the magnetic pole points toward as it rotates on or around the <term>terrella</term> or the earth. In the large diagram that follows, this is indicated by straight lines. In the middle latitude of 45 degrees, the magnetic rotation is directed toward the equator, and there the arc from its endpoint to the pole is a quadrant of a circle. However, at latitudes above this (*ante hunc*, i.e., nearer the equator), all the arcs of revolution are greater than a quadrant; at latitudes below this (*post hunc*, i.e., higher, farther from the equator), they are less. In the former case, the needle rotates quickly; in the latter, it gradually rotates more slowly. Each region has its own arc of revolution. Within this arc is the endpoint toward which the needle turns, according to the numerical degree of latitude of the place. Therefore, a straight line drawn from the region to a point in that arc corresponding to the numerical degree of latitude indicates the magnetic direction; it also shows the degree of inclination at the intersection of the quadrant of dip that serves (*inservit*) that specific region. Subtract the arc of the quadrant of dip (from the center to the line of magnetic direction), and what remains is the arc of dip beneath the horizon. Thus, in the rotation of the <term>versorium</term> *N*, whose line of magnetic direction extends to *D*, if you subtract arc *RM* from the quadrant of dip *SM*, what remains will be the arc of dip—that is, it shows how much the needle dips at 45 degrees latitude.

->*Observing the magnetic dip at sea.*<-

Place the dip instrument upon our variation instrument, with a wooden ball being placed between the round movable compass box and the dip instrument; but first remove (*eximito*) the versorium <note>Gilbert's term for a pivoted magnetic needle.</note>, so that it does not interfere with the dip instrument. In this way, when the sea is in motion, the compass box will remain upright on the level of the horizon. The dip compass is to be directed, by means of a small versorium at its base, to the point of the variation; the plane of the upright compass conforms to the great circle of that variation (commonly called the magnetic meridian). Thus, the dip instrument, by virtue of its rotational property, shows the degree of the dip.

*In a dip instrument, the magnetic needle which descends when on a meridian circle hangs perpendicular when it lies on a parallel.*

The magnetic needle, in its proper position, while it aligns itself with the earth by its rotational property, dips to a certain extent in an oblique sphere <note>An "oblique sphere" refers to locations between the equator and the poles where the celestial or magnetic poles are at an angle to the horizon.</note>. But when the plane of the instrument is moved from the plane of the meridian, the needle (which points poleward) no longer remains at the degree of its dip, but inclines more toward the center, for the directional force is greater than the dip force; and all power of dip is taken away if the plane of the instrument is on a parallel. For then the needle, its axis being transverse, cannot take its proper position, and so points perpendicular to the earth and remains only in its own meridian, or in what is commonly called the magnetic meridian.

# CHAPTER IX.

## DEMONSTRATION OF DIRECTION, OR OF VARIATION FROM THE TRUE DIRECTION, TOGETHER WITH DIP, SIMPLY BY THE MOVEMENT IN WATER, DUE TO THE POWER OF CONTROLLING AND ROTATING.

Pass through a round cork three finger-breadths of thin iron *wire*, so that the cork may support the iron in water. Let the water be contained in a vase or large glass goblet. With a very sharp knife, pare the cork away gradually (still preserving its roundness) until it stands motionless a finger-breadth or two under the surface, with the wire evenly balanced. Then stroke one end of the wire on the north pole of a loadstone, and the other end on the south pole (very carefully, so that the cork is not moved even slightly out of its place), and put the instrument back in the water. The wire will dip with a circular movement on its center below the plane of the horizon, according to the latitude of the place; and even as it dips, it will show (the true direction being disrupted) the point of variation.

The loadstone with which it is rubbed should be a powerful one, such as is required in all magnetic demonstrations.

When the wire, having been thus placed in the water and treated with the loadstone, comes to a standstill in the line of the dip, its lower end remains at the point of variation in an arc of a great circle, or meridian, passing through the zenith, the point of variation on the horizon, and through that lowermost point of the heavens called the nadir. # CHAPTER X.

## OF VARIATION OF DIP.

WE have already spoken of direction and of variation as a sort of derangement of direction. Now we observe a similar irregular movement in the dip, when it descends below the limits or when, as sometimes happens, it does not reach its proper bounds. Thus, the variation of the dip is an arc of the magnetic meridian between the true and the apparent dip. For just as magnetized bodies are pulled to one side because of the earth's elevations, so too the needle (its rotation being slightly increased) dips beyond the proper measure. And as variation is a deviation in direction, so, for the same reason, there is some error of dip, although it is usually a minor one. Sometimes, too, even if there is no variation of direction on the horizon, there may nevertheless be a variation of the dip; namely, when some magnetically powerful mass of earth projects directly on the meridian line (that is, on the meridian itself), or when such elevations have less force than is required by the general con-

## CHAPTER XI.

### OF THE FORMAL MAGNETIC ACT SPHERICALLY POURED FORTH.

<margin>*</margin> WE have repeatedly spoken of the poles of the earth and the terrella and of the equinoctial circle; most recently, we treated the dip of magnetized bodies toward the earth and toward the terrella, and the causes for it. But having labored long and hard with various and numerous devices to reach the cause of this dip, we have by good fortune discovered a new and admirable science of the spheres themselves—a science surpassing the marvels of all magnetic virtues. For such is the property of magnetic spheres that their force is poured forth and diffused beyond their surfaces spherically, the form being elevated above the bounds of physical nature; and the mind that has diligently studied this natural philosophy will discover the definite causes of the movements and revolutions. The powers of a terrella, too, are of the same kind throughout the whole sphere of its influence, and the spheres (of influence) themselves, at whatever distance from the body of the

terrella, have, in proportion to their diameter and the amount of their surface area, limits to their forces; or, in other words, there are points where magnetic bodies turn toward them. These bodies do not point toward the same part or point of the terrella at every distance from it (unless they are on the axis of the spheres and the terrella), but instead always tend toward those points on the spheres (of influence) that are at an equal distance along an arc from their common axis. It is by these spheres and in accordance with their size that it is made to rotate and is directed, both while its center stands still and while it moves along any arc of that sphere. Still, we do not mean that the magnetic forms and spheres exist in the air, water, or any other non-magnetic medium, as though the air or water adopted them or were shaped by them; for the forms are only poured out and actually exist when magnetic bodies are present. Hence, a magnetic body within the forces and limits of the spheres is affected, and in the various spheres, magnetic bodies control and stimulate other magnetic bodies just as if the spheres of influence were solid material loadstones. For the magnetic force does not travel through the whole of the medium, nor does it exist as it would in a continuous body; so the spheres are magnetic, yet they are not physical spheres existing on their own.

### DEMONSTRATION.

Upon the instrument diagram described above, place a small board or a strong disk of brass or tin on which the magnetic spheres are inscribed, as shown in the diagram. In the middle, make a hole proportioned to the size of the <term>terrella</term>, so that the board may lie evenly on the middle of it along the meridian circle above the wood. Then, in one of the spheres of influence, place a small <term>versorium</term> one barleycorn long. As the versorium moves into various positions within that same circle, it will always correspond to the dimensions of that sphere rather than those of the <term>terrella</term>, as seen in the diagram of the effused magnetic forms. While some writers suggest that the causes of the loadstone's wonderful effects are the hidden and mysterious virtues of things, and others regard a property of the loadstone’s substance as the cause, we have discovered the primary substantial form—not in some vague approximation of truth or in controversial reasoning, but, as in many other demonstrations, through this most indisputable diagram of the magnetic forces effused by the form. Here, we grasp the true efficient cause. And this form, though it is perceived by none of our senses and is therefore less perceptible to the intellect, now appears manifest and visible before our very eyes through this formal act, which proceeds from it just as light proceeds from a source of light. And here it should be noted that a magnetic needle moved over the earth, over a <term>terrella</term>, or over the effused spheres, rotates completely twice in one circuit of its center, like an <term>epicycle</term> around its circle.

### CHAPTER XII.

#### THE MAGNETIC FORCE IS ANIMATE, OR IMITATES A SOUL; IN MANY RESPECTS IT SURPASSES THE HUMAN SOUL WHILE THAT IS UNITED TO AN ORGANIC BODY.

The loadstone is shown through many experiments to be wonderful and, as it were, animate. This one prominent property is the same as that which the ancients believed to be a soul in the heavens, in the globes, in the stars, and in the sun and moon. For they believed that such diverse movements could not be produced, nor such vast bodies revolve in fixed times, nor such wonderful powers be infused into other bodies without a divine and animate nature; by this means, the whole world flourishes with the most beautiful diversity through this primary form of the globes themselves. The ancient philosophers—such as Thales, Heraclitus, Anaxagoras, Archelaus, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Parmenides, Plato, and all the Platonists (and not just Greek philosophers, but also the Egyptians and Chaldeans)—all seek a certain universal soul in the world and declare the entire world to be endowed with a soul. Aristotle held that the universe is not animate, but the heavens only; he claimed his elements were inanimate, but the stars were animate to him. As for us, we find this soul only in the globes and in their <term>homogenic</term> parts; and although this soul is not the same in all globes (for that in the sun or in certain stars is much superior to that in other less noble globes), nevertheless, the souls in very many globes agree in their powers. ## CHAPTER I.

### OF THE GLOBE OF EARTH AS A LOADSTONE.

UNTIL now we have spoken of the loadstone and magnetic bodies, how they work together and act on each other, and how they align themselves with the terrella and the earth. ### CHAPTER II.

#### THE MAGNETIC AXIS OF THE EARTH REMAINS INVARIABLE.

THE earth’s magnetic axis, just as it passed through the center of the earth in the very beginnings of the moving world, so today it extends through the center to the same points on the surface, with the equinoctial line and plane also remaining the same. For these natural boundaries cannot be altered except by a vast destruction of the terrestrial mass, as is easily shown by magnetic demonstrations. Therefore, the opinion held by Dominicus Maria of Ferrara—a man of rare ability and the teacher of Nicolaus Copernicus—is to be rejected. It was based on certain observations and was as follows: “Some years ago,” he writes, “while considering Ptolemy’s geography, I found the elevations of the north pole given by him for several regions to fall short by one degree and ten minutes of what they are in our time. This difference can by no means be attributed to an error in the table, for it is not believable that the whole book should be equally wrong throughout the figures contained in the tables; therefore, we must suppose the north pole has been brought toward the vertical point. Thus, a long-term observation began to disclose to us things hidden from our ancestors—not through any laziness on their part, but because they lacked observations over a long period by their predecessors. For the elevations of the pole were observed in very few places before Ptolemy’s time, as he himself testifies in the beginning of his *Cosmographia*: ‘Hipparchus alone,’ he writes, ‘has handed down to us the latitudes of a few places; but many

The Pythagorean Philolaus held that the earth was one of the stars and turned in an oblique circle toward the fire, just as the sun and moon have their paths. Philolaus was an illustrious mathematician and a very experienced investigator of nature. But when philosophy began to be handled by many and was made public, then theories adapted to the understanding of the common crowd, or supported by sophistical subtleties, found their way into the minds of many; like a torrent, they swept everything before them once they had gained favor with the multitude. Consequently, many fine discoveries of the ancients were rejected and discredited—or at the very least, they were no longer studied and developed.

Therefore, Copernicus was the first among the moderns (a man most worthy of the highest scholarly praise) who undertook to illustrate the *phenomena* of bodies in motion with new hypotheses. These logical demonstrations are either followed or observed by other authors—men highly knowledgeable in all types of learning—to more surely discover the alleged (*φαινομένην*) “symphony” of motion. Thus, the suppositions and purely imaginary spheres postulated by Ptolemy and others to determine the times and periods of movements do not necessarily have to be accepted in the physical lectures of philosophers.

It is, then, an ancient opinion handed down from olden times—but now developed by great thinkers—that the whole earth completes a diurnal rotation in the span of twenty-four hours. But since we see the sun, the moon, the other planets, and the whole heavenly host appear and disappear within the span of one day, then either the earth whirls in a daily motion from west to east, or the entire heavens and the rest of the universe necessarily speed around from east to west. In the first place, it is not probable that the highest heaven and all those visible splendors of the fixed stars are swept around in this rapid, headlong career. Besides, what genius has ever found in one and the same (Ptolemaic) sphere those stars which we call fixed, or has ever given rational proof that there are any such adamantine spheres at all? No man has ever shown this; nor is there any doubt that just as the planets are at various distances from the earth, so, too, are those mighty and multitudinous luminaries arranged at various heights and at distances most remote from the earth. They are not set in any spherical framework or firmament (as is supposed), nor in any vaulted structure. 

As for the intervals (between the spheres) imagined by some authors, they are matters of speculation, not of fact; those other intervals do far surpass them and are far more remote. And, situated as they are in the heavens, at various distances, in the thinnest ether, or in that most subtle <term>fifth essence</term>, or in a vacuum—how shall the stars keep their places in the mighty swirl of these enormous spheres composed of a substance about which no one knows anything? 

Astronomers have observed 1022 stars; besides these, innumerable other stars appear minute to our senses. Regarding still others, our sight grows dim, and they are hardly discernible except by the keenest eye. Nor is there any man possessing the best power of vision who will not—while the moon is below the horizon and the atmosphere is clear—feel that there are many more stars, indeterminable and flickering by reason of their faint light, obscured because of the distance. Hence, we may well believe that these are many and that they can never be fully taken in by the eye. What, then, is the inconceivably great space between us and these remotest fixed stars? And what is the vast, immeasurable amplitude and height of the imaginary sphere in which they are supposed to be set? How far away from the earth

It is evident, therefore, that all the heavenly bodies are set in their destined places; within them are gathered whatever elements tend toward their own centers, and around them all their parts are assembled. But if they have motion, it will be the motion of each around its own center, like the earth’s rotation; or it will be by a progression in an orbit, like that of the moon. In such a vast and scattered flock, there will be no single circular motion. And among the stars, those situated near the equator would seem to be carried around with the greatest speed, while others nearer the pole have a slower movement; and still others, as if motionless, have only a small revolution. Yet no differences in their light, mass, or color are perceptible to us; for they are just as brilliant, clear, resplendent, or faint (dark, *fuscæ*) toward the poles as they are near the equator and the zodiac. Yet in times past, it was supported by the calculation and comparison of movements and was generally accepted by mathematicians, while the nagging rabble of pseudo-philosophers egged them on.

The motions of the heavenly bodies (that is, of the planets) all seem to be eastward, following the order of the zodiac signs; and mathematicians and common philosophers also believe that the fixed stars progress in the same way with a very slow movement. Because of their ignorance of the truth, they feel compelled to add a ninth sphere to these stars. But now this inadmissible *primum mobile*—this fiction, this something beyond any logical reasoning and evidenced by no visible star, being purely a product of imagination and mathematical hypothesis accepted and believed by philosophers and elevated into the heavens far beyond all the stars—must necessarily, by a contrary impulse, wheel from east to west, against the tendency of all the rest of the universe.

Whatever in nature moves naturally is impelled by its own forces and by a harmonious agreement with other bodies. Such is the motion of parts toward a whole, and of the globes and stars throughout the universe in accord with each other; such is the circular propulsion of the planets' bodies, each observing and encouraging the other's path. But regarding this *primum mobile* with its opposing and most rapid course—where are the bodies that encourage it or propel it? Where is the nature that acts in concert with it? And what mad force lies beyond the *primum mobile*? For the <term>agent force</term> resides in the bodies themselves, not in space, and not in the voids between them.

For on the convexity of the firmament, it would travel over more than eighteen hundred such circles; but what structure of iron can be imagined so strong or so tough that it would not be wrecked and shattered to pieces by such mad and unimaginable velocity? The Chaldeans believed the heavens to be light. But in light there is no such firmness—not in the fire-firmament of Plotinus, nor in the fluid or watery heavens of God-inspired Moses, nor in the supremely thin and transparent firmament that stands between our eyes and the lights of the stars but does not block them. # THE EARTH HAS A CIRCULAR MOTION.

From these arguments, therefore, we infer with certainty, and not with mere probability, the daily rotations of the earth; for nature always acts with fewer rather than with many means; and because it is more accordant with reason that the one small body, the earth, should make a daily revolution than that the whole universe should be whirled around it. I pass over the earth’s other movements, for here we treat only of the daily rotation, by which it turns toward the sun and produces the natural day (of twenty-four hours) which we call *nycthemeron*. And, indeed, nature would seem to have given a motion quite in harmony with the shape of the earth, for since the earth is a globe, it is far easier and far more fitting that it should revolve on its natural poles than that the whole universe—whose boundaries we do not know and cannot know—should be whirled around. It is easier and more fitting than that there should be fashioned a sphere of the <term>primum mobile</term>—a concept not accepted by the ancients, and which even Aristotle never thought of or admitted as existing beyond the sphere of the fixed stars; finally, it is a concept which the Holy Scriptures do not recognize, just as they do not recognize a revolution of the entire firmament.

<meta>This page continues the argument for the Earth's daily rotation, specifically focusing on how the magnetic behavior of the Earth's parts (lodestones) demonstrates an inherent capacity for circular motion that reflects the movement of the entire planet.</meta>

# THE EARTH HAS A CIRCULAR MOTION.

A lodestone placed in a wooden vessel is put in water so that it may float freely, rotate, and move about. If the pole *B* of the lodestone is made to point, unnaturally, toward the south *F*, the <term>terrella</term> revolves around its center in a circular motion on the plane of the horizon toward the north *E*, where it comes to rest, and not at *C* or at *D*. So acts a small stone weighing only four ounces; and a powerful lodestone of 100 pounds will make the same movement just as quickly; and the largest mountain of lodestone would revolve in the same way were it to be set afloat on a wide stream or in the deep sea; and yet a magnetic body is far more hindered by water than the whole earth is by the air. The whole earth would act in the same way, were the north pole turned aside from its true direction; for that pole would go back, in the circular motion of the whole, toward <term>Cynosura</term>.

Yet this motion is nothing but that circular motion by which the parts naturally tend to their own places. The whole earth aligns with <term>Cynosura</term> by its steadfast nature; and similarly each true part of the earth seeks a similar place in the world, and turns with circular motion to that position. The natural movements of the whole and of the parts are alike: hence, since the parts move in a circle, the whole, too, has the power of circular motion. A spherical lodestone, when floated in water, moves circularly on its center to become (as it seems) conformed to the earth on the plane of the equator. Thus, too, would it move on any other great circle if it were free to move, so that in the <term>dip compass</term> there is circular movement on the meridian (if there is no variation), or, if there is variation, on a great circle drawn from the zenith through the variation point.

But if, by the daily rotation of the earth, the moon did not pass quickly, the sea would rise excessively in some parts and many coasts would be overwhelmed by mighty tides. Therefore, lest the earth should perish and be destroyed in various ways, she rotates by virtue of her magnetic and primary energy. Such are the movements in the rest of the planets, with the motion and light of other bodies especially urging them. For the moon also turns around during its <term>menstrual circuit</term> <note>monthly orbit</note> so that it may successively receive the sun's light on all its parts—light which it enjoys and with which it is refreshed, just like the earth itself. Nor could the moon, without grave harm and certain destruction, endure the unceasing fall of light on only one of its sides.

Thus, each of the moving globes has circular motion, either in a great circular orbit, or on its own axis, or in both ways. But the idea that all the fixed stars, the planets, and all the higher heavens revolve simply for the earth's sake is a ridiculous supposition to the mind of a philosopher. Therefore, the earth revolves and not the whole heavens; this movement brings growth and decay, provides the occasion for the generation of living things, and arouses internal heat to productiveness. Because of this, matter flourishes to receive forms, and from this primary revolution of the earth, natural bodies receive their first impulse and original action. ## CHAPTER V.

### ARGUMENTS OF THOSE WHO DENY THE EARTH'S MOTION; AND REFUTATION THEREOF.

It will not be unnecessary to also weigh the arguments of those who deny that the earth moves, so that we may better satisfy the crowd of philosophers who believe that the stability and immobility of the globe are proved by undeniable arguments. Aristotle does not allow that the earth moves in a circle; for, he says, if it did, then every part of it would have the same motion. But since all separated parts tend toward the center in straight lines, he argues that circular motion would be something imposed by force, would be contrary to nature, and would not be perpetual. But we have already proven that all true parts of the earth do move circularly, and that all magnetic bodies (when properly arranged) are carried around in a circle. Planetary globes do not move in a circle around the center of the earth; nor is the earth the center—even if it were at the center—but rather a body positioned around the center.

And it is inconsistent that the Peripatetics' heavenly bodies should depend on something as frail and perishable as the earth's center.

Now creation results from motion, and without motion all nature would be sluggish. The sun's motions and the moon's motions produce changes; the earth's motion awakens the inner life of the globe; animals themselves do not live without motion and the constant working of the heart and the arteries. As for the claim that the only movement in the earth is a single motion in a straight line toward the center, and that the movement of an individual body is unique and solitary—the arguments for this have no weight. This is because motion in a straight line is merely the tendency toward their origin, not just for the earth, but also for the components of the sun, the moon, and all other celestial bodies; however, these also move in a circle. <term>Joannes Costeus</term>, who is uncertain about the cause of the earth's motion, considers the magnetic energy to be internal, active, and controlling; he holds the sun to be an external motivating cause; nor is the earth so lowly and worthless a body as it is commonly rumored to be. Therefore, according to him, the <term>diurnal motion</term> is produced by the earth, for the earth's sake and for the earth's benefit.

Those (if they exist) who assert that this movement of the earth takes place not only in longitude but also in latitude speak nonsense; for nature has established definite poles in the earth and has set fixed, rather than chaotic, revolutions. Thus the moon revolves toward the sun in its monthly course, while always pointing its specific poles toward specific parts of the heavens. As for the objection that the surface unevenness produced by mountains and valleys would prevent daily rotation, it is of no weight; for mountains do not ruin the roundness of the earth—compared with the entire earth, mountains are but tiny bumps. Furthermore, the earth does not rotate without carrying its <term>effluences</term> <note>atmospheric vapors or magnetic emissions</note> along with it. Beyond the effluences, there is no resistance. The earth's motion is performed with as little effort as the motions of the other heavenly bodies; nor is it inferior in dignity to some of these. ## CHAPTER VI.

### ON THE CAUSE OF THE FIXED TIME OF THE TOTAL REVOLUTION OF THE EARTH.

THE causes of the daily motion are to be found in the magnetic energy and in the alliance of bodies: that is to say, why a revolution of the earth is performed in the span of 24 hours. For no ingenious invention—whether of the <term>clepsydra</term>¹ <note>a water clock</note>, or of hourglasses, or of timepieces with toothed wheels driven by the tension of a steel spring—can show any variation in time. But the daily revolution, once completed, begins again. Now we will define a day as a complete revolution of a meridian of the earth from sun to sun. This is a little less than the total revolution; for in 365¼ turnings of a meridian to the sun, a year is completed. Because of this fixed and

Thus, since the sun itself is the mover and inciter of the universe, the other planets that are situated within the sphere of its forces—being impelled and set in motion—do also, with their own forces, determine their own courses and revolve in their own periods, according to the extent of their greater rotation, the differences of the forces emitted, and the perception of a greater good. Because of this, Saturn, having a longer path to travel, revolves in a longer time, while Venus revolves in nine months, and Mercury in 80 days, according to *Copernicus*; and the moon makes the circuit of the earth in 29 days, 12 hours, and 44 minutes. We have stated that the earth turns on its center, creating one day in its revolution toward the sun. The moon goes around the earth in a monthly course, and when it returns to conjunction with the sun after its previous conjunction, it constitutes one month, or one lunar day. The mean distance of the moon’s orbit, according to the calculations of *Copernicus* and other later astronomers, is distant from the earth’s center about 29 5/6 diameters of the earth. A solar revolution of the moon in its orbit takes 29 days, 12 hours, and 44 minutes. The sun is the cause of both the earth’s and the moon’s motions. Diameters bear a constant ratio to circumferences. And the moon’s orbit is a little more than twice 29½ times the length of the great circles on the earth.

Thus the moon and the earth agree in a twofold ratio of motion, and the earth rotates in its daily motion in the space of 24 hours; because the moon has a motion proportioned to the earth, and the earth has a motion agreeing in a twofold proportion with the moon’s motion. There is some difference in minutes, for the distances of the stars are not sufficiently determined in minutes, nor are astronomers agreed upon them. So, then, the earth rotates in the space of 24 hours, even as the moon does in her monthly course, by a magnetic compact of both, the globes being impelled forward according to the ratio of their orbits, as Aristotle admits (*De Caelo*, Book II, Chap. X). “It comes about,” says he, “that the motions of each are performed in a ratio, namely, in the same intervals whereby some are quicker, others slower.” But as between the moon and the earth, it is more reasonable to believe that they are in agreement, because, being neighboring bodies, they are very similar in nature and substance, and because the moon has a more manifest effect on the earth than any of the other stars, except the sun; also the moon alone of all planets directs its movements as a whole toward the earth’s center, and is closely related to the earth, and as it were held by ties to the earth.

Such, then, is the symmetry and harmony of the moon’s and the earth’s movements, very different from the oft-mentioned harmony of the celestial motions, which requires that

the closer any sphere is to the *primum mobile* and to the imaginary and fictitious rapid first motion, the less it resists it (*contranitatur*) and the more slowly it is carried by its own motion from west to east; but the farther away it is, the more rapidly and freely it performs its motion. Consequently, the moon (being farthest from the *primum mobile*) revolves with the greatest speed. These absurdities have been accepted for the sake of the *primum mobile*, and so that it might appear to have some effect in slowing the movements of the lower heavens; as if the motion of the stars resulted from retardation rather than being innate and natural to them, and as if the rest of the heavens (with the exception of the *primum mobile*) were constantly driven by a mighty force with a frantic impulse. It is far more probable that the stars revolve symmetrically, in a state of mutual concert and harmony.¹

<note>¹ Dr. William Whewell says (“Hist. of the Ind. ## CHAPTER VII.

### OF THE EARTH'S <term>PRIMARY MAGNETIC NATURE</term>, WHEREBY ITS POLES ARE MADE DIFFERENT FROM THE POLES OF THE <term>ECLIPTIC</term>.

HAVING shown the nature and causes of the earth’s <term>diurnal revolution</term>, produced partly by the energy of its magnetic property and partly by the influence of the sun and its light, we must now discuss the distance of the earth’s poles from those of the <term>ecliptic</term>—a condition very necessary for human welfare. For if the poles of the world or the earth were fixed at the poles of the <term>zodiac</term>, then the <term>equator</term> would lie exactly under the line of the ecliptic, and there would be no change of <term>seasons</term>—neither winter, nor summer, nor spring, nor autumn—but the state of things would remain forever unchanging. Hence (for the everlasting good of humanity) the earth’s <term>axis</term> tilted from the pole of the zodiac just enough to allow for biological growth and variety. Thus the <term>declination</term> of the <term>tropics</term> and the <term>inclination</term> of the earth’s pole always stay near the 24th degree, but at present it is only 23 degrees 28 minutes, or, according to others, 29 minutes; formerly, however, the declination was 23 degrees 52 minutes, and that is the furthest limit of declination observed so far. This has been wisely ordered by nature and settled by the earth’s primary pre-eminence. For if those poles—those of the earth and the ecliptic—were much farther apart, then as the sun approached the tropic, all things would be wasted and ruined in any high latitude of the other and neglected portion of the globe, because of the prolonged

### CHAPTER VIII.

#### OF THE <term>PRECESSION OF THE EQUINOXES</term> BY REASON OF THE <term>MAGNETIC MOVEMENT</term> OF THE EARTH’S POLES IN THE <term>ARCTIC</term> AND <term>ANTARCTIC CIRCLES</term> OF THE <term>ZODIAC</term>.

The early astronomers, not noticing the inequality of years, made no distinction between the <term>equinoctial</term> or <term>solstitial</term> revolving year and the year determined from a fixed star. They also considered the Olympian years, which were reckoned from the rising of the <term>Dog Star</term> or <term>Sirius</term> (*Canicula*), to be the same as those reckoned from the solstice. <term>Hipparchus the Rhodian</term> was the first to notice that there is a difference between the two, and found another year, calculated from fixed stars, of greater length than the equinoctial or solstitial year; therefore, he supposed that the stars also have a subsequent motion, though a very slow one and not easily noticed. After Hipparchus, <term>Menelaus</term> (a Roman geometer), then <term>Ptolemy</term>, and, a long time afterward, <term>Machometes Aracensis</term> and several others, have held in all their writings that the fixed stars and the whole fir-

And surely it must seem more probable that the appearances of the heavens are produced by a deflection and inclination of the small body, the earth, than by a whirling of the whole system of the universe—especially as this movement is ordered for the good of the earth alone, and is of no benefit at all to the fixed stars or the planets. For by this motion, the rising and setting of stars in all horizons are changed, as well as their culminations in the <term>zenith</term>, so that stars that once were vertical are now some degrees distant from the zenith. Provision has been made by nature for the earth’s soul or its magnetic energy—just as in tempering, receiving, and diverting the sun’s rays and light in fitting seasons, it was necessary that the bearings of the earth’s pole should be 23 degrees and more distant from the poles of the <term>ecliptic</term>; so that now, in regulating and in receiving in due order and succession the luminous rays of the fixed stars, the earth’s poles should revolve at the same distance from the ecliptic in the <term>arctic circle</term> of the ecliptic, or rather that they should creep with slow gait, because the actions of the stars do not always persist in the same parallel circles, but have a slower change; for the influences of the stars are not so powerful that the desired course should be more rapid. ### CHAPTER IX.
#### ON THE ANOMALY OF THE PRECESSION OF THE EQUINOXES AND THE OBLIQUITY OF THE ZODIAC.

THE change in the equinoxes is not always uniform, but becomes sometimes more rapid and sometimes slower; for the earth’s poles travel at unequal rates in the Arctic and in the Antarctic zodiacal circles, and recede from the center line on both sides.

It was Copernicus, however, who first provided the true explanation of the phenomenon known as the *precession of the equinoxes*, and Newton who discovered its physical cause (G. J. Astronomers, in accounting for this inequality of precession and of declination of the tropics, have offered various theories. Thebitius, to establish a law for these great inequalities in the movements of the stars, held that the eighth sphere does not advance by continuous motion from west to east, but that it has a sort of tremulous motion (*motu quodam trepidationis concuti*) whereby the leading stars in Aries and in Libra of the eighth heaven describe around the leading stars of Aries and Libra of the ninth sphere certain small circles with diameters equal to about nine degrees. But as this "motion of trepidation" <note>See note, Book III, Chap. I.</note> is full of absurdities and impossible motions, this movement has gone out of fashion. Other astronomers, therefore, are compelled to ascribe motion to the eighth sphere, and on top of this to construct a ninth heaven, or even a tenth and an eleventh. <note>See note, Book VI, Chap. III.</note> We must pardon errors in mathematicians, for one may be permitted, in the case of movements difficult to account for, to offer any hypotheses whatever in order to establish a law and to bring in a rule that will make the facts agree. But the philosopher can never admit such enormous and monstrous celestial constructions.

Now, although we see in all this how reluctant these mathematicians are to attribute any motion to the earth—which is a very small body—nevertheless they drive and whirl the heavens, which are vast and immense beyond human comprehension and human imagination. They construct three heavens and postulate three inconceivable monstrosities to account for a few unexplained motions. Ptolemy, comparing his own observations with those of Timochares and Hipparchus (of whom one lived 260 years before his time and the other 460 years), deemed this to be the motion of the eighth sphere and of the entire firmament. He proved it with many phenomena related to the poles of the zodiac; and, still thinking its motion was uniform, he held that the fixed stars travel only one degree in 100 years beneath the *primum mobile*. Seven hundred and fifty years after him, Abitegnius found that one degree is traveled over in 66 years, so that the entire period would be 23,760 years. Alphonsus claimed this motion was even slower—1 degree 28 minutes in 200 years; and thus the course of the fixed stars would proceed, but at an unequal rate. Finally, Copernicus—through his own observations and those of Timochares, Aristarchus the Samian, Menelaus, Ptolemy, Machometes Aracensis, and Alphonsus—discovered the anomalies of the motion of the earth's axis. However, I have no doubt that other anomalies will also appear some centuries from now, for it is difficult to note such a slow movement except over periods of many ages; therefore, we are still ignorant of the mind of nature and what she aims at through this inequality of motion. ## *True movement and natural axis (or poles) of the earth directed toward the arctic circle of the zodiac.*

*B*; in the second part, more slowly from *B* to *C*; in the third, with the same slowness from *C* to *D*; in the fourth, more rapidly again from *D* to *E*; in the fifth, with equal speed from *E* to *F*; again more slowly from *F* to *G*; with the same slowness from *G* to *H*; in the last eighth, more rapidly again from *H* to *I*. This is Copernicus’s *intorta corolla* <note>1</note> with the mean motion fused into a curved line, which is the true path of the

<note>1 See *Nicolaus Copernicus of Torun, On the Revolutions of the Celestial Spheres*, Nuremberg 1543, pages 66, 67, or the Amsterdam edition of 1617, pages 154-157. The *intorta corolla* is not an inverted but an irregular crown: a figure representing the successive positions produced by the projection of the Earth’s pole upon the stellar sphere, resembling a crown, but distorted by the irregularities of motion. (Consult also Rheticus, “First Account of the Books of Revolutions of Copernicus”; Kepler, “On the Full Equation of Time and the Motion of the Eighth Sphere.”)</note>

<meta>This page concludes the discussion of the Earth's axial movements, specifically how the pole's motion relates to the periods of precession and obliquity, and brings the entire treatise on magnetism to a close.</meta>

<header>WILLIAM GILBERT.</header>

motion. And so the pole reaches the extreme limit of variation of the <term>precession of the equinoxes</term> twice, but the limit of inclination or <term>obliquity</term> once only. Thus do the moderns—and in particular Copernicus, the restorer of astronomy—describe the variations of the movement of the earth's axis, so far as the same is made possible by the observations of the ancients down to our day; but we still lack many and more exact observations to fix anything positively as to the anomaly of the movement of the precessions, as also of the <term>obliquity of the zodiac</term>. For since the time when this anomaly was first noted in various observations, only one half of a period of obliquity has passed. Hence all these points touching the unequal movement of precession and obliquity are undecided and undefined, and so we cannot assign with certainty any natural causes for the motion.

Therefore we here bring our arguments and magnetic experiments to an end and conclusion.
